title_en: Hangzhou Builds a Legal System for Collaborative Intellectual Property Protection of New Business Models
body_en: Report from this newspaper In recent years, the Hangzhou Municipal Administration for Market Regulation in Zhejiang Province has focused on the pain points and difficulties in intellectual property protection for new business formats, innovatively built a collaborative legal protection system, and launched a series of practical measures, achieving significant results and injecting strong momentum into high-quality economic and social development. The bureau has taken the lead nationwide in exploring and establishing a preventive protection mechanism for enterprise names, implementing front-end preventive protection for enterprise names with a certain market influence, such as "Six Little Dragons." It has improved backend dispute resolution standards and issued the "Several Provisions on Administrative Handling of Trademark and Market Entity Name Disputes," clarifying the boundaries of administrative handling for various disputes between trademarks and names, effectively resolving problems that have long plagued enterprises and law enforcement practices. In the field of data intellectual property protection, the bureau has built a full-process collaborative protection model of data "registration + enforcement." It has jointly issued the "Guiding Opinions on Collaborative Registration of Data Property Rights, Data Intellectual Property Rights, and Data Assets in Hangzhou" with the Municipal Bureau of Data and the Municipal Bureau of Finance, strengthening data rights confirmation and protection. At the same time, by publishing ten typical cases of administrative law enforcement for data protection, it has promoted a good pattern of collaborative protection between administration and judiciary, providing strong support for the high-quality development of Hangzhou's data industry. For the emerging field of live streaming, the Hangzhou Municipal Administration for Market Regulation has innovatively released the nation's first "Guiding Principles for Risk Control and Legal Affairs in Collaborative Intellectual Property Protection for Live Streaming (Trial)." This "Guideline" links network service providers, live streaming room operating agencies, intellectual property rights holders, and public security and judicial departments, building an intellectual property protection system throughout the entire live streaming process, achieving a balance between safeguarding public interests and stimulating industry innovation. A series of innovative measures have achieved remarkable results. In the 2025 Global Innovation Index's ranking of the world's top 100 innovation clusters, Hangzhou ranked 13th globally, a new historical high. Unitree Robotics won the only 2025 World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Global Award in China. The medical and health symptom screening data case collected by Lianxin Technology was selected as one of the top ten typical cases in the second batch of data intellectual property registrations in 2025. The Hangzhou Intellectual Property Protection Center achieved excellent results in national and provincial assessments, ranking second nationwide and first in the province, respectively. In 2025, Hangzhou completed 8,305 data intellectual property registrations, ranking first in the province. It launched the first "three-certificate collaborative" registration platform in China focusing on data property rights, data intellectual property rights, and data assets. Related innovative practices have been deeply reported by multiple authoritative media, attracting widespread attention and positive responses from all sectors of society. □ Yu Jingjing

body_en: [Financial Calendar] State Council Information Office holds press conference on the "Spatial Coordination Plan for the Modern Capital Metropolitan Area (2023-2035)" Ministry of Commerce holds press conference to introduce recent key work in the business sector Cannes World AI Summit New Stock Listing: Haisheng Medical (Beijing Stock Exchange) Financial Reports: Lenovo Group, Hua Hong Semiconductor ►►According to Xinhua News Agency, on February 11, the State Council held its 18th special study session themed "Deepening and Expanding 'AI+' and Comprehensively Empowering Thousands of Industries." title_en: Beijing Municipal Administration for Market Regulation summons 12 third-party online train ticket sales platforms.
body_en: Recently, the Beijing Municipal Administration for Market Regulation organized a meeting with 12 major platforms involved in online train ticket sales, including Ctrip, Qunar, Fliggy, Tongcheng, Meituan, JD.com, TravelSky, Gaotie Guanjia, Didi, Gaode Maps, Baidu Maps, and Tencent Maps. The meeting focused on prominent issues in online train ticket sales that have caused strong public concern, and was conducted as an administrative interview. During the interview, the Beijing Municipal Administration for Market Regulation clearly outlined four compliance requirements for the platforms. First, strictly implement corporate social responsibility and establish a correct business philosophy to "help more and hinder less" for travelers. Second, comprehensively review business models and service processes, prohibit explicit or implicit suggestions that consumers can obtain priority ticket purchase privileges through paid services, promptly rectify misleading advertisements such as "accelerator packs," "dual channels," and "ticket availability monitoring" after tickets are sold out, and voluntarily accept social supervision. Third, comprehensively review and rectify platform pages, remove products suspected of misleading advertising, adjust page promotional content, and prohibit the use of 12306 images, text, trademarks, etc., to mislead consumers into believing that the platform has a specific business cooperation with 12306. Fourth, diligently implement clear pricing, prominently display value-added service content and prices, promptly rectify issues where the displayed train ticket price differs from the actual payment due to inconspicuous value-added service reminders, and effectively protect consumers' right to know.

title_en: Cui Zhongfu presided over the review meeting for the industry standards "Pharmaceutical Logistics - Cargo Safety Assurance Requirements" and "Logistics Service Specifications for Investigational Drugs".
body_en: Cui Zhongfu Presided Over the Review Meeting for the Industry Standards "Requirements for Safety Assurance of Pharmaceutical Logistics Cargo" and "Specifications for Logistics Services of Investigational Drugs" Publication Date: 2026-02-12 14:40:58 Standardization Department Follow China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing WeChat Qzone Sina Weibo Copy Link On February 10, 2026, the National Logistics Standardization Technical Committee organized a review meeting in Beijing for the industry standards "Requirements for Safety Assurance of Pharmaceutical Logistics Cargo" (Project Plan Number: 303-2024-001) and "Specifications for Logistics Services of Investigational Drugs" (Project Plan Number: 303-2024-002). Cui Zhongfu, Chief Economist of the China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing and Executive Deputy Director of the National Logistics Standardization Technical Committee, presided over the meeting. The industry standard "Requirements for Safety Assurance of Pharmaceutical Logistics Cargo" was drafted by units including the Pharmaceutical Logistics and Supply Chain Branch of the China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing and Sinopharm Holding Suzhou Co., Ltd. This standard specifies the basic requirements for safety assurance in pharmaceutical logistics, including warehousing safety, packaging safety, loading and unloading safety, transportation and distribution safety, information security, and risk and emergency management. It is applicable to the safety assurance of pharmaceutical logistics provided by logistics service providers. The development of this standard will regulate the safety management of pharmaceutical logistics, promote the standardized development of pharmaceutical logistics safety assurance work, enhance the level of pharmaceutical logistics safety assurance, and promote high-quality industry development. The industry standard "Specifications for Logistics Services of Investigational Drugs" was drafted by units including the Pharmaceutical Logistics and Supply Chain Branch of the China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing and Kexin Hai (Beijing) Medical Supplies Trading Co., Ltd. This standard specifies the service providers, service assurance, service content, information management, safety and emergency management, and service evaluation and improvement for logistics services of investigational drugs. It is applicable to the logistics services and management of investigational drugs. The development of this standard will provide unified specifications for the logistics services of investigational drugs, clarify the operational requirements for each link, and contribute to improving the professional and standardized level of logistics services for investigational drugs, thereby supporting high-quality industry development. An expert group composed of some members of the National Logistics Standardization Technical Committee and its Pharmaceutical Logistics Sub-technical Committee, standardization experts, and experts in the field of pharmaceutical logistics listened to the report from the standard drafting group and reviewed the submitted draft standards, compilation explanations, and the summary and handling table of solicited opinions. They unanimously agreed that both standards passed the review. title_en: Interpretation of the National Standard "Composition and Calculation Methods of Green Logistics Indicators"
body_en: National Standard "Green Logistics Indicator Composition and Accounting Methods" Interpretation Publication Date: 2026-02-12 14:46:45 Standardization Department Follow China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing (CFLP) WeChat Qzone Sina Weibo Copy Link I. Standard Overview Standard Number: GB/T37099—2026 (replacing GB/T37099—2018) Standard Name: "Green Logistics Indicator Composition and Accounting Methods" Publication Date: January 28, 2026 Implementation Date: May 1, 2026 II. Background of Standard Revision General Secretary Xi Jinping pointed out in the report of the 20th National Congress of the Communist Party of China: "Promoting the green and low-carbon development of the economy and society is a key link in achieving high-quality development." Since the "14th Five-Year Plan," under the scientific guidance of Xi Jinping's thought on ecological civilization, China has been accelerating the comprehensive green transformation of economic and social development, coordinating carbon reduction, pollution control, green expansion, and growth, and speeding up the modernization of harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature. The Central Committee of the Communist Party of China and the State Council also clearly required in the "Action Plan for Effectively Reducing the Overall Logistics Costs of Society" to "accelerate the green transformation of logistics." Currently, the green transformation of China's logistics industry has entered a critical stage. While some leading enterprises have formed demonstrations in areas such as new energy substitution, circular packaging, and carbon management, problems such as the difficulty in quantifying, benchmarking, and verifying green practices remain prominent, which to some extent restricts the precise implementation of policy guidance, market incentives, and industry collaboration. The national standard "Green Logistics Indicator Composition and Accounting Methods" (GB/T37099—2018), released and implemented in 2018, first proposed the concept of green logistics and laid an important foundation for promoting the green development of the industry. However, in the face of new requirements of the "dual carbon" strategy, the rapid penetration of digital and intelligent technologies, the widespread application of new energy equipment, and the in-depth practice of ESG concepts, the 2018 version of the standard urgently needs to be strengthened in terms of management guidance, technological application, and greenhouse gas accounting. For example, in terms of management, the original standard lacked sufficient guidance for the systematic top-level design of green logistics; in response to technological frontiers, it lacked targeted measurement indicators for new practices such as new energy equipment, green building materials, and digital-intelligent operations; in terms of accounting accuracy, the accounting boundaries for greenhouse gases and different pollutants need further refinement to support precise emission reduction and compliance management for enterprises. III. Main Content of the Standard This standard establishes the composition of green logistics indicators for logistics activities, describes the indicator descriptions and accounting methods, and is applicable to the selection and accounting of green logistics indicators for enterprises with logistics activities. (I) Terms and Definitions. The standard provides terms and definitions for "green logistics," "renewable energy," "joint distribution," "greenhouse gas," "atmospheric pollutant," "gaseous pollutant," "new energy transport vehicle," "new energy loading and unloading equipment," "clean and environmentally friendly transport vehicle," and "green building materials." Compared with the 2018 version, the changes are: - The definitions of "green logistics," "renewable energy," and "joint distribution" have been modified to better align with current industry practices. - Terms such as "floor area ratio," "degradable plastic," "reusable material," and "reduced packaging" have been removed to enhance the professional focus of the indicators. - Definitions for "new energy transport vehicle," "new energy loading and unloading equipment," "clean and environmentally friendly transport vehicle," and "green building materials" have been added to reflect the trend of equipment upgrades. (II) Green Logistics Indicator Composition. The standard defines four major categories of first-level indicators: "Management," "Resources," "Operations," and "Environment." These indicators aim to strengthen systematic management, refine green resource management, improve intelligent operation levels, and accurately account for environmental impacts, in order to fully respond to the "dual carbon" goals and the needs of high-quality industry development. Specifically: 1. Management Indicators. The second-level indicator "Management" has been changed to the first-level indicator "Management Indicators" to highlight its top-level design and leading role in the entire green logistics system. Two new second-level indicators, "Organization and Planning" and "Systems and Frameworks," have been added to guide enterprises from scattered green practices to systematic green management. The original third-level indicators "Logistics Management System," "Logistics Operation Plan," and "Logistics Informatization Level" have been removed, as their core content has been covered and elevated by the "Organization and Planning" and "Systems and Frameworks" indicators, thus avoiding indicator duplication. 2. Resource Indicators. (1) Facilities: "Greenery coverage rate of logistics nodes" has replaced "greenery rate of warehouse areas." This not only includes ground greening but also encourages vertical greening on roofs and facades, providing a more comprehensive dimension and effectively guiding the improvement of ecological functions at nodes. "Usage rate of green building materials," "renewable energy generation and storage systems," and "rainwater recycling and utilization systems" have been added, extending greenness to the entire life cycle of building material production and building operation. "Green building materials" reduce embodied carbon at the source; "renewable energy and storage systems" promote clean energy use at nodes; "rainwater recycling" promotes water resource circulation, jointly building energy-saving, low-carbon, and circular green infrastructure. "Logistics node site selection" and "floor area ratio" have been removed, as these are essentially mandatory or prerequisite constraints for territorial spatial planning and architectural design, with low relevance to green logistics. (2) Equipment: "Proportion of clean energy loading and unloading equipment" has been changed to "Proportion of new energy loading and unloading equipment." Loading and unloading operations are mostly concentrated within logistics nodes such as warehouses and stations, with relatively fixed operating environments, providing favorable conditions for the priority promotion and application of new energy equipment such as pure electric and hydrogen energy. "Proportion of high-efficiency lighting in warehouses and stations" has been changed to "Proportion of high-energy-efficiency equipment," covering all energy-consuming equipment, not limited to lighting, guiding more comprehensive energy efficiency improvements. "Application rate of energy metering devices" has been added, providing a data foundation for accurate energy consumption accounting and energy-saving renovation, and is a prerequisite for the effective implementation of other equipment-related indicators. (3) Energy: "Energy consumption per unit volume of warehouses and stations" has been changed to "Energy consumption per unit volume of logistics nodes." The term "logistics nodes" is more unified and scientific. "Fuel consumption per hundred tons (cubic meters/vehicle) kilometer of transport vehicles" has been changed to "Energy consumption per ton-kilometer of transport vehicles." Energy consumption is unified to the standard unit of "ton-kilometer," and by converting to standard coal, the energy consumption of different energy types and transportation modes becomes comparable, making the accounting fairer and more scientific. (4) Packaging: "Usage rate of biodegradable plastic packaging materials" has been changed to "Usage rate of biodegradable packaging." "Usage rate of reduced packaging materials" has been changed to "Usage rate of reduced packaging." The evaluation focus has shifted from "material properties" to "actual application." This guides enterprises to not only consider what materials they purchase but also to ensure their actual use in logistics operations, making the indicators more aligned with operational reality. "Usage rate of recycled packaging materials" and "Usage rate of environmentally friendly inks" have been added, supplementing the dimensions of "recycling" and "non-toxicity" on the basis of "reduction" and "degradation." "Recycled materials" encourage the use of recycled materials to form a closed loop; "environmentally friendly inks" reduce the emission of toxic and harmful substances during production and disposal, achieving full-chain environmental protection. "Usage rate of reusable packaging materials" has been removed, as its content overlaps with the newly added "Usage rate of recycled packaging materials," and the consideration of packaging "reuse" has been incorporated into the "Proportion of circulation and reuse of turnover equipment" and "Recycling rate of logistics packaging" within the operational indicators. 3. Operation Indicators. (1) Facility and Equipment Utilization: "Throughput per unit area (volume) of warehouses and stations" has been changed to "Utilization rate per unit area (volume) of logistics nodes." This guides enterprises to achieve higher intensity and effective utilization within a unit space, which is more in line with the intensive and compact development principles of green logistics. "Utilization rate of transport vehicle load (volume)" has been removed, as the utilization efficiency of transport vehicles is already reflected by the more comprehensive and scientific "actual load rate" indicator. "Utilization rate of mechanical equipment" has been removed, as this indicator is too broad and has low relevance to green logistics. (2) Logistics Operations: "Actual load rate" has been added to improve the efficiency of single vehicle transportation and reduce empty runs. "Enclosed coverage rate of bulk cargo" controls dust pollution. "Proportion of freight turnover volume by rail and water transport" guides long-distance transportation towards lower-emission modes. "Proportion of recycled water usage" promotes water conservation. "Cargo damage rate" and "Compliance rate of handling unqualified products (including waste)" have been removed, as these indicators are mainly related to quality safety and compliant disposal, which are basic requirements for enterprise operations, rather than measures of the green level and resource efficiency of the logistics process. (3) A new second-level indicator, "Digital and Intelligent Operations," has been added, with sub-indicators including "Usage rate of electronic waybills," "Coverage rate of intelligent equipment," "Rate of intelligent monitoring of energy consumption," and "Coverage rate of intelligent dispatch." This introduces the dimension of "digital and intelligent" for the first time. These indicators guide process paperlessness, operation automation, energy consumption visualization, and dispatch optimization, clarifying that intelligent technology is an indispensable catalyst for achieving green transformation. 4. Environmental Indicators. (1) Greenhouse Gases: The original "Greenhouse gas emissions per unit of business volume" has been split into "Greenhouse gas emissions per unit of business volume for transportation activities" and "Greenhouse gas emissions per unit of business volume for logistics nodes." The emission mechanisms, accounting methods, and emission reduction paths for transportation activities and logistics nodes are distinctly different. Splitting the accounting clarifies the responsibility boundaries. (2) Solid and Liquid Pollution: "Solid and liquid pollution" has been changed to two independent second-level indicators: "Solid Waste" and "Liquid Pollutants." Referring to the "Law of the People's Republic of China on the Prevention and Control of Environmental Pollution by Solid Waste," "solid pollutants" have been revised to "solid waste." Furthermore, solid waste and liquid pollutants differ in their form, hazard characteristics, treatment standards, and regulatory requirements, making separate settings more scientific and rigorous. (3) Noise Pollution: "Noise exposure control rate at work stations" has been added. This indicator guides enterprises not only to be responsible for surrounding communities but also to proactively take engineering or management measures to protect frontline employees who are long-term exposed to noise environments, reflecting the people-oriented concept of green development. IV. Significance of Standard Implementation This standard provides enterprises with logistics activities with a complete, unified, and operable set of technical tools. Its implementation will have the following three levels of positive impacts: (I) Effectively Reduce Operating Costs for Logistics Enterprises. By implementing this standard, enterprises can accurately measure and compare energy and resource consumption in various links such as warehousing, transportation, and packaging according to unified accounting methods. This helps enterprises identify operational shortcomings characterized by high energy consumption and low efficiency, transforming green practices into sustainable economic benefits for the enterprise. (II) Effectively Improve the Working Environment and Fulfill Social Responsibilities. By implementing this standard, enterprises can increase the use of new energy equipment, implement enclosed operations for bulk cargo, and reduce pollutants and noise sources. This can promote the effective improvement of the frontline working environment, ensure the occupational health and safety of workers, enhance employee belonging and social recognition, and fulfill social responsibilities to the surrounding communities and the environment. (III) Accurately Quantify Environmental Performance and Support Green Transformation. By implementing this standard, environmental indicators become measurable, manageable, and verifiable. At the same time, the adoption of consistent accounting standards across the entire industry provides real, transparent, and verifiable data support for the national promotion of "dual carbon" strategic goals, effectively promoting the high-quality development of the logistics industry. title_en: Notice of the State Administration for Market Regulation on Printing and Distributing the "Guidelines for Anti-Monopoly Compliance of Internet Platforms"
body_en: Notice of the State Administration for Market Regulation on Issuing the "Guidelines for Anti-Monopoly Compliance of Internet Platforms" To the Market Supervision Bureaus (Departments, Commissions) of all provinces, autonomous regions, municipalities directly under the Central Government, and the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps: The "Guidelines for Anti-Monopoly Compliance of Internet Platforms" are hereby issued to you. Please publicize and implement them in conjunction with your actual situation. State Administration for Market Regulation January 28, 2026 (This document is publicly released) Guidelines for Anti-Monopoly Compliance of Internet Platforms Chapter 1 General Provisions Article 1 Purpose and Basis To support and guide platform operators in effectively preventing anti-monopoly compliance risks, improving anti-monopoly compliance management systems, protecting the legitimate rights and interests of relevant parties, maintaining fair market competition order, and promoting the innovation and healthy development of the platform economy, these Guidelines are formulated in accordance with the "Anti-Monopoly Law of the People's Republic of China" (hereinafter referred to as the "Anti-Monopoly Law") and other laws and regulations. Article 2 Relevant Concepts For the purposes of these Guidelines, "internet platform" refers to a business organizational form that, through network information technology, enables mutually dependent bilateral or multilateral parties to conduct transactions or other activities under the rules provided by a specific carrier, thereby jointly creating value. For the purposes of these Guidelines, "platform operator" refers to an operator that provides internet platform services such as venues, transaction matching, and information exchange to natural persons, legal persons, and other market entities. For the purposes of these Guidelines, "platform-based operator" refers to an operator that provides goods or services (hereinafter collectively referred to as "goods") within an internet platform. For the purposes of these Guidelines, "anti-monopoly compliance risk" refers to the possibility of platform operators and their employees incurring legal liability, economic or reputational losses, and other negative consequences due to violations of the relevant provisions of the "Anti-Monopoly Law." For the purposes of these Guidelines, "anti-monopoly compliance management" refers to organized, planned, and full-process management activities targeting the business and management behaviors of platform operators and the performance of duties by their employees, with the aim of preventing and controlling anti-monopoly compliance risks. Article 3 Necessity of Compliance Management Internet platforms exhibit significant network effects and involve multiple parties, including platform operators, platform-based operators, consumers, and practitioners. Platform operators typically possess certain managerial attributes, leveraging data, algorithms, technological, capital advantages, and platform rules to enhance market power and influence the platform's competitive ecosystem. Therefore, it is essential to strengthen anti-monopoly compliance management. Platform operators who violate the "Anti-Monopoly Law" will bear corresponding legal liabilities and face related commercial and credit risks. By strengthening anti-monopoly compliance management, platform operators can avoid risks arising from monopolistic practices and cultivate a positive brand image and core competitive advantages. Enhancing anti-monopoly compliance awareness and improving anti-monopoly compliance management systems will help platform operators elevate the level and quality of competition, optimize resource allocation, improve operational efficiency, protect the legitimate rights and interests of multiple parties, promote the continuous optimization of the platform's competitive ecosystem, and achieve innovative development of the platform economy. Article 4 Basic Principles Platform operators shall, in accordance with these Guidelines, conduct anti-monopoly compliance management work based on the following basic principles, aiming for fair rules, benevolent algorithms, and compliant competition: (1) Principle of Specificity. Identify, assess, and control compliance risks in a targeted manner by considering factors such as the industry, business model, governance structure, and market competition conditions of the platform operator, and conduct anti-monopoly compliance management accordingly. (2) Principle of Comprehensiveness. Promote full-process compliance, covering pre-event, in-event, and post-event stages, achieving full coverage of business areas, departments, and employees, and integrating decision-making, execution, and supervision. Establish a coordinated and interconnected comprehensive compliance system. (3) Principle of Penetration. Ensure penetration across the platform operator's headquarters, branches, and holding subsidiaries. Improve the headquarters' guidance, coordination, and supervision mechanisms, and reinforce the compliance management responsibilities of each branch. Achieve hierarchical, business, and rule/algorithm penetration. (4) Principle of Sustainability. Improve the long-term mechanism for anti-monopoly compliance, ensure the continuous and effective implementation of compliance management systems, prevent "one-off" or "phased" compliance, regularly assess the platform operator's own compliant operations, and promptly update and improve anti-monopoly compliance management systems. Article 5 Overall Compliance Requirements Platform operators shall earnestly assume primary responsibility for anti-monopoly compliance, improve anti-monopoly compliance systems, strengthen anti-monopoly compliance management, compete lawfully, operate compliantly, and shall not engage in monopolistic practices prohibited by the "Anti-Monopoly Law" by leveraging data, algorithms, technology, capital advantages, or platform rules. Chapter 2 Risk Identification Section 1 Monopolistic Agreements Monopolistic agreements refer to agreements, decisions, or other concerted actions that exclude or restrict competition. The "Anti-Monopoly Law" prohibits operators from reaching monopolistic agreements. Platform operators shall comply with the "Anti-Monopoly Law" and the "Provisions on Prohibiting Monopolistic Agreements" to avoid reaching monopolistic agreements in the course of providing platform services or conducting self-operated businesses, as well as organizing other operators to reach monopolistic agreements or providing substantial assistance. When identifying the risks of monopolistic agreements, platform operators shall first analyze whether the relevant conduct falls under the circumstances stipulated in Articles 17, 18(1), and 19 of the "Anti-Monopoly Law," and then analyze whether such conduct meets the conditions for non-prohibition or exemption stipulated in the "Anti-Monopoly Law." Article 6 Horizontal Monopolistic Agreements Platform operators that are in competition with each other shall avoid reaching horizontal monopolistic agreements by fixing or changing prices, restricting production (sales) volume, dividing markets, restricting new technologies (products), or jointly boycotting transactions through the following means: (1) Engaging in communication of intent and exchange of information regarding competitively sensitive information through meetings, phone calls, text messages, emails, shared documents, instant messaging tools, shared data pools, interoperability agreements, cloud storage platforms, artificial intelligence, etc. (2) Collecting and exchanging competitively sensitive information such as pricing models, commission rates, preferential policies, customer lists, traffic allocation mechanisms, and research and development, investment, production, marketing, and promotion strategies. (3) Coordinating behaviors related to user segmentation, dynamic pricing, traffic allocation, and product ranking through data, algorithms, technology, and platform rules. Risk Example: Algorithmic collusion between platforms Platform operators that are in competition with each other use algorithms to reach monopolistic agreements through communication of intent, exchange of sensitive information, and coordinated behavior. For example, platform operators A and B, which are in competition, collude through algorithms to unify pricing mechanisms, commission rates, etc., thereby reaching a horizontal monopolistic agreement that excludes or restricts market competition. Article 7 Vertical Monopolistic Agreements Platform operators shall avoid reaching vertical monopolistic agreements, such as fixing resale prices or restricting minimum resale prices, with their trading counterparts through the following means: (1) Automating the setting of resale prices using technological means such as big data analysis and artificial intelligence. (2) Unifying resale prices through platform rules related to API calls, data usage, traffic allocation, promotional activities, store management, and user services. (3) Directly or indirectly restricting resale prices through user profiling and predictive algorithms. Article 8 Organizing and Providing Substantial Assistance Platform operators shall avoid organizing platform-based operators or other operators to reach monopolistic agreements or providing substantial assistance for reaching monopolistic agreements through the following means: (1) Organizing or coordinating communication of intent among platform-based operators or between platform-based operators and other operators through data sharing, issuing notices, signing agreements, etc. (2) Providing necessary support or creating key facilitating conditions for platform-based operators or other operators to obtain competitively sensitive information or achieve coordinated behavior. Risk Example: Organizing and assisting platform-based operators to reach monopolistic agreements A platform operator organizes or coordinates platform-based operators that are in competition with each other to reach horizontal agreements, or provides substantial assistance by offering necessary support or creating key conditions. For example, platform operator A signs price adjustment agreements with content that is the same or similar with platform-based operators that are in competition with each other. In this process, it facilitates communication of intent and exchange of competitively sensitive information among platform-based operators, ultimately leading to consistent pricing behavior that excludes or restricts market competition. Section 2 Abuse of Dominant Market Position Abuse of dominant market position refers to conduct by an operator with a dominant market position, such as selling at unfairly high prices, purchasing at unfairly low prices, selling below cost without justifiable reasons, refusing to trade, imposing trading restrictions, tying, attaching other unreasonable conditions, or practicing differential treatment. The "Anti-Monopoly Law" prohibits operators with a dominant market position from engaging in such conduct. Platform operators with a significant market share or market power are encouraged to regularly assess whether they hold a dominant market position in the relevant market. Platform operators shall comply with the "Anti-Monopoly Law" and the "Provisions on Prohibiting Abuse of Dominant Market Position" to avoid engaging in such conduct in the course of providing platform services or conducting self-operated businesses. When identifying the risks of abuse of dominant market position, platform operators shall first define the relevant market, assess whether they hold a dominant market position in the relevant market, and whether they are implementing relevant conduct. Then, they shall consider whether there are justifiable reasons and whether the relevant conduct excludes or restricts market competition to specifically analyze whether it constitutes abuse of dominant market position. Article 9 Factors for Consideration of Dominant Market Position When assessing whether they hold a dominant market position in the relevant market, platform operators may consider the following factors: (1) The platform operator's market share and the competitive landscape of the relevant market. When determining the platform operator's market share, the proportion of transaction value, transaction volume, sales revenue, registered users, active users, click-through rates, usage time, number of platform-based operators, or other indicators in the relevant market may be considered, along with the duration for which such market share has been maintained. When analyzing the competitive landscape of the relevant market, the development status of the relevant market, the number and market share of competing platform operators, the characteristics of platform competition, the degree of platform differentiation, economies of scale, the situation of potential competing platform operators, and innovation and technological changes may be considered. (2) The platform operator's ability to control the market. The platform operator's ability to control upstream and downstream markets or other related markets, to hinder or influence the entry of other platform operators into the relevant market, the relevant business models, network effects, and the ability to influence or determine prices, traffic, or other transaction conditions may be considered in conjunction with factors such as the diversity of online and offline businesses and vertical integration. (3) The platform operator's financial and technical capabilities. Investor status, asset scale, capital sources, profitability, financing capacity, technological innovation and application capabilities, intellectual property rights held, ability to process relevant data, and the extent to which these financial and technical capabilities can promote business expansion or consolidate and maintain market position may be considered. (4) The degree of dependence of platform-based operators and other operators on the platform operator for transactions. The trading relationship, transaction volume, and duration of transactions between platform-based operators and other operators and the platform operator, lock-in effects, user stickiness, the possibility of switching to other platforms, and switching costs may be considered. (5) The ease or difficulty for other platform operators to enter the relevant market. Market access, platform economies of scale, scale of capital investment, technical barriers, user multi-homing, user switching costs, ease or difficulty of data acquisition, and user habits may be considered. (6) Other factors based on the characteristics of the platform economy that determine a platform operator's dominant market position. Article 10 Unfairly High or Low Prices Platform operators with a dominant market position shall avoid abusing their market dominance by selling goods at unfairly high prices or purchasing goods at unfairly low prices through the following means: (1) Charging platform-based operators fees, such as commissions, registration fees, service fees, membership fees, technical service fees, information service fees, and marketing promotion fees, that are significantly higher than those charged by other platform operators in similar businesses under the same or similar market conditions, or increasing the above-mentioned fees charged to platform-based operators by more than a normal margin when costs are basically stable. (2) Charging platform-based operators unfairly high fees by splitting service items or increasing fee categories. (3) Paying platform-based operators prices for goods that are significantly lower than those paid by other platform operators in similar businesses under the same or similar market conditions. When determining whether market conditions are the same or similar, factors such as platform type, business model, transaction stage, cost structure, and specific transaction circumstances may generally be considered. Risk Example: Unfairly high platform prices A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its market dominance to charge platform-based operators unfairly high fees by leveraging platform rules, technology, and algorithms. For example, platform operator A, which has a dominant market position, continuously increases service fees by more than a normal margin for many years while its costs remain basically stable, thereby charging platform-based operators unfairly high fees and harming their interests. Article 11 Selling Below Cost Platform operators with a dominant market position shall avoid abusing their market dominance by selling goods or providing services at prices below cost without justifiable reasons, through excessive subsidies or cross-subsidies, thereby excluding or restricting market competition. When analyzing whether conduct constitutes selling below cost, the focus shall generally be on whether the platform operator is crowding out competing platform operators by selling at prices below cost, and whether it is likely to obtain improper benefits under unfair competitive conditions, harm fair market competition, and infringe upon the legitimate rights and interests of consumers after crowding out competing platform operators. When calculating costs, the cost interrelationships among the relevant markets involved in the platform's multi-sided markets and their reasonableness may be comprehensively considered. Risk Example: Selling below cost on a platform A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its market dominance by providing services at prices below cost without justifiable reasons, through excessive subsidies or preferential policies exceeding reasonable limits, thereby excluding or restricting market competition. For example, platform operator A, which has a dominant market position, provides platform-based operators with free entry and substantial subsidies for a period significantly exceeding the reasonable duration of commercial practice. After competing platform operators exit the relevant market, it significantly increases entry fees and other related fees, thereby obtaining improper benefits and harming fair market competition and the legitimate rights and interests of consumers. Article 12 Refusal to Trade Platform operators with a dominant market position shall avoid abusing their market dominance by refusing to trade with trading counterparts without justifiable reasons, thereby excluding or restricting market competition, through the following means: (1) Terminating, delaying, or interrupting transactions with trading counterparts by delisting products, blocking accounts, setting complex transaction processes, restricting traffic, shutting down interfaces, or interrupting data sharing. (2) Refusing to trade with trading counterparts by setting unreasonable transaction conditions, service fees significantly higher than market reasonable levels, ceasing to provide application updates, interrupting data updates, or delaying the signing of cooperation agreements. (3) Substantially reducing the transaction volume with trading counterparts by restricting traffic acquisition or order acceptance through traffic allocation algorithms, product release rules, etc. (4) Imposing unreasonable restrictions and obstacles that make it difficult for trading counterparts to conduct transactions by formulating unreasonable marketing, research and development, or other platform rules, or using discriminatory algorithms. (5) Refusing to trade with trading counterparts on reasonable terms by controlling specific data, models, or application platforms that constitute essential facilities. Risk Example: Blocking and filtering A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its market dominance by blocking and filtering trading counterparts at the application, transmission, or network layers without justifiable reasons, thereby preventing them from entering the relevant market and excluding or restricting market competition. For example, platform operator A, which has a dominant market position, prevents trading counterparts from conducting specific businesses or participating in market competition without justifiable reasons by restricting link redirection or port access. Article 13 Tying Platform operators with a dominant market position shall avoid abusing their market dominance by imposing trading restrictions without justifiable reasons, requiring trading counterparts to trade only with themselves or their designated operators, or to refrain from trading with specific operators, thereby excluding or restricting market competition, through the following means: (1) Setting exclusive cooperation terms in platform rules for merchant entry, platform services, content release, application development, etc., requiring platform-based operators to cooperate only with the platform or to release specific goods or content only on this platform. (2) Requiring platform-based operators not to cooperate with specific competing platforms or not to participate in promotional activities of specific competing platforms through activity rules, cooperation agreements, or in-platform notices. (3) Implementing restrictions through punitive measures such as blocking stores, de-ranking search results, restricting traffic, deducting deposits, imposing fines, canceling eligibility for promotional activities, delaying launches, differential fees, delayed payment periods, or reducing rating levels. (4) Indirectly implementing restrictions through incentive measures such as subsidies, discounts, preferential offers, traffic resource support,赠送增值服务 (gifting value-added services), or improving rating levels. Risk Example: "Choose One of Two" behavior A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its market dominance by forcing trading counterparts to choose between the platform operator and other competing platform operators without justifiable reasons, and by enforcing such "choose one of two" behavior through punitive or incentive measures, thereby excluding or restricting market competition. For example, platform operator A, which has a dominant market position, requires platform-based operators to commit not to cooperate with competing platforms without justifiable reasons, and punishes platform-based operators that fail to comply with the commitment by de-ranking their search results, delisting their products, restricting their traffic, or deducting their deposits, thereby restricting the platform-based operators' freedom of choice and achieving the effect of excluding or restricting market competition. Article 14 Tying or Attaching Other Unreasonable Conditions Platform operators with a dominant market position shall avoid abusing their market dominance by tying or attaching other unreasonable trading conditions without justifiable reasons, thereby excluding or restricting market competition, through the following means: (1) Using standard terms, pop-up windows, or mandatory operational steps that are difficult to choose, change, or refuse, requiring platform-based operators or consumers to use designated products in conjunction with their services. (2) Forcing platform-based operators, consumers, or others to accept other products by taking punitive measures such as de-ranking search results, restricting traffic, creating technical barriers, shutting down services, or canceling authorization. (3) Forcing or indirectly forcing platform-based operators, consumers, or others to participate in promotional or preferential activities, accept unreasonable matching prices, or bear expenses or risks that should be borne by the platform operator. (4) Attaching unreasonable restrictions on transaction conditions and methods, service provision methods, payment methods and means, or after-sales services. (5) Forcing the collection of unreasonable fees such as technical service fees or traffic promotion fees that are not clearly disclosed, in addition to the transaction price, or collecting unreasonable fees beyond the transaction price through repeated charges. (6) Forcing the collection of non-essential user information or attaching trading conditions, transaction processes, or service items unrelated to the subject matter of the transaction. Risk Example: "Lowest Price on the Entire Network" A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its market dominance by requiring platform-based operators to provide the lowest prices on the entire network without justifiable reasons, thereby excluding or restricting market competition. For example, platform operator A, which has a dominant market position, requires platform-based operators not to sell products at prices higher than those on other competing platforms without justifiable reasons. If a platform-based operator lowers its prices on other platforms, it must also lower its prices on platform A to the same or a lower level, and takes measures to ensure the implementation of such requirements, thereby achieving the effect of excluding or restricting competition. Platform operators that do not have a dominant market position and require platform-based operators to provide them with trading conditions equal to or more favorable than those offered to competing platforms regarding product prices, quantities, etc., may constitute monopolistic agreements. Article 15 Differential Treatment Platform operators with a dominant market position shall avoid abusing their market dominance by implementing differential treatment towards trading counterparts, such as platform-based operators or consumers, with the same trading conditions without justifiable reasons, thereby excluding or restricting market competition, through the following means: (1) Implementing differentiated standards, rules, or algorithms in platform entry, fee collection, or marketing promotion for trading counterparts with the same trading conditions, such as product categories, order quantities, or rating levels. (2) Implementing differentiated transaction prices, payment terms, or transaction methods based on user preferences, transaction history, terminal devices, or usage habits, by using algorithms that analyze payment capacity, user stickiness, or price sensitivity. The term "same trading conditions" in the preceding paragraph refers to situations where there are no substantial differences affecting transactions between trading counterparts in terms of transaction security, transaction costs, creditworthiness, transaction stage, or transaction duration. Differences in private information, transaction history, individual preferences, or consumption habits obtained by platform operators during transactions do not affect the determination that trading counterparts have the same conditions. Risk Example: Platform differential treatment A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its market dominance by implementing differential treatment in prices, policies, or other aspects towards platform-based operators, consumers, or other trading counterparts with the same trading conditions without justifiable reasons, thereby excluding or restricting market competition. For example, platform operator A has a dominant market position and, without justifiable reasons, charges platform-based operators with the same scale, products, and creditworthiness significantly different commission rates, thereby achieving the effect of excluding or restricting market competition. Article 16 Justifiable Reasons When assessing whether there are justifiable reasons as stipulated in Articles 11 to 15 of these Guidelines, platform operators may consider the following factors: (1) For a reasonable period, to develop other businesses on the platform, to promote new products into the market, or to conduct promotional activities. (2) Compliance with fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory platform rules, or to prevent undue reduction of interests of operators in the platform economy. (3) Necessity for protecting the legitimate rights and interests of trading counterparts, consumers, or practitioners, or for maintaining a reasonable business model. (4) Compliance with legitimate industry practices and trading habits, or necessity for improving the use value or efficiency of goods. (5) Necessity for protecting intellectual property rights, trade secrets, personal information, or specific resource investments made for transactions. (6) Necessity for protecting transaction security, data security, or network security. (7) Objective factors such as force majeure. (8) Other reasons that can prove the justification of the conduct. Reasons such as consistency with the practices of competing platform operators, following consumption trends, maintaining market price stability, or maintaining the integrity of the platform ecosystem are generally not considered justifiable reasons as stipulated in Articles 11 to 15 of these Guidelines. Section 3 Concentration of Undertakings Concentration of undertakings includes the following situations: (1) merger of undertakings; (2) acquisition of control over other undertakings through the acquisition of equity or assets; (3) acquisition of control over other undertakings or the ability to exert decisive influence over other undertakings through contracts or other means. Article 17 Declaration of Concentration of Undertakings Where the concentration of undertakings reaches the declaration standards stipulated in the "Regulations of the State Council on the Declaration Standards for Concentration of Undertakings," the undertakings shall declare to the anti-monopoly enforcement agency of the State Council in advance and shall not implement the concentration without declaration. The anti-monopoly enforcement agency of the State Council shall handle illegal concentrations of undertakings in accordance with the law. Article 18 Compliance with Concentration of Undertakings Platform operators may refer to the "Guidelines for Anti-Monopoly Compliance of Undertakings" and the "Guidelines for Anti-Monopoly Compliance of Concentration of Undertakings" to identify, assess, and control the anti-monopoly compliance risks of concentration of undertakings, avoid concentrations of undertakings that have or may have the effect of excluding or restricting competition, and prevent legal liabilities arising from illegal implementation of concentrations. Section 4 Abuse of Administrative Power to Exclude or Restrict Competition The "Anti-Monopoly Law" prohibits administrative organs and organizations authorized by laws and regulations to manage public affairs (hereinafter referred to as administrative bodies) from abusing administrative power to exclude or restrict competition. Platform operators may refer to the "Guidelines on Anti-Monopoly in the Field of Platform Economy" to avoid actively or passively engaging in monopolistic practices under the coordination, promotion, or requirement of administrative bodies. Where platform operators believe that administrative organs abuse administrative power to exclude or restrict competition, they may report to the anti-monopoly enforcement agency or apply for administrative reconsideration in accordance with the law. Article 19 Monopolistic Practices Coordinated or Promoted by Administrative Bodies Platform operators shall avoid actively participating in monopolistic practices prohibited by the "Anti-Monopoly Law" that are coordinated or promoted by administrative bodies, or engaging in monopolistic practices by utilizing cooperation agreements, memorandums of understanding, or other documents signed with administrative bodies. Article 20 Monopolistic Practices Required by Administrative Bodies When platform operators receive documents such as measures, decisions, announcements, notices, opinions, letters, or meeting minutes that are required to be executed by administrative bodies, they shall pay close attention to whether the content of the documents carries anti-monopoly compliance risks. If risks exist, they shall report to the anti-monopoly enforcement agency when necessary. Chapter 3 Risk Management Article 21 Risk Assessment Platform operators may establish a risk assessment indicator system based on the characteristics of their industry and market competition conditions, combined with their own business scale and business model, to comprehensively assess anti-monopoly compliance risks. Platform operators are encouraged to implement classified and tiered management based on risk assessment,
