For example, platform operators A and B, which are in competition, collude through algorithms to unify pricing mechanisms, commission rates, etc., thereby reaching a horizontal monopolistic agreement that excludes or restricts market competition. Article 7 Vertical Monopolistic Agreements Platform operators shall avoid reaching vertical monopolistic agreements, such as fixing resale prices or restricting minimum resale prices, with their trading counterparts through the following means: (1) Automating the setting of resale prices using technological means such as big data analysis and artificial intelligence. (2) Unifying resale prices through platform rules related to API calls, data usage, traffic allocation, promotional activities, store management, and user services. (3) Directly or indirectly restricting resale prices through user profiling and predictive algorithms. Article 8 Organizing and Providing Substantial Assistance Platform operators shall avoid organizing platform-based operators or other operators to reach monopolistic agreements or providing substantial assistance for reaching monopolistic agreements through the following means: (1) Organizing or coordinating communication of intent among platform-based operators or between platform-based operators and other operators through data sharing, issuing notices, signing agreements, etc. (2) Providing necessary support or creating key facilitating conditions for platform-based operators or other operators to obtain competitively sensitive information or achieve coordinated behavior. Risk Example: Organizing and assisting platform-based operators to reach monopolistic agreements A platform operator organizes or coordinates platform-based operators that are in competition with each other to reach horizontal agreements, or provides substantial assistance by offering necessary support or creating key conditions. For example, platform operator A signs price adjustment agreements with content that is the same or similar with platform-based operators that are in competition with each other. In this process, it facilitates communication of intent and exchange of competitively sensitive information among platform-based operators, ultimately leading to consistent pricing behavior that excludes or restricts market competition. Section 2 Abuse of Dominant Market Position Abuse of dominant market position refers to conduct by an operator with a dominant market position, such as selling at unfairly high prices, purchasing at unfairly low prices, selling below cost without justifiable reasons, refusing to trade, imposing trading restrictions, tying, attaching other unreasonable conditions, or practicing differential treatment. The "Anti-Monopoly Law" prohibits operators with a dominant market position from engaging in such conduct. Platform operators with a significant market share or market power are encouraged to regularly assess whether they hold a dominant market position in the relevant market. Platform operators shall comply with the "Anti-Monopoly Law" and the "Provisions on Prohibiting Abuse of Dominant Market Position" to avoid engaging in such conduct in the course of providing platform services or conducting self-operated businesses. When identifying the risks of abuse of dominant market position, platform operators shall first define the relevant market, assess whether they hold a dominant market position in the relevant market, and whether they are implementing relevant conduct. Then, they shall consider whether there are justifiable reasons and whether the relevant conduct excludes or restricts market competition to specifically analyze whether it constitutes abuse of dominant market position. Article 9 Factors for Consideration of Dominant Market Position When assessing whether they hold a dominant market position in the relevant market, platform operators may consider the following factors: (1) The platform operator's market share and the competitive landscape of the relevant market. When determining the platform operator's market share, the proportion of transaction value, transaction volume, sales revenue, registered users, active users, click-through rates, usage time, number of platform-based operators, or other indicators in the relevant market may be considered, along with the duration for which such market share has been maintained. When analyzing the competitive landscape of the relevant market, the development status of the relevant market, the number and market share of competing platform operators, the characteristics of platform competition, the degree of platform differentiation, economies of scale, the situation of potential competing platform operators, and innovation and technological changes may be considered. (2) The platform operator's ability to control the market. The platform operator's ability to control upstream and downstream markets or other related markets, to hinder or influence the entry of other platform operators into the relevant market, the relevant business models, network effects, and the ability to influence or determine prices, traffic, or other transaction conditions may be considered in conjunction with factors such as the diversity of online and offline businesses and vertical integration. (3) The platform operator's financial and technical capabilities. Investor status, asset scale, capital sources, profitability, financing capacity, technological innovation and application capabilities, intellectual property rights held, ability to process relevant data, and the extent to which these financial and technical capabilities can promote business expansion or consolidate and maintain market position may be considered. (4) The degree of dependence of platform-based operators and other operators on the platform operator for transactions. The trading relationship, transaction volume, and duration of transactions between platform-based operators and other operators and the platform operator, lock-in effects, user stickiness, the possibility of switching to other platforms, and switching costs may be considered. (5) The ease or difficulty for other platform operators to enter the relevant market. Market access, platform economies of scale, scale of capital investment, technical barriers, user multi-homing, user switching costs, ease or difficulty of data acquisition, and user habits may be considered. (6) Other factors based on the characteristics of the platform economy that determine a platform operator's dominant market position. Article 10 Unfairly High or Low Prices Platform operators with a dominant market position shall avoid abusing their market dominance by selling goods at unfairly high prices or purchasing goods at unfairly low prices through the following means: (1) Charging platform-based operators fees, such as commissions, registration fees, service fees, membership fees, technical service fees, information service fees, and marketing promotion fees, that are significantly higher than those charged by other platform operators in similar businesses under the same or similar market conditions, or increasing the above-mentioned fees charged to platform-based operators by more than a normal margin when costs are basically stable. (2) Charging platform-based operators unfairly high fees by splitting service items or increasing fee categories. (3) Paying platform-based operators prices for goods that are significantly lower than those paid by other platform operators in similar businesses under the same or similar market conditions. When determining whether market conditions are the same or similar, factors such as platform type, business model, transaction stage, cost structure, and specific transaction circumstances may generally be considered. Risk Example: Unfairly high platform prices A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its market dominance to charge platform-based operators unfairly high fees by leveraging platform rules, technology, and algorithms. For example, platform operator A, which has a dominant market position, continuously increases service fees by more than a normal margin for many years while its costs remain basically stable, thereby charging platform-based operators unfairly high fees and harming their interests. Article 11 Selling Below Cost Platform operators with a dominant market position shall avoid abusing their market dominance by selling goods or providing services at prices below cost without justifiable reasons, through excessive subsidies or cross-subsidies, thereby excluding or restricting market competition. When analyzing whether conduct constitutes selling below cost, the focus shall generally be on whether the platform operator is crowding out competing platform operators by selling at prices below cost, and whether it is likely to obtain improper benefits under unfair competitive conditions, harm fair market competition, and infringe upon the legitimate rights and interests of consumers after crowding out competing platform operators. When calculating costs, the cost interrelationships among the relevant markets involved in the platform's multi-sided markets and their reasonableness may be comprehensively considered. Risk Example: Selling below cost on a platform A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its market dominance by providing services at prices below cost without justifiable reasons, through excessive subsidies or preferential policies exceeding reasonable limits, thereby excluding or restricting market competition. For example, platform operator A, which has a dominant market position, provides platform-based operators with free entry and substantial subsidies for a period significantly exceeding the reasonable duration of commercial practice. After competing platform operators exit the relevant market, it significantly increases entry fees and other related fees, thereby obtaining improper benefits and harming fair market competition and the legitimate rights and interests of consumers. Article 12 Refusal to Trade Platform operators with a dominant market position shall avoid abusing their market dominance by refusing to trade with trading counterparts without justifiable reasons, thereby excluding or restricting market competition, through the following means: (1) Terminating, delaying, or interrupting transactions with trading counterparts by delisting products, blocking accounts, setting complex transaction processes, restricting traffic, shutting down interfaces, or interrupting data sharing. (2) Refusing to trade with trading counterparts by setting unreasonable transaction conditions, service fees significantly higher than market reasonable levels, ceasing to provide application updates, interrupting data updates, or delaying the signing of cooperation agreements. (3) Substantially reducing the transaction volume with trading counterparts by restricting traffic acquisition or order acceptance through traffic allocation algorithms, product release rules, etc. (4) Imposing unreasonable restrictions and obstacles that make it difficult for trading counterparts to conduct transactions by formulating unreasonable marketing, research and development, or other platform rules, or using discriminatory algorithms. (5) Refusing to trade with trading counterparts on reasonable terms by controlling specific data, models, or application platforms that constitute essential facilities. Risk Example: Blocking and filtering A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its market dominance by blocking and filtering trading counterparts at the application, transmission, or network layers without justifiable reasons, thereby preventing them from entering the relevant market and excluding or restricting market competition. For example, platform operator A, which has a dominant market position, prevents trading counterparts from conducting specific businesses or participating in market competition without justifiable reasons by restricting link redirection or port access. Article 13 Tying Platform operators with a dominant market position shall avoid abusing their market dominance by imposing trading restrictions without justifiable reasons, requiring trading counterparts to trade only with themselves or their designated operators, or to refrain from trading with specific operators, thereby excluding or restricting market competition, through the following means: (1) Setting exclusive cooperation terms in platform rules for merchant entry, platform services, content release, application development, etc., requiring platform-based operators to cooperate only with the platform or to release specific goods or content only on this platform. (2) Requiring platform-based operators not to cooperate with specific competing platforms or not to participate in promotional activities of specific competing platforms through activity rules, cooperation agreements, or in-platform notices. (3) Implementing restrictions through punitive measures such as blocking stores, de-ranking search results, restricting traffic, deducting deposits, imposing fines, canceling eligibility for promotional activities, delaying launches, differential fees, delayed payment periods, or reducing rating levels. (4) Indirectly implementing restrictions through incentive measures such as subsidies, discounts, preferential offers, traffic resource support,赠送增值服务 (gifting value-added services), or improving rating levels. Risk Example: "Choose One of Two" behavior A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its market dominance by forcing trading counterparts to choose between the platform operator and other competing platform operators without justifiable reasons, and by enforcing such "choose one of two" behavior through punitive or incentive measures, thereby excluding or restricting market competition. For example, platform operator A, which has a dominant market position, requires platform-based operators to commit not to cooperate with competing platforms without justifiable reasons, and punishes platform-based operators that fail to comply with the commitment by de-ranking their search results, delisting their products, restricting their traffic, or deducting their deposits, thereby restricting the platform-based operators' freedom of choice and achieving the effect of excluding or restricting market competition. Article 14 Tying or Attaching Other Unreasonable Conditions Platform operators with a dominant market position shall avoid abusing their market dominance by tying or attaching other unreasonable trading conditions without justifiable reasons, thereby excluding or restricting market competition, through the following means: (1) Using standard terms, pop-up windows, or mandatory operational steps that are difficult to choose, change, or refuse, requiring platform-based operators or consumers to use designated products in conjunction with their services. (2) Forcing platform-based operators, consumers, or others to accept other products by taking punitive measures such as de-ranking search results, restricting traffic, creating technical barriers, shutting down services, or canceling authorization. (3) Forcing or indirectly forcing platform-based operators, consumers, or others to participate in promotional or preferential activities, accept unreasonable matching prices, or bear expenses or risks that should be borne by the platform operator. (4) Attaching unreasonable restrictions on transaction conditions and methods, service provision methods, payment methods and means, or after-sales services. (5) Forcing the collection of unreasonable fees such as technical service fees or traffic promotion fees that are not clearly disclosed, in addition to the transaction price, or collecting unreasonable fees beyond the transaction price through repeated charges. (6) Forcing the collection of non-essential user information or attaching trading conditions, transaction processes, or service items unrelated to the subject matter of the transaction. Risk Example: "Lowest Price on the Entire Network" A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its market dominance by requiring platform-based operators to provide the lowest prices on the entire network without justifiable reasons, thereby excluding or restricting market competition. For example, platform operator A, which has a dominant market position, requires platform-based operators not to sell products at prices higher than those on other competing platforms without justifiable reasons. If a platform-based operator lowers its prices on other platforms, it must also lower its prices on platform A to the same or a lower level, and takes measures to ensure the implementation of such requirements, thereby achieving the effect of excluding or restricting competition. Platform operators that do not have a dominant market position and require platform-based operators to provide them with trading conditions equal to or more favorable than those offered to competing platforms regarding product prices, quantities, etc., may constitute monopolistic agreements. Article 15 Differential Treatment Platform operators with a dominant market position shall avoid abusing their market dominance by implementing differential treatment towards trading counterparts, such as platform-based operators or consumers, with the same trading conditions without justifiable reasons, thereby excluding or restricting market competition, through the following means: (1) Implementing differentiated standards, rules, or algorithms in platform entry, fee collection, or marketing promotion for trading counterparts with the same trading conditions, such as product categories, order quantities, or rating levels. (2) Implementing differentiated transaction prices, payment terms, or transaction methods based on user preferences, transaction history, terminal devices, or usage habits, by using algorithms that analyze payment capacity, user stickiness, or price sensitivity. The term "same trading conditions" in the preceding paragraph refers to situations where there are no substantial differences affecting transactions between trading counterparts in terms of transaction security, transaction costs, creditworthiness, transaction stage, or transaction duration. Differences in private information, transaction history, individual preferences, or consumption habits obtained by platform operators during transactions do not affect the determination that trading counterparts have the same conditions. Risk Example: Platform differential treatment A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its market dominance by implementing differential treatment in prices, policies, or other aspects towards platform-based operators, consumers, or other trading counterparts with the same trading conditions without justifiable reasons, thereby excluding or restricting market competition. For example, platform operator A has a dominant market position and, without justifiable reasons, charges platform-based operators with the same scale, products, and creditworthiness significantly different commission rates, thereby achieving the effect of excluding or restricting market competition. Article 16 Justifiable Reasons When assessing whether there are justifiable reasons as stipulated in Articles 11 to 15 of these Guidelines, platform operators may consider the following factors: (1) For a reasonable period, to develop other businesses on the platform, to promote new products into the market, or to conduct promotional activities. (2) Compliance with fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory platform rules, or to prevent undue reduction of interests of operators in the platform economy. (3) Necessity for protecting the legitimate rights and interests of trading counterparts, consumers, or practitioners, or for maintaining a reasonable business model. (4) Compliance with legitimate industry practices and trading habits, or necessity for improving the use value or efficiency of goods. (5) Necessity for protecting intellectual property rights, trade secrets, personal information, or specific resource investments made for transactions. (6) Necessity for protecting transaction security, data security, or network security. (7) Objective factors such as force majeure. (8) Other reasons that can prove the justification of the conduct. Reasons such as consistency with the practices of competing platform operators, following consumption trends, maintaining market price stability, or maintaining the integrity of the platform ecosystem are generally not considered justifiable reasons as stipulated in Articles 11 to 15 of these Guidelines. Section 3 Concentration of Undertakings Concentration of undertakings includes the following situations: (1) merger of undertakings; (2) acquisition of control over other undertakings through the acquisition of equity or assets; (3) acquisition of control over other undertakings or the ability to exert decisive influence over other undertakings through contracts or other means. Article 17 Declaration of Concentration of Undertakings Where the concentration of undertakings reaches the declaration standards stipulated in the "Regulations of the State Council on the Declaration Standards for Concentration of Undertakings," the undertakings shall declare to the anti-monopoly enforcement agency of the State Council in advance and shall not implement the concentration without declaration. The anti-monopoly enforcement agency of the State Council shall handle illegal concentrations of undertakings in accordance with the law. Article 18 Compliance with Concentration of Undertakings Platform operators may refer to the "Guidelines for Anti-Monopoly Compliance of Undertakings" and the "Guidelines for Anti-Monopoly Compliance of Concentration of Undertakings" to identify, assess, and control the anti-monopoly compliance risks of concentration of undertakings, avoid concentrations of undertakings that have or may have the effect of excluding or restricting competition, and prevent legal liabilities arising from illegal implementation of concentrations. Section 4 Abuse of Administrative Power to Exclude or Restrict Competition The "Anti-Monopoly Law" prohibits administrative organs and organizations authorized by laws and regulations to manage public affairs (hereinafter referred to as administrative bodies) from abusing administrative power to exclude or restrict competition. Platform operators may refer to the "Guidelines on Anti-Monopoly in the Field of Platform Economy" to avoid actively or passively engaging in monopolistic practices under the coordination, promotion, or requirement of administrative bodies. Where platform operators believe that administrative organs abuse administrative power to exclude or restrict competition, they may report to the anti-monopoly enforcement agency or apply for administrative reconsideration in accordance with the law. Article 19 Monopolistic Practices Coordinated or Promoted by Administrative Bodies Platform operators shall avoid actively participating in monopolistic practices prohibited by the "Anti-Monopoly Law" that are coordinated or promoted by administrative bodies, or engaging in monopolistic practices by utilizing cooperation agreements, memorandums of understanding, or other documents signed with administrative bodies. Article 20 Monopolistic Practices Required by Administrative Bodies When platform operators receive documents such as measures, decisions, announcements, notices, opinions, letters, or meeting minutes that are required to be executed by administrative bodies, they shall pay close attention to whether the content of the documents carries anti-monopoly compliance risks. If risks exist, they shall report to the anti-monopoly enforcement agency when necessary. Chapter 3 Risk Management Article 21 Risk Assessment Platform operators may establish a risk assessment indicator system based on the characteristics of their industry and market competition conditions, combined with their own business scale and business model, to comprehensively assess anti-monopoly compliance risks. title_en: Meituan's market value once fell below HK$500 billion, and the industry competition landscape is gradually becoming clear.
body_en: On February 13th, Meituan's stock price continued to fall, with intraday declines exceeding 4.5%, and its market value once dropped below HK$500 billion. By the close of trading on February 13th, Meituan's stock price was HK$82.5. Since January, Meituan's stock price has been on a continuous decline, and the current price is down 22.5% from the high of HK$106.5 on January 13th. Wang Pengbo, a senior analyst in the financial industry at BoTong Consulting, told Yicai Global that Meituan's stock price adjustment since January is mainly influenced by three factors: industry competition, mergers and acquisitions, and profit expectations, among which phased competitive pressure and market sentiment have a relatively greater impact. In particular, competition within the industry has intensified, and subsidy behaviors have led to an increase in related expenses, exerting some pressure on short-term profits. Business integration from acquisitions also incurs phased costs, causing market concerns about short-term performance. Wang Pengbo believes that regulatory norms are more about guiding the long-term healthy development of the industry and have limited impact on the overall value of the company, as the company's core barriers have not changed. On February 5th, Meituan announced in a Hong Kong Stock Exchange filing that it had completed the acquisition of 100% of the equity of Dingdong Maicai's China business for an initial consideration of approximately US$717 million (approximately RMB 4.98 billion). In terms of food delivery competition, Taobao Flash Purchase distributed free order coupons to users through the Qianwen App in February, leading to a surge in orders for milk tea shops. In addition, the food delivery industry has recently faced regulatory challenges, and competition among platforms has once again drawn attention. Before the Spring Festival, market supervision administrations in cities such as Bengbu, Deyang, and Jinhua issued a notice on the operating order of the Spring Festival food delivery market, requiring platforms to balance the interests of consumers, merchants, delivery personnel, and the platforms themselves, and to protect the legitimate rights and interests of all parties. In January, the Office of the National Anti-Monopoly and Anti-Unfair Competition Committee of the State Council conducted an investigation and assessment of the market competition in the food delivery platform services industry in accordance with the Anti-Monopoly Law of the People's Republic of China. Regarding the future stock price trend of Meituan, Wang Pengbo stated that although Meituan's stock price will remain in a phase of volatile consolidation in the short term, the space for further significant weakening is limited, and there is no basis for a continuous downward trend. The industry competition landscape is gradually becoming clearer, and business integration after the acquisition and profit recovery are progressing normally. As competition becomes more rational, cost control measures take effect, and business integration proceeds smoothly, the company's valuation will gradually return to its fundamentals, and it has the conditions for volatile recovery in the medium to long term. A research report released by GF Securities in February shows that Meituan has strong operational barriers in its food delivery business and will maintain a leading position in the local life services industry in the long term. Short-term competition in the food delivery sector will continue to put pressure on profits. Looking ahead to 2026, it is expected that the profitability of food delivery will improve compared to the loss level in the second half of 2025. Chen Liteng, an analyst at the E-commerce Research Center of the Network Economy, believes that Meituan still possesses relatively stable core advantages. Its nationwide instant delivery network, the dual-sided ecosystem barrier formed by a massive user base and merchants, the synergistic effect of businesses such as food delivery and in-store travel, and the addition of fresh supply chain and pre-warehouse capabilities after the acquisition of Dingdong are fundamental supports that are difficult to replicate quickly. If competition returns to rationality and business synergies are realized, performance and valuation are expected to gradually recover; in the long term, it will be determined by the pace of profit recovery and the growth momentum of new businesses, showing a differentiated trend, and requiring continuous tracking of key performance and competition landscape signals.

title_en: Internet Platform Anti-Monopoly Compliance Guidelines Released
body_en: People's Daily, Beijing, February 13th (Reporter Sun Hongli) According to the website of the State Administration for Market Regulation, to support and guide platform operators in effectively preventing antitrust compliance risks, improving antitrust compliance management systems, protecting the legitimate rights and interests of relevant parties, maintaining fair market competition order, and promoting the innovative and healthy development of the platform economy, the "Guidelines for Antitrust Compliance of Internet Platforms" (hereinafter referred to as the "Guidelines") were released today. Internet platforms have obvious network effects and involve multiple parties, including platform operators, platform-based merchants, consumers, and practitioners. Platform operators typically have certain managerial attributes, strengthening market power through data and algorithms, technology, capital advantages, and platform rules, thereby influencing the platform's competitive ecosystem. It is essential to effectively strengthen antitrust compliance management. The "Guidelines" require platform operators to follow four major principles: targeted, comprehensive, penetrating, and continuous, in carrying out antitrust compliance management work to achieve fair rules, algorithms for good, and competitive compliance. They must earnestly assume the primary responsibility for antitrust compliance, improve antitrust compliance systems, strengthen antitrust compliance management, compete lawfully, operate compliantly, and must not engage in monopolistic behaviors prohibited by the "Anti-Monopoly Law" by leveraging data and algorithms, technology, capital advantages, or platform rules. The "Guidelines" stipulate four types of monopolistic risks: monopolistic agreements, abuse of dominant market position, monopolistic concentration of undertakings, and abuse of administrative power to exclude or restrict competition. They also list eight risk examples, including algorithmic collusion between platforms, organizing and assisting platform-based merchants in reaching monopolistic agreements, unfair high pricing by platforms, platform sales below cost, blocking and shielding, "choose one of two" practices, "lowest price across the network," and differential treatment by platforms. The following is the full text of the "Guidelines": **Guidelines for Antitrust Compliance of Internet Platforms** **Chapter 1 General Provisions** **Article 1 Purpose and Basis** To support and guide platform operators in effectively preventing antitrust compliance risks, improving antitrust compliance management systems, protecting the legitimate rights and interests of relevant parties, maintaining fair market competition order, and promoting the innovative and healthy development of the platform economy, these Guidelines are formulated in accordance with the "Anti-Monopoly Law of the People's Republic of China" (hereinafter referred to as the "Anti-Monopoly Law") and other laws and regulations. **Article 2 Relevant Concepts** For the purposes of these Guidelines, "Internet platform" refers to a business organizational form that, through network information technology, enables interdependent bilateral or multilateral parties to trade or engage in other activities under the rules provided by a specific carrier, thereby jointly creating value. "Platform operator" as used in these Guidelines refers to an operator that provides Internet platform services such as operating venues, transaction matching, and information exchange to natural persons, legal persons, and other market entities. "Platform-based merchant" as used in these Guidelines refers to a merchant that provides goods or services (hereinafter collectively referred to as "goods") within an Internet platform. "Antitrust compliance risk" as used in these Guidelines refers to the possibility of platform operators and their employees incurring legal liabilities, causing economic or reputational losses, or other negative consequences due to violations of relevant provisions of the "Anti-Monopoly Law." "Antitrust compliance management" as used in these Guidelines refers to organized, planned, and full-process management activities targeting the business and management behaviors of platform operators and the performance of duties by their employees, with the aim of preventing and controlling antitrust compliance risks. **Article 3 Necessity of Compliance Management** Internet platforms have obvious network effects and involve multiple parties, including platform operators, platform-based merchants, consumers, and practitioners. Platform operators typically have certain managerial attributes, strengthening market power through data and algorithms, technology, capital advantages, and platform rules, thereby influencing the platform's competitive ecosystem. It is essential to effectively strengthen antitrust compliance management. Platform operators that violate the "Anti-Monopoly Law" will bear corresponding legal responsibilities and incur related commercial and credit risks. Strengthening antitrust compliance management by platform operators can avoid risks arising from engaging in monopolistic behaviors, cultivate a good brand image, and enhance core competitive advantages. Enhancing antitrust compliance awareness and improving antitrust compliance management systems by platform operators are conducive to raising the level and quality of competition, optimizing resource allocation, improving operational efficiency, protecting the legitimate rights and interests of multiple parties, promoting the continuous optimization of the platform's competitive ecosystem, and achieving the innovative development of the platform economy. **Article 4 Basic Principles** Platform operators shall follow the basic principles below and refer to these Guidelines in carrying out antitrust compliance management work to achieve fair rules, algorithms for good, and competitive compliance: (1) **Targeted Principle.** Identify, assess, and control compliance risks in a targeted manner by considering factors such as the industry, business model, governance structure, and market competition conditions of the platform operator, and carry out antitrust compliance management accordingly. (2) **Comprehensive Principle.** Promote compliance throughout the entire chain, including ex-ante, in-process, and ex-post stages, achieving full coverage of business areas, departments, and employees, and integrating all aspects of decision-making, execution, and supervision to build a coordinated and comprehensive compliance system. (3) **Penetrating Principle.** Connect the headquarters, branches, and holding subsidiaries of platform operators, improve the guidance, coordination, and supervision mechanisms of the headquarters, and reinforce the compliance management responsibilities of each branch to achieve penetration across levels, businesses, and rules/algorithms. (4) **Continuous Principle.** Improve the long-term mechanism for antitrust compliance, ensure the continuous and effective implementation of compliance management systems, prevent "one-off" or "phased" compliance, regularly assess the platform operator's own compliance operations, and promptly update and improve antitrust compliance management systems. **Article 5 Overall Compliance Requirements** Platform operators shall earnestly assume the primary responsibility for antitrust compliance, improve antitrust compliance systems, strengthen antitrust compliance management, compete lawfully, operate compliantly, and must not engage in monopolistic behaviors prohibited by the "Anti-Monopoly Law" by leveraging data and algorithms, technology, capital advantages, or platform rules. **Chapter 2 Risk Identification** **Section 1 Monopolistic Agreements** A monopolistic agreement refers to an agreement, decision, or other concerted action that excludes or restricts competition. The "Anti-Monopoly Law" prohibits operators from reaching monopolistic agreements. Platform operators shall comply with the "Anti-Monopoly Law" and the "Provisions on Prohibiting Monopolistic Agreements" and avoid reaching monopolistic agreements in the process of providing platform services or conducting self-operated businesses, as well as organizing other operators to reach monopolistic agreements or providing substantial assistance. When identifying the risk of monopolistic agreements, platform operators typically first analyze whether the relevant behavior falls under the circumstances stipulated in Articles 17, 18(1), and 19 of the "Anti-Monopoly Law," and then analyze whether such behavior meets the conditions for non-prohibition or exemption stipulated in the "Anti-Monopoly Law." **Article 6 Horizontal Monopolistic Agreements** Platform operators that are in competition with each other shall avoid reaching horizontal monopolistic agreements that fix or change prices, restrict production or sales volume, divide markets, restrict new technologies or products, or jointly boycott transactions through the following means: (1) Engaging in communication and information exchange regarding competitively sensitive information through meetings, phone calls, text messages, emails, shared documents, instant messaging tools, shared data pools, interoperability agreements, cloud storage platforms, artificial intelligence, etc. (2) Collecting and exchanging competitively sensitive information such as pricing models, commission rates, preferential policies, customer lists, traffic allocation mechanisms, and research and development, investment, production, marketing, and promotion strategies. (3) Achieving coordinated behavior in user segmentation, dynamic pricing, traffic allocation, and product ranking through data, algorithms, technology, and platform rules. **Risk Example:** Algorithmic collusion between platforms Platform operators that are in competition with each other use algorithms to reach monopolistic agreements through communication, exchange of sensitive information, and coordinated behavior. (6) Forcing the collection of non-essential user information or attaching transaction conditions, transaction processes, or service items unrelated to the subject matter of the transaction. **Risk Example:** "Choose one of two" practices A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its dominant market position by forcing trading counterparts to choose between the platform operator and other competing platform operators without justifiable reasons, and enforcing such "choose one of two" practices through punitive or incentive measures, thereby excluding or restricting market competition. For example, platform operator A, which has a dominant market position, without justifiable reasons, requires platform-based merchants to promise not to cooperate with competing platforms and punishes those who fail to comply by demoting their search rankings, delisting their products, restricting their traffic, or deducting their security deposits, thereby restricting the merchants' freedom of choice and resulting in the exclusion or restriction of market competition. **Article 14 Tying or Attaching Other Unreasonable Conditions** Platform operators with a dominant market position shall avoid abusing their dominant market position by tying or attaching other unreasonable transaction conditions without justifiable reasons, thereby excluding or restricting market competition, through the following means: (1) Using format clauses, pop-ups, or mandatory operational steps that are difficult to select, change, or refuse, requiring platform-based merchants or consumers to use designated goods in conjunction with the use of their services. (4) Attaching unreasonable restrictions on transaction conditions and methods, service provision methods, payment methods and means, after-sales services, etc. (5) Charging unreasonable fees such as technical service fees or traffic promotion fees that are not clearly disclosed in addition to the transaction price, or charging unreasonable fees in addition to the transaction price through repeated charges. (6) Forcing the collection of non-essential user information or attaching transaction conditions, transaction processes, or service items unrelated to the subject matter of the transaction. **Risk Example:** "Lowest price across the network" A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its dominant market position by requiring platform-based merchants to provide the lowest price across the network without justifiable reasons, thereby excluding or restricting market competition. For example, platform operator A, which has a dominant market position, without justifiable reasons, requires platform-based merchants not to sell goods at a higher price on other competitive platforms than on its platform. If prices are lowered on other platforms, they must also be lowered to the same or a lower level on platform A, and measures are taken to ensure compliance with such requirements, resulting in the exclusion or restriction of competition. Platform operators that do not have a dominant market position but require platform-based merchants to provide trading conditions equal to or more favorable than those offered to competitive platforms in terms of product prices, quantities, etc., may constitute a monopolistic agreement. **Article 15 Differential Treatment** Platform operators with a dominant market position shall avoid abusing their dominant market position by implementing differential treatment towards trading counterparts, such as platform-based merchants or consumers, whose trading conditions are the same, without justifiable reasons, thereby excluding or restricting market competition, through the following means: (1) Implementing differentiated standards, rules, or algorithms in terms of platform entry, fee collection, or marketing promotion for trading counterparts with the same trading conditions, such as product categories, order quantities, or rating levels. (2) Implementing differentiated transaction prices, payment terms, or transaction methods based on algorithms that analyze user preferences, transaction history, terminal devices, usage habits, payment capacity, user stickiness, and price sensitivity. For the purposes of the preceding paragraph, "same trading conditions" means that there are no substantial differences affecting transactions in terms of transaction security, transaction costs, creditworthiness, transaction stage, or transaction duration among trading counterparts. Differences in privacy information, transaction history, individual preferences, and consumption habits obtained by platform operators during transactions do not affect the determination that the trading counterparts have the same conditions. **Risk Example:** Differential treatment by platforms A platform operator with a dominant market position abuses its dominant market position by implementing differential treatment in terms of prices or policies towards trading counterparts, such as platform-based merchants or consumers, whose trading conditions are the same, without justifiable reasons, thereby excluding or restricting market competition. title_en: Market Supervision Administration summons 7 platform companies to curb "involutionary" competition
body_en: On February 13th, the State Administration for Market Regulation interviewed platform companies including Alibaba, Douyin, Baidu, Tencent, JD.com, Meituan, and Taobao Flash Sale. The administration required these platform companies to strictly abide by laws and regulations such as the "Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China," the "Price Law of the People's Republic of China," the "Law of the People's Republic of China on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests," and the "E-commerce Law of the People's Republic of China." They were also urged to proactively fulfill their primary responsibilities and further regulate platform promotional activities. Relevant platform companies were reminded to eliminate all forms of "involutionary" competition, jointly maintain a fair competitive market environment, and promote the innovation and healthy development of the platform economy. (CCTV Reporter Li Jingjing)

title_en: Hong Kong tech stocks plunge at the start of the year, is the Hang Seng Tech Index also becoming "old and slow"? | Market Watch
body_en: On February 20th, the fourth day of the Lunar New Year, which was the first trading day for Hong Kong stocks in the Year of the Dragon, the Hang Seng Tech Index once fell by over 2.5% to 5222 points, hitting a new adjustment low in nearly five months. Some investors exclaimed, "Have the major constituent stocks of the Hang Seng Tech Index also become 'old men'?" Alibaba (09988.HK) once fell by more than 4%, Baidu Group (09888.HK) once fell by over 6%, and Tencent Holdings (00700.HK) once fell by over 2%. In stark contrast, some newly listed stocks related to artificial intelligence and chips, including Zhipu (02513.HK), MINIMAX (00100.HK), and Montage Technology (06809.HK), continued to surge and hit new highs. As of the midday closing on that day, the Hang Seng Tech Index closed at 5245 points, down 2.28%, with a turnover of 22.5 billion Hong Kong dollars; the Hang Seng Index fell 0.61% to close at 26544 points, with a turnover of 91.7 billion Hong Kong dollars. Industry insiders analyzed that competition in businesses such as food delivery and red envelopes was fierce around the Spring Festival, and investors began to worry about the return on investment in artificial intelligence. It is expected that Hong Kong technology and internet stocks will remain weak, and it is estimated that until Tencent and other companies announce their earnings in March, technology and internet stocks will restart share buybacks, and stock prices will gradually stabilize. Wu Lixian, a strategist at Everbright Securities International, analyzed for Yicai Global that technology and internet stocks are still dragging down Hong Kong stocks. Investors are concerned about the business development of companies like Alibaba and Baidu, and related stocks have fallen significantly. Currently, technology stocks as a whole are not the main focus of capital, and coupled with the lack of support from southbound funds, it is expected that Hong Kong stocks may continue to weaken in the short term. The short-term support for the Hang Seng Index is around 26000 to 26200 points. Li Zeming, Investment Director of Red Ant Capital, believes that investors' doubts about the effectiveness of AI infrastructure construction are growing. Compared to the same period last year, the cost of AI infrastructure construction has increased significantly, but profits and revenue have not grown at the same rate in the commercialization process. The prices of infrastructure such as chips, storage, power generation equipment, and energy storage are continuously soaring, while competition in the downstream AI application end is intensifying. The leading advantages and moats of some companies are not obvious and are easily replaced by competitors. Investors may need to establish new valuation models to deal with such problems. In addition, AI applications are developing rapidly and have shown a trend of replacing traditional software and traditional SaaS (Software as a Service). Li Zeming stated that for some leading technology and internet stocks, the market is worried about their excessive upstream AI investment and difficulty in obtaining corresponding returns, and on the other hand, it is worried about businesses like gaming being disrupted by AI, leading to valuation difficulties. Businesses like food delivery are also facing fierce competition. In the short term, technology and internet stocks still face certain downward pressure, but as stock prices gradually reflect negative factors, they may gradually form a bottom. It is expected that future rebound catalysts may include policy benefits and interest rate cuts by the Federal Reserve. On a stock-specific level, it is expected that companies will restart share buybacks after announcing their earnings, which will provide some support for stock prices. Liu Gang, an analyst at CICC, stated that overseas, short-term disturbances have relatively weakened. The US CPI data in January provided some positive news, which helped alleviate the pressure from the Federal Reserve's hawkish stance. The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds has fallen to 4.05%, a decrease of 25 basis points from the high of 4.3% at the end of January. Although interest rate cuts are still "far away," the decline in long-term interest rates has the same effect as interest rate cuts on interest-rate-sensitive demand and the denominator of Hong Kong stocks, the latter of which also achieves its effect by guiding long-term interest rates. title_en: Li Wenlong: Building a strong financial nation also requires building a strong digital financial nation | Big Names Talk in the Year of the Horse
body_en: The "15th Five-Year Plan" proposals advocate for accelerating the construction of a strong financial nation, vigorously developing technological finance, green finance, inclusive finance, pension finance, and digital finance, with a particular emphasis on "digital finance." This represents a significant upgrade and breakthrough compared to the "14th Five-Year Plan," which outlined eleven areas for building a modern strong nation: "culture, education, talent, sports, science and technology, manufacturing, quality, cyberspace, transportation, trade, and the ocean," but did not mention a "strong financial nation." In reality, from the perspective of the global economic division of labor, building a strong financial nation holds extreme top-level value and strategic guidance. Furthermore, against the backdrop of the global economy's accelerated shift towards the digital economy, it is even more crucial to prioritize the construction of a "strong digital financial nation." This is key for China to gain a leading advantage in current and future global digital economic development. I. Finance is the apex of the economic division of labor system, determining whether the Chinese nation can truly rise. From a global industrial perspective, in the traditional economic division of labor pyramid, agriculture and resource industries are at the bottom, and manufacturing is in the middle. Since the financial industry provides the channels and methods for financing and payment in global economic activities, and determines the carriers and forms of wealth, it is the lifeline of the economy and thus sits at the apex of the global economic pyramid. From the perspective of global national economic division, for a long time, even as the manufacturing industries of the UK and the US have continuously shrunk and their influence has been limited, due to the Anglo-Saxon groups of the US and UK and Jewish financiers controlling the global financial system, they have occupied the apex of the pyramid. Consequently, the US and UK have exerted the greatest influence globally, able to arbitrarily use finance as a tool of control and deterrence. In contrast, although Germany and Japan have developed manufacturing industries, they have never been able to reach the top-tier financial advantage of the US and UK. Currently, China, as a manufacturing powerhouse, is in a significantly weaker position in the international financial arena. International financial payments and payment tools are controlled by Europe and the US, preventing China from reaching the apex of the global economic pyramid. This poses a huge long-term pressure and challenge to China's global rise. Therefore, while being a manufacturing powerhouse is extremely important, if China is currently complacent about being a global manufacturing power or stops there, it may at best develop into a "larger Germany" or a "larger Japan" in the future, potentially blocking China's path and steps to becoming a global financial power and hindering its true rise to become a world-class strong nation. II. The global economy is accelerating its shift towards the digital economy, and the explosion of digital finance based on data elements and digital assets is an inevitable trend. Currently, the global traditional economy is irreversibly accelerating its shift towards the digital economy, which is a universally recognized development trend. In the digital economy, digitalization has generated a large number of data elements and data resources, becoming the core assets of the digital economy, ranking alongside traditional real estate, movable property, and traditional financial assets as the four major asset classes. With the massive emergence of digital assets, accumulating and participating in economic activities at a faster pace than traditional assets, digital finance activities surrounding digital assets will become increasingly active and explosive. This includes, under compliance and regulatory conditions, leveraging blockchain technology to link industries, with digital finance activities possessing high levels of trustworthiness, liquidity, tradability, and traceability. These are bound to become the main financial manifestations of the global digital economy. III. Digital finance plays a core role in the digital economy. In the traditional economic division of labor pyramid, agriculture and resource industries are at the bottom, manufacturing is in the middle, and finance is at the apex. Correspondingly, in the digital economy division of labor pyramid, digital agriculture and digital manufacturing are at the middle and lower levels, while digital finance will undoubtedly be at the apex of the digital economy pyramid. In view of this, while paying attention to the development of other digital industries, it is necessary to have a clear understanding and high regard for the strategic position and top-tier advantage of digital finance in the digital economy. This is crucial for China to set its core goals and correct direction for building a modern strong nation. IV. A strong digital financial nation is crucial for truly achieving global rise in the digital economy. Currently, China holds a leading position in the foundational areas of the global digital economy, particularly in social governance and manufacturing. However, it remains relatively weak in the digital finance sector. Specifically, the international influence and application of the digital yuan are still in their early stages, and compliant digital finance applications supported by blockchain technology have just begun. Fortunately, in the current global digital economy division of labor pyramid, the layout of digital finance has not yet been fully solidified, presenting significant opportunities for China. At the same time, it is important to be vigilant, as the United States has accelerated its efforts to secure a top-tier advantage in the digital economy pyramid, aiming to establish global leadership in digital finance. Given this situation, China should make building a strong digital financial nation its core objective for becoming a strong financial nation. This is crucial for the Chinese nation to truly achieve global rise in the digital economy. title_en: Institutional investors collectively anticipate a "good start" for A-shares in the Year of the Horse, outlining two main themes for the spring rally.
body_en: The strong performance of Hong Kong stocks on the last day of the Spring Festival holiday has led institutions to be highly optimistic about a "red opening" for A-shares in the Year of the Horse. On February 23rd, both the Hang Seng Index and the Hang Seng Tech Index strengthened. title_en: Institutional Outlook丨Post-holiday spring rally expected to continue; media sector poised to benefit from new AI application dividends
body_en: The A-share market saw a slight increase in the week before the holiday, with the Shanghai Composite Index rising by 0.41%, the Shenzhen Component Index by 1.39%, and the ChiNext Index by 1.22%. How will the A-share market perform going forward? Here's what institutions have to say: ① Galaxy Securities: A-share market likely to trend upwards after the holiday. Galaxy Securities' research report suggests that after the Spring Festival, driven by policy expectations, liquidity support, and industry trend catalysts, the market is likely to trend upwards with some volatility. However, short-term market sentiment may be affected by overseas uncertainties. Around the Two Sessions, the A-share market's core driver will likely be policy catalysts, with funds rotating around policy-oriented industry themes and opportunities, characterized by "policy hot spot rotation and rapid style shifts." In March, the market logic will gradually shift from "policy expectations" to "earnings realization." The disclosure of listed companies' 2025 annual reports and subsequent 2026 first-quarter reports will serve as anchors for the market. Stocks with better-than-expected earnings may attract focused investment. In terms of allocation opportunities, focus on: Theme 1, the "anti-involution" concept driven by improved supply-demand dynamics and industry profit recovery, as well as dividend assets with valuation safety margins. The allocation logic remains clear, and it is recommended to pay attention to non-ferrous metals (precious metals) and petrochemicals benefiting from price increases, as well as sectors like basic chemicals, steel, cement, building materials, and finance. Theme 2, during the Spring Festival holiday, hot topics like robots and large AI models received widespread attention, and structural highlights may emerge after the holiday. As the global landscape undergoes unprecedented changes, and China's economic fundamentals shift towards new productive forces, key "15th Five-Year Plan" areas such as semiconductors, artificial intelligence, new energy, military industry, and aerospace are worth watching. ② CITIC Securities: Spring rally expected to continue after the holiday, with price increases remaining a core allocation theme for the first quarter. CITIC Securities' research report indicates that February of this year is a significant turning point. The leap in AI coding capabilities has officially brought the scale of effective global code into an exponential expansion phase. However, the expansion speed of the total value of social physical production and total income, under current physical AI technology conditions, lags far behind the expansion speed of AI-generated code. The world is likely to first experience a period of code volume expansion, excess execution power, intensified competition, and a decline in the return on capital investment. Based on the degree of physical dependence and regulatory/emotional barriers of different industries, we can categorize industries into four types: Damaged (low physical dependence, low regulatory/emotional barriers), Reshaped (low dependence, high barriers), Fortress (high dependence, high barriers), and Beneficiary (high physical dependence, low regulatory/emotional barriers). In the coming period, the gap in returns between beneficiaries of physical scarcity and those damaged by code expansion may widen, and this divergence trend will continue. This is a new factor that must be considered when analyzing market trends and sector allocation. From a short-term market perspective, the A-share industry structure is dominated by manufacturing and finance. Under the impact of AI, the influence on these sectors is relatively smaller compared to the US and Hong Kong stock markets. The inflow of funds and the desire for market gains have not changed, and the spring rally is expected to continue after the holiday, with price increases remaining one of the core allocation themes for the first quarter. ③ Huaxin Securities: Media sector is expected to benefit from new AI application dividends. Huaxin Securities' research report states that the 2026 Spring Festival Gala was a highly concentrated year for AI, and an important watershed and node for AI applications. After the Spring Festival Gala, AI competition will become more intense, with various companies continuously launching new models and products. The market performance of Hong Kong stocks, from Zhipu to Minimax, highlights market sentiment. After the Spring Festival, the AI sector in A-shares is expected to continue its momentum, with the media sector likely to benefit from new AI application dividends. From Doubao AI interactions to embodied intelligence applications, the performances during the Spring Festival Gala have lowered the public's perception of technological applications and significantly popularized cutting-edge technologies among audiences in lower-tier markets in China. 2026 will also become a pivotal year for the media industry to move towards "intelligent media." The benefits of the media sector from AI, ranging from GEO in digital marketing advertising to AIGC in content, will continue to provide new supply. Seedance 2.0 has lowered the threshold for content generation but also raised the aesthetic standards of content. With the maturity of AI technology, the next wave of competition is expected to shift from AI entry point competition to user attention economy competition. The media sector can focus on areas such as film, games, Chinese animation, TV series, music, reading, digital marketing advertising, e-commerce, digital creativity, and immersive experiences. ④ Huaxi Securities: After the long holiday, A-shares will experience a "red envelope rally." Huaxi Securities' research report anticipates a "red envelope rally" for A-shares after the holiday. Firstly, during the Spring Festival, external uncertainties such as the situation in Iran and Trump's tariff policies somewhat suppressed market risk appetite, leading to a strengthening of safe-haven assets. However, driven by the stellar performance of the technology sector, global stock markets generally rose. Secondly, against the backdrop of a rebound in the US dollar index, the RMB exchange rate remained stable and appreciated moderately, which helps strengthen expectations for medium- to long-term funds to increase their allocation to Chinese assets. Thirdly, during the Spring Festival, numerous catalysts were released in technology fields such as robots, large AI models, and storage, boosting market expectations for a technology rally after the holiday. ⑤ Zheshang Securities: Mixed bullish and bearish factors, with a tendency towards stronger volatility; hold positions and observe, with more watching and less action. Zheshang Securities' research report indicates that the market experienced a pullback after a surge before the holiday, showing stronger volatility, with major broad-based indices exhibiting "large weak, small strong" characteristics. Looking ahead, during the holiday period, overseas markets presented a mix of bullish and bearish factors: on one hand, during the Spring Festival, the FTSE A50 futures rose by 1.39%, the Nasdaq and S&P 500 closed higher, the AI application sector in Hong Kong stocks surged, and the offshore RMB exchange rate broke through 6.89. On the other hand, the Hang Seng Index and the Hang Seng Tech Index fell by 0.58% and 2.78% respectively, and internet giants like Alibaba, Baidu, and Meituan performed poorly. Considering the A-share market's pullback after a surge before the holiday, its volatile trend, the mixed bullish and bearish factors during the holiday, and the historical demand for fund returns after the Spring Festival, the probability of a trend-setting opportunity appearing at the A-share opening after the holiday is low. In the short to medium term, it is expected to be characterized by stronger volatility, with localized opportunities likely to emerge in AI applications with overseas market mapping and robots with Spring Festival Gala mapping. From a quarterly perspective, the opportunity for a "systematic slow bull market" remains optimistic. In terms of allocation, based on the judgment of "mixed bullish and bearish factors, with a tendency towards stronger volatility; hold positions and observe, with more watching and less action," institutions suggest: For timing, short-term positions should adopt a "more watching and less action" approach, waiting for opportunities, while medium-term positions should continue to hold with a "systematic slow bull market" mindset. In terms of sectors, focus on relatively low-valued sectors such as securities, building materials, and banks, while also paying attention to AI applications and robot sectors in the short term. For individual stocks, prioritize those that have lagged in gains since the "924 rally," have the potential for catch-up gains, and have managed to break above their annual moving averages.

The FTSE China A50 futures rose by over 1.5%. On the 23rd, Hong Kong stocks surged across the board, with gold and precious metals concept stocks strengthening. Tongguan Gold rose by over 12%, while Chifeng Gold and Zhaojin Mining rose by over 7%. Technology, internet, consumer electronics, and lithium battery sectors led the gains, with optical communication concept stocks such as Yangtze Optical Fibre and Cable, Accelink Technologies, and Comlink Technology surging. The AI large model sector fell against the trend, while the pharmaceutical and real estate sectors weakened slightly. Driven by risk aversion sentiment, international gold and silver prices continued to rise, with international gold futures achieving four consecutive days of gains. COMEX gold rose by 1.7%, COMEX silver by 8.5%, and CME Bitcoin futures fell by 1.3%. ICE Brent crude oil and WTI crude oil rose by 5.6%. Additionally, the US dollar index fell significantly by 0.9%, the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds rose by 4 basis points, the offshore RMB against the US dollar remained flat, and the Japanese yen depreciated by 1.5% against the US dollar. 02 US Supreme Court Rules on Tariff Case, China Responds On February 20th, US Eastern Time, the US Supreme Court announced its ruling on a tariff lawsuit, determining that the retaliatory tariffs and fentanyl tariffs imposed by the US government on relevant trading partners under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) were illegal. On February 23rd, the spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce responded to a reporter's question, stating that China has noted the US Supreme Court's ruling on the tariff lawsuit and is conducting a comprehensive assessment of the relevant content and impact. China has consistently opposed unilateral tariff increases in all forms and has repeatedly emphasized that trade wars have no winners and protectionism has no way out. The unilateral measures imposed by the US, such as retaliatory tariffs and fentanyl tariffs, violate both international trade rules and US domestic law, and are not in the interest of any party. Facts have repeatedly proven that cooperation between China and the US benefits both sides, while confrontation harms both. China urges the US to revoke the relevant unilateral tariff measures imposed on its trading partners. We also note that the US is preparing to take alternative measures, such as trade investigations, in an attempt to maintain tariffs on its trading partners. China will continue to pay close attention to this and firmly safeguard China's interests. 03 US Customs: Will Stop Collecting Tariffs Tomorrow! Trump: Tariff Rate to Increase to 15% According to CCTV News on February 23rd, the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) announced that it will stop collecting tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) starting February 24th, US Eastern Time. On the 22nd, CBP stated through its cargo system message service that tariffs imposed under IEEPA will no longer be effective, and will not be collected for goods entering the consumer market or withdrawn from warehouses for consumption from February 24th, US Eastern Time. The announcement also stated that the suspension of these tariffs does not affect any other tariffs imposed by the Trump administration. On February 21st, local time, Trump posted on his social media platform "Truth Social" that he would increase the tariff rate on global goods from 10% to 15%. Trump stated, "Based on a comprehensive, detailed, and complete review of the US Supreme Court's ruling on tariffs on the 20th – a ruling that is absurd, poorly worded, and extremely anti-American – the current uniform tariff of 10% imposed on all countries will be increased to a fully permissible and legally tested level of 15%." Additionally, sales of AI-related products doubled year-on-year, with mobile phones, laptops, toys, and smart glasses being particularly popular among consumers. Among them, Jihua Group indirectly invested in Unitree Robotics and Galaxy General at the same time, and Zhongji Innolight indirectly invested in Unitree Robotics and Magic Atom. The report believes that the gradual implementation of the "triple balance" for electric vehicles and the global explosion of energy storage demand will drive continuous growth in lithium demand. In terms of performance, as the industry's supply and demand gradually improve, the profitability of companies in the lithium battery industry chain is comprehensively recovering. According to Wind data, among the 71 A-share lithium battery listed companies that have disclosed their performance forecasts or reports, 51 have achieved year-on-year net profit growth (including reduced losses), and 19 have turned losses into profits. For details, please refer to: "Significantly Raised! Lithium Batteries Receive Positive News!" 07 "Unprecedented in the World"! It is understood that Nvidia's GTC 2026 conference will be held from March 16th to 19th, local time, in San Jose, California, focusing on the new era of the AI infrastructure race. Huang stated, "We have prepared several world-first new chips. Nothing is easy, as all technologies have reached their limits." However, he did not disclose the specific model, but clearly hinted that this new hardware will push current physical limits to the extreme. Tech media NeoWin interpreted this as the mysterious chip being a mature product based on the Rubin architecture. In addition, data released by South Korean customs on the 23rd showed that exports in the first 20 days of February increased by 47.3% year-on-year, higher than the revised 34% increase for the entire month of January. Among them, chip exports surged by 134% year-on-year, continuing their strong momentum. This indicates that despite the ongoing trade uncertainties brought about by US tariff policies, chip demand remains robust. 08 Chinese Scientists Achieve New Progress in Optical Communication and 6G Chinese scientists have recently made breakthrough progress in the fields of optical communication and 6G, achieving the first cross-network integration between optical fiber communication and wireless communication systems internationally. The self-developed "Optical Fiber-Wireless Integrated Fusion Communication System" has set a new record for data transmission rates. This achievement was published online in Nature on the morning of the 19th. 09 IPO Registration and New Stock Subscriptions The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) has approved the IPO registration for one company. The CSRC has approved the GEM initial public offering registration for Wuxi Rich Intelligent Equipment Co., Ltd. This week (February 24th - February 27th), there are 2 new stocks to be issued: Tuesday: Haifeiman; Wednesday: Gude Electric Materials. 10 Over 70 Billion Yuan in Market Value of Restricted Shares to be Unlocked This Week Data shows that this week (February 24th - February 27th), a total of 44 companies will have their restricted shares unlocked sequentially, with a total of 3.524 billion shares to be unlocked. Based on the latest closing prices, the total market value of unlocked shares is 74.518 billion yuan. In terms of market value of unlocked shares, the top three are: Huaxi Nonferrous Metals (18.255 billion yuan), *ST Songfa (10.919 billion yuan), and Doli Technologies (8.997 billion yuan). In terms of the proportion of unlocked shares, the top three are: Doli Technologies (73.6%), Yangzhou Jinquan (73.45%), and Kuntai Shares (72.39%). Editor: Liu Junyu Proofreader: Liu Rongzhi

title_en: During the Spring Festival holiday, Hong Kong stocks first declined and then rose, with listed company performance disclosures dominating the first quarter trend | Market Observation
body_en: Global stock markets rebounded as some US tariffs were deemed "invalid," leading to a significant surge in Hong Kong stocks on February 23rd. The Hang Seng Index rose by 2.53% to close at 27,082 points, with a turnover of HK$172.9 billion. The Hang Seng Tech Index, which hit a new low in its adjustment on February 20th, rebounded sharply by 3.34% on the 23rd, closing at 5,385 points with a turnover of HK$46.8 billion. Industry insiders stated that the frequent policy changes regarding tariffs by US President Trump, along with geopolitical uncertainties in regions like Iran, will cause significant short-term volatility in Hong Kong stocks. Looking ahead, the gradual release of company earnings reports will increasingly drive the performance of Hong Kong stocks in the first quarter. It is anticipated that the resumption of share buybacks by tech companies after their earnings announcements will support the market. Yu Fenghui, an advisor at the Hong Kong Stock 100 Research Center, told Yicai Global that after the Lunar New Year holiday, the Hong Kong stock market exhibited considerable uncertainty. Today's rebound demonstrates the market's rapid recovery capability, a phenomenon that typically reflects investor sentiment fluctuations and high sensitivity to external information. Global stock markets have recently reacted strongly to interest rate changes, economic growth expectations, and specific industry news (such as AI-related developments). Short-term market movements are more driven by technical and capital factors rather than substantive changes in fundamentals. Looking forward, the upcoming wave of company earnings disclosures will provide a more solid fundamental basis for the market. Investors should closely monitor company earnings announcements and their future outlooks to accurately grasp market trends. Given the complex and evolving global economic landscape, investors should also maintain a cautious approach, allocate assets prudently, and avoid over-concentration in any single sector. Wong Chi-wing, CEO of Broad Capital International, stated that the US Supreme Court's ruling deeming tariffs imposed by President Trump under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act as illegal and invalid was a significant trigger for the rebound in Hong Kong stocks, seen as a signal of easing trade friction. Coupled with capital inflows and the continuation of themes like AI and robotics, market sentiment has rapidly repaired. However, uncertainties remain regarding Trump's new tariff policies and potential tax refund lawsuits. Looking ahead, the earnings disclosure period for listed companies (from late February to April) is crucial. If the earnings of technology, consumer, and resource sectors exceed expectations, earnings-driven growth will dominate the market. Conversely, if the earnings of heavyweight stocks fall short of expectations, it could trigger a market pullback. Regarding the upcoming earnings disclosure period for tech stocks, Li Zemin, Chief Investment Officer at Blue Water Capital Management Limited, expects it to be a mixed bag. Major tech companies, particularly leading firms like Tencent and Alibaba, are about to release their earnings. While overall performance is expected to be positive for the fourth quarter of 2025, and despite short-term concerns about their capital expenditures and cash flows, the earnings announcements are expected to alleviate these worries. Due to the quiet period before earnings, these companies have been unable to conduct share buybacks recently, and the resumption of buybacks after earnings will provide support for their stock prices.

title_en: Hong Kong stock market commodity prices surge, what reference does this have for A-share trends after the holiday?
body_en: Hong Kong stocks welcomed a "good start" on the second trading day of the Lunar Year of the Horse. On February 23rd, both the Hang Seng Index and the Hang Seng Tech Index saw significant gains, with market sentiment showing a notable recovery. On the market, sector differentiation was evident: tech stocks and semiconductor concepts generally rose, while commodity sectors performed particularly strongly, with gold and oil stocks collectively advancing and leading the market. Meanwhile, previously popular AI and robotics sectors experienced a pullback. Industry analysis suggests that the surge in Hong Kong's commodity sectors is not an isolated phenomenon. It is strongly supported by the sustained rise in international gold and oil prices, and is also closely related to the increased demand for safe-haven assets driven by the escalation of tensions between the US and Iran during the Spring Festival. Hong Kong Commodity Market Surges On February 23rd, the Hong Kong stock market performed robustly, marking a "good start" for the Year of the Horse. By the close of trading, the Hang Seng Index rose by 2.53%, and the Hang Seng Tech Index surged by 3.34%, indicating a clear recovery in market sentiment. Sector performance showed significant differentiation. Hong Kong tech stocks generally rose. By the close of trading, Meituan-W (83690.HK) was up 5.26%, Alibaba (09988.HK) was up 3.47%, and Tencent (00700.HK) was up 3.07%. Semiconductor concept stocks strengthened, with Hua Hong Semiconductor (01347.HK) rising by 4.51%. The commodity sector performed particularly brilliantly.
