title_en: Precise regulation maintains a fair and competitive market order.
body_en: The review of operator concentration is an important part of strengthening antitrust enforcement and maintaining a fair competition order. Data shows that in 2025, the State Administration for Market Regulation concluded 706 cases of operator concentration, a year-on-year increase of 9.8%, demonstrating the full market competition in China and the trend of economic development towards new and better quality. The world-leading review efficiency also makes the implementation of high-quality investment and M&A projects more efficient. Xu Lefu, Director of the Second Anti-Monopoly Bureau of the State Administration for Market Regulation, introduced that in order to allow good investment and M&A projects to be completed sooner with less waiting, market regulatory departments strictly implement the one-notification-within-five-days system, with an average case acceptance time of 17.9 days and an average review time of 26.8 days. Transactions involving private enterprises, state-owned enterprises, and foreign enterprises were unconditionally approved in 244, 379, and 297 cases respectively, supporting the healthy development of enterprises of all ownership types and serving the overall economic development. The "Guidelines for the Review of Non-Horizontal Operator Concentration" and other systems were issued, and the pilot delegation of review to local authorities was converted to formal delegation. The operator concentration antitrust business system was effectively operated, and a historical case query function was launched to provide more convenience and transparency for enterprises. Fair competition in the people's livelihood sector has always been the top priority of regulation. Public utilities are closely related to people's lives. While many places are promoting the integration of public utilities and improving service quality, some monopoly risks are also hidden. In January 2026, the State Administration for Market Regulation prohibited the establishment of a joint venture between Foshan Bluebird Gas and Foshan Nanguan Gas, which was the first prohibition of operator concentration in the public utility sector, drawing a clear regulatory "red line" for M&A in the people's livelihood sector. Strengthening enforcement deterrence is an important means of maintaining market order. Since 2025, the State Administration for Market Regulation has investigated 13 cases of illegal implementation of operator concentration, publicly imposed administrative penalties on 5 cases, with a total fine of 8.7 million yuan. From the perspective of enterprise entities and industry types, 6 cases involved state-owned enterprises, 4 involved private enterprises, and 3 involved foreign-invested enterprises, covering sectors such as retail, engineering and construction, semiconductors, human resource services, and power cables. From the perspective of discretionary circumstances, the 5 cases with public penalties did not have the effect of excluding or restricting competition, and were fined less than 5 million yuan. One case was given a lighter penalty due to "voluntary surrender," and 5 cases had their fines reduced due to "first-time violation," "active cooperation with the investigation," and "establishment of an antitrust compliance system." Hu Pinjie, Deputy Director of the Second Anti-Monopoly Bureau of the State Administration for Market Regulation, introduced that the illegal situations mainly involve four types of behavior: first, operators that meet the reporting standards but implement concentration without prior declaration according to law; second, operators that implement concentration during the review stage without approval after declaration; third, operators that violate the review decision with additional restrictive conditions; and fourth, concentrations that do not meet the reporting standards but there is evidence that they have or may have the effect of excluding or restricting competition, and the State Administration for Market Regulation has legally required declaration, but the operators implement concentration without declaration according to law. "Punishment is not the goal. We hope to use law enforcement to urge enterprises to operate in accordance with the law and regulations, earnestly fulfill their declaration obligations and conditional commitments, and maintain a fair market competition order." Hu Pinjie reminded all operators to pay attention to 3 compliance requirements. First, report everything that should be reported. Concentrations that meet the reporting standards must fulfill the prior declaration obligation; those that do not meet the reporting standards but are required to declare must also declare according to law; concentrations that are not declared or implemented without approval after declaration are prohibited. Second, strictly abide by commitments. For concentrations that have or may have the effect of excluding or restricting competition, if they are not prohibited, the enforcement agency will approve them with additional restrictive conditions based on the commitments submitted by the operators; violations of conditional review decisions and commitments will be investigated for legal responsibility. Finally, it is also important to do a good job of overseas compliance. Antitrust is a universally accepted international rule. "Going out" enterprises must strictly abide by local antitrust laws and regulations when participating in international competition in overseas markets.

title_en: Two highlights of the construction of China's antitrust legal system in 2025
body_en: Since the amendment of China's Anti-Monopoly Law in 2022, the State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) has continuously improved and strengthened the systematic construction of the anti-monopoly legal system. It has not only formulated a series of supporting normative legal documents but also successively issued guidelines and directives aimed at guiding business operators in building anti-monopoly compliance. This has concretized abstract legal provisions, enabling business operators in the market to have laws to follow and to abide by them. In the just-passed year of 2025, the SAMR revised and issued several important supporting normative legal documents and compliance guidelines, covering aspects such as monopolistic agreements, concentrations of undertakings, the fair competition review system, and the abuse of administrative power by administrative organs to exclude or restrict competition. Two aspects of institutional development are particularly noteworthy: First, the revised and reissued "Provisions on Prohibiting Monopolistic Agreements" clarifies the standards for the implementation of the "safe harbor" system for vertical monopolistic agreements for the first time. Second, the "Guidelines on Non-Horizontal Concentrations of Undertakings" provides a detailed explanation and interpretation of the concept, types, review standards, and analytical framework for non-horizontal concentrations of undertakings for the first time. Highlight 1: Implementation of the "Safe Harbor" System for Vertical Monopolistic Agreements. This pro-competitive effect is particularly evident in industries with complex industrial products (such as automobiles) and luxury goods. On the other hand, in practice, business operators, especially small and medium-sized ones, have their own experiences with RPM agreements. They believe that RPM agreements not only enable them to quickly promote products with the help of numerous distributors but also ensure that the market recognition and competitiveness of their products are not severely damaged by the unbridled price competition among distributors. Therefore, there has been widespread questioning among market operators regarding the general prohibition of RPM agreements. In particular, the analytical methods used by the SAMR and the People's Courts in anti-monopoly cases involving RPM agreements have sometimes conflicted. In view of this, the Anti-Monopoly Law revised in 2022 added a clause containing the "safe harbor" system, namely Article 18, Paragraph 3, which clearly stipulates: "Where an undertaking can prove that its market share in the relevant market is below the standard set by the anti-monopoly enforcement agency of the State Council and meets other conditions stipulated by the anti-monopoly enforcement agency of the State Council, the concentration shall not be prohibited." However, for several years, due to ongoing disputes, the SAMR, as the administrative enforcement agency of the Anti-Monopoly Law, has not set clear standards for the "safe harbor" system, leaving this provision at an abstract legal level and lacking operability. The provisions divide vertical monopolistic agreements into two categories: RPM agreements and other non-RPM vertical monopolistic agreements, each with different applicable standards. Specifically, for RPM agreements, the provisions set relatively strict "safe harbor" standards, requiring undertakings implementing RPM agreements to ensure that during the term of the agreement, the market share of all undertakings (undertakings and their trading counterparts) in their respective relevant markets is below 5% annually. If there are multiple trading counterparts, their market shares in the same relevant market need to be aggregated. The annual turnover of the goods involved in the RPM agreement reached between the undertaking and its trading counterpart must be below 100 million yuan. Similar to the first condition, if any party involves multiple persons, their turnover also needs to be aggregated. On the other hand, compared to the stricter safe harbor standards for RPM agreements, the safe harbor standards for other non-RPM vertical monopolistic agreements are much more lenient, only stipulating that if an undertaking claims to apply the "safe harbor" system, it should prove that the market share of the undertaking and its trading counterpart in the relevant market during the agreement period is below 15% annually. In addition to these different "safe harbor" standards for two types of vertical monopolistic agreements, the provisions also reserve space for different standards applicable to special industries, special fields, or specific types of agreements. The provisions clarify that if the SAMR has other regulations on the safe harbor standards for vertical monopolistic agreements in specific industries, specific fields, or specific types, those regulations shall apply. Currently, the "Provisions on Prohibiting Abuse of Intellectual Property Rights to Exclude or Restrict Competition" issued by the SAMR previously contains special provisions on market share. In the future, the SAMR does not rule out the possibility of setting different "safe harbor" standards for vertical monopolistic agreements in specific industries, specific fields, or specific types based on specific circumstances. Second, if the market share of an undertaking in the relevant market is between 35% and 50%, it is inclined to believe that the concentration has or may have the effect of excluding or restricting competition. Third, if the market share of an undertaking in the relevant market is between 25% and 35%, it is generally considered that the possibility of the concentration having the effect of excluding or restricting competition is low, but based on the market competition conditions of individual cases, it is necessary to analyze whether the concentration has the effect of excluding or restricting competition. Fourth, if the market share of an undertaking in the relevant market is below 25%, it is generally presumed that the concentration does not have the effect of excluding or restricting competition. Of course, the above standards are only for preliminary judgment. In specific cases, the Guidelines also clearly point out that enforcement agencies need to consider other influencing factors. Second, the issuance of the "Guidelines on Review of Non-Horizontal Concentrations of Undertakings" also has significant implications for business operator compliance. Traditionally, enforcement agencies have focused on horizontal concentrations in the field of anti-monopoly review of concentrations of undertakings. Therefore, business operators have often been cautious about anti-monopoly review when engaging in horizontal mergers and acquisitions, but have not paid enough attention to compliance issues related to non-horizontal concentrations of undertakings. These can provide predictable and reliable compliance guidance for business operators engaged in mergers and acquisitions, establishing joint ventures, etc., in the future. In addition to the "safe harbor" system for vertical monopolistic agreements and the concretization of the anti-monopoly review analytical framework for non-horizontal concentrations of undertakings, which have been重点 discussed, in 2025, the SAMR also revised and issued the "Provisions on Prohibiting Abuse of Administrative Power to Exclude or Restrict Competition," "Regulations on Reporting Concentrations of Undertakings," "Implementation Measures for the Regulations on Fair Competition Review," and "Basis for Discretionary Administrative Penalties for Illegal Concentrations of Undertakings (Trial)" and other legal normative documents. In terms of anti-monopoly regulation in key industries, in addition to officially releasing the "Anti-Monopoly Guidelines for the Pharmaceutical Field," the SAMR also issued the "Guidelines for Anti-Monopoly Compliance in the Internet Platform Field (Draft for Comment)" and the "Anti-Monopoly Guidelines for the Public Utilities Sector (Draft for Comment)" for the internet platform and public utilities sectors, respectively. The issuance and implementation of numerous normative documents, guidelines, and directives have further improved China's anti-monopoly legal system. title_en: From "Telling Stories" to "Submitting Homework": Under the AI Frenzy, Who is Swimming Naked and Who is Building Walls?
body_en: The market's volatility is intensifying, driven by alternating waves of AI enthusiasm and fear. The US stock market rebounded on February 24th, led by technology stocks, as renewed optimism about artificial intelligence overshadowed concerns about the disruptive potential of this emerging technology, leading to a significant rally in software stocks. However, SanDisk, a recently popular storage stock, faced a short-seller attack, with its stock price falling by more than 8% at one point on the 24th. Citron Research, a well-known short-selling firm, announced it holds a short position in the storage chip manufacturer, citing three reasons for its bearish outlook: cyclical pressures in the storage market, increased competition from Samsung, and the departure of its long-term investors. The AI craze is gradually returning to rationality. As of the close on February 24th, the Nasdaq index was down 1.63% year-to-date, a stark contrast to the consecutive annual gains of over 20% in the past three years. The harsh reality of the capital markets is that they are no longer willing to pay for "storytelling" visions and are instead charging for the reality of "delivering results." The winners of the future will not necessarily be today's highest-valued giants, but rather those companies that can rebuild their moats amidst technological shifts and transform AI into sustainable revenue. With software stocks rebounding and storage stocks plummeting, the recent US stock market's attitude towards AI has been oscillating between concern and anticipation. Li Huihui, a professor of management practice at emlyon business school, is more inclined to interpret this "swing" as the market repricing two curves: one is the new demand curve brought about by AI, and the other is the substitution curve of AI for old business models. The significant drop in software stocks in February, with the sector losing approximately $1 trillion in market value in a single week, was largely due to premature concerns about "AI substitution," which pushed valuations to extremes rather than a sudden deterioration of fundamentals. The market worried that AI intelligences would directly disrupt the livelihoods of many SaaS companies. However, Li Huihui believes this panic is premature. In the B2B enterprise market, the core barriers for software lie in deep workflow integration and data compliance. AI currently acts as a super plugin and enabler, far from completely overturning and replacing existing solutions. The recent rebound reflects smart money realizing they had overreacted. The core trigger for Citron's short attack was the significant discounted sale by a major shareholder and the disruption of the traditional supply-demand balance for NAND flash memory chips. However, the market may be confusing a core issue: SanDisk primarily focuses on NAND for consumer electronics and traditional data centers, while the real bottleneck for current AI large model computing power is HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) and advanced DRAM. Leading global storage manufacturers are now aggressively shifting production capacity towards HBM, which represents the true core assets for AI. How to view the current market sentiment? Li Huihui's assessment is that the AI sector has fully entered a "dual high" phase: "high valuation and high growth" coexist. In this extremely tense environment, any minor micro-level disturbance, even a slightly disappointing monthly data point, will be infinitely amplified by macro sentiment, leading to sharp, wide-ranging fluctuations. However, from a broader perspective, he remains steadfastly optimistic. As long as the Moore's Law for computing hardware continues to advance and the parameter scale and emergent capabilities of large models continue to break through, the bull market logic driven by underlying technological innovation remains intact. The short-term back-and-forth is merely capital repricing different assets. For years, the US stock market indices have been dominated by "asset-light, recurring revenue technology business models" that enjoy near-zero marginal costs and growing profit margins. However, under the AI wave, these once-favored asset-light tech giants are transforming into "capital-intensive, cash-flow-hungry enterprises." Li Huihui told reporters that if the market continues to focus solely on the alarming capital expenditures (Capex) in tech giants' financial reports, it is underestimating the dimensions of this game. His core argument is that this is not simply a shift to "asset-heavy" but rather tech giants are passively evolving into "intelligent utilities." In the past, companies like Apple and Google enjoyed P/E ratios of forty to fifty times due to their asset-light, zero-marginal-cost expansion. But now, computing power has become a fundamental infrastructure for society. When giants invest hundreds of billions of dollars to become a "computing power grid" and "intelligence water plant" for all humanity, their business model irreversibly transforms into a utility. In traditional capital markets, the reasonable P/E ratios for utility companies are generally in the range of 15 to 20 times. Therefore, Li Huihui believes that tech giants will continue to be strong, but the era of "rising and falling together" is over. The market will not see a smooth upward curve but rather a slower slope, greater volatility, and more pronounced differentiation. Giants that can transform computing power into "quantifiable, sustainable inference revenue/subscription revenue" will continue to outperform the index. However, companies that are merely piling up GPUs, experiencing delivery delays, and failing to achieve high utilization rates will be priced by the market as "asset-heavy cyclical stocks," with their stock prices being suppressed when interest rates rise and Capex is revised upwards. The investment in Capex is to protect the tech giants' existing search empires and advertising moats from being directly replaced by native large models like OpenAI or Anthropic. The "return" on this colossal investment is not reflected in incremental profits but in "the core business not being disrupted." Preserving the core business is the greatest ROI for this capital. In the medium to long term, Capex ROI will become the main determinant of market capitalization. Li Huihui suggests focusing on three key metrics: the speed of increase in depreciation/revenue, the point at which free cash flow turns positive, and the monetization efficiency per unit of computing power (whether the growth rate of inference revenue can outpace the growth rate of computing power supply). If two out of these three metrics are achieved, the market will provide tech giants with a higher safety net; conversely, in a "dual high" environment, any setbacks will be amplified into significant drawdowns. Amidst high US asset prices, Wall Street warnings are incessant. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has expressed concerns about the US economy, noting that high asset prices and intense competition in the banking sector remind him of the pre-2008 crisis era. After years of rapid ascent, what are the potential risks facing US stocks? Li Huihui believes the current market faces potential risks in the following three areas. Firstly, the current problem with US stocks is tight pricing. The S&P 500's forward valuation is around 22 times, making it highly sensitive to marginal changes in interest rates, earnings, or policy. There are also structural hidden dangers in the US stock market: the top 10 companies in the S&P 500 now account for over 40% of the index's weight. If the earnings expectations of just one or two of these leaders are revised downwards, the index's pullback will be amplified. The market is currently treating "good news as the norm" at this level. Secondly, from a credit perspective, the overall delinquency rate for US households rose to 4.8% at the end of last year, with pressure from credit cards and student loans persisting. Although bank lending standards have not tightened across the board, they have become more cautious regarding real estate development loans. Finally, Wall Street private equity giants are aggressively lending to businesses, particularly those leveraged by buyouts, traditional software companies, B2B service providers, and mid-sized enterprises. These loans are highly opaque, and many are high-interest floating-rate loans. The market is currently fixated on how much incremental wealth AI can generate, while severely underestimating AI's destructive power as a deflationary force. If large models and AI agents disrupt the livelihoods of many traditional SaaS companies, IT outsourcing firms, and process service providers within the next one to two years, these traditional companies burdened with massive private debt will see their recurring revenue collapse instantly, and their cash flow will immediately break down. When widespread corporate defaults occur, it will directly drag down major Wall Street banks. Luca Paolini, Chief Strategist at Pictet Asset Management, told 21st Century Business Herald reporters that before October last year, almost all AI-related tech stocks were rising, albeit at different paces, but in the same direction. For a period, AI trading drove everything, and investors would buy any company related to AI, regardless of what they did. The market is now becoming more discerning. Paolini analyzes that chip manufacturers are booming, AI stocks related to Google are performing well, while stocks related to OpenAI are struggling slightly. The market now seems to be trying to pick winners and losers. This means that a basket of AI stocks will not perform as well as before, and we will see fewer gains. Investors' focus is shifting from "how much growth" to "how to achieve growth." For example, companies like Oracle, which have issued a large amount of debt, have been "punished" by the market. Competition continues. Paolini believes that the most important thing in the future will not only be to create the best language models but also to be able to integrate various aspects of AI into businesses, which can affect almost any industry – pharmaceuticals, law, education, with immense potential. Therefore, the focus will be more on applications rather than just the language models that support AI. Can US stocks continue to rise in the future? Li Huihui believes that the US stock market index still has upward momentum, but it will exhibit a "K-shaped melt-up." The current pricing system of US stocks has been severely distorted by passive funds (ETFs). As long as US pension funds continue to invest in broad market indices, these indiscriminate purchases will mechanically flow into the few largest tech giants by weight. This will cause the index to continue to rise due to liquidity inertia, creating a false impression of prosperity. However, beneath the surface of the index repeatedly hitting new highs, the stock prices of small and medium-sized enterprises and traditional companies lacking technological moats and being "dimensionally reduced" by AI have actually entered a brutal bear market. Meanwhile, the balance sheets of "systemically important" giants with absolute pricing power and hundreds of billions in cash are thick enough to withstand external shocks. title_en: Food Safety Special Press Conference Transcript
body_en: On the afternoon of February 26, the State Administration for Market Regulation held a special press conference on food safety. The following is the transcript of the press conference: Wang Qiuping, Spokesperson for the State Administration for Market Regulation and Director of the Department of Publicity and Information: Ladies and gentlemen, media friends, good afternoon! The festive atmosphere of the New Year is still strong and warm. First, I would like to extend my New Year greetings to all of you! When families reunite, safety is paramount. Today, we are holding our first special press conference on food safety after the Spring Festival. I am very happy to meet with you all again for a commitment to safeguarding the safety of our "cloud" dining tables. Food safety is the cornerstone of people's well-being and the watchword for every household. Currently, live-streaming e-commerce is booming, and online consumption is vibrant. The rapid development of new business models, while convenient for people's lives, also poses higher requirements and stricter challenges for food safety. As consumption moves to the "cloud," kitchens connect to "fingertips," and delicious food travels through screens to reach dining tables, safeguarding must stay ahead of risks; safety must be the most solid foundation. To reinforce the responsibilities of online business entities, the State Administration for Market Regulation has recently formulated two "Regulations" targeting online catering and food sales. They are the "Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Online Catering Service Providers Implementing Food Safety Primary Responsibility" and the "Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Online Food Sales Operators Implementing Food Safety Primary Responsibility." These two "Regulations" aim to weave a tighter web of responsibility, ensuring that "traffic" and "quality" go hand in hand. Safety on the tip of the tongue, responsibility in the palm of your hand. To help you understand the content of the two "Regulations," we have invited Mr. Sun Huichuan, Food Safety Supervisor of the State Administration for Market Regulation, Mr. Si Guang, Director of the Department of Food Production and Operation, Mr. Yu Lu, Director of the Department of Catering Food, Mr. Liu Songtao, Director of the Department of Special Food, and Ms. Wang Dan, Deputy Director of the Department of Regulations. These officials will provide in-depth interpretations and answer your questions. We look forward to your active participation. First, I would like to invite Mr. Sun Huichuan to introduce the main content and background of the two "Regulations." Sun Huichuan, Food Safety Supervisor of the State Administration for Market Regulation: Dear media friends, good afternoon! First, I will briefly introduce the relevant situation of the "Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Online Catering Service Providers Implementing Food Safety Primary Responsibility." In recent years, the online catering industry has developed rapidly, and "ordering takeout" has become one of the daily dining consumption methods for the public, especially young people. According to data from China's Catering Industry Annual Report, the scale of China's takeout market is expected to exceed 1.4 trillion yuan, with a year-on-year growth rate of over 10%, accounting for about 24% of the total revenue of the catering industry, becoming an important growth pole for the industry. As netizens say, ordering takeout is very simple now, but getting "reassuring takeout" or "quality takeout" is not always easy. Through daily supervision, we have found that some takeout merchants provide fake addresses, upload fake photos, and even have fake qualifications. How can such takeout be reassuring?! At the same time, some takeout platforms are solely focused on expanding their market share, blindly approving merchants, and indiscriminately tolerating dishonest merchants and problematic takeout, disregarding their platform responsibilities and food safety. In response to these situations, to further improve the food safety level of catering takeout, the State Administration for Market Regulation has formulated and issued the "Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Online Catering Service Providers Implementing Food Safety Primary Responsibility," focusing on three aspects to enhance the "reassurance index" of takeout. First, it tightly grips the "key" of the platform's primary responsibility. The "Regulations" detail the platform's management responsibilities for merchant qualification review, information disclosure, process control, and problem handling throughout the entire chain, requiring takeout platforms to be responsible upon registration, managed upon going online, and fulfill their responsibilities during operation. Food safety responsibilities must be embedded in every link, every process, and every decision of platform operations. We want to warn takeout platforms that they cannot just collect commissions and shirk responsibility; they cannot just focus on traffic and ignore quality. Takeout platforms must truly assume the primary responsibility of being the "gatekeeper" of takeout food safety. Second, it focuses on the "key point" of standardized operation by merchants. The "Regulations" clarify that merchants must have a real physical operating store, and their business scope, address, and qualification certificates must be consistent; merchants must strictly implement requirements for raw material control, facility maintenance, and operating procedures, and are not allowed to process food outside the operating area or entrust others to process it; merchants that do not provide dine-in services must be marked with a special label. We want to warn all takeout merchants that "no face-to-face" does not mean "dishonest," and "no door-to-door" does not mean "no one is watching." Food safety is the bottom line for merchants, and legal compliance is their responsibility. Third, it builds a "protective net" for punishing illegal and irregular acts. Takeout platforms are essentially e-commerce platforms. The "Regulations" are linked with the "E-commerce Law," incorporating takeout platforms into the unified regulatory framework for e-commerce platform operators, further strengthening the platform's legal responsibilities in information reporting, data sharing, and consumer rights protection. At the same time, the penalties for illegal and irregular acts by platforms and merchants have been significantly increased, with fines up to 200,000 yuan. If the main responsible person of a platform intentionally violates the law, with serious nature and severe consequences, they may also be fined between one and ten times their income from the previous year. Next, I will briefly introduce the relevant situation of the "Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Online Food Sales Operators Implementing Food Safety Primary Responsibility." Currently, with the vigorous development of the platform economy, food has become one of the main commodities in online "shopping carts," from daily necessities like rice, oil, salt, soy sauce, vinegar, and tea to beverages and fresh meat products. However, at the same time, problems such as counterfeit and shoddy products and false marketing have occurred frequently and have not been eradicated, seriously affecting people's sense of food safety and consumer confidence, and also hindering the high-quality development of the food industry. From a regulatory perspective, current laws and regulations have relatively few specific provisions on the safety of online food sales, especially the specific responsibilities of platform enterprises in food safety management. The relevant requirements are not well-suited to the actual situation of online sales, leading to prominent issues where enterprises have no rules to follow and regulators have no basis for enforcement. In this regard, the State Administration for Market Regulation is committed to "addressing shortcomings" and has specifically formulated the "Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Online Food Sales Operators Implementing Food Safety Primary Responsibility." It focuses on three aspects: platform providers, online food sellers, and regulatory departments, revolving around the three keywords of "responsibility," "collaboration," and "enforcement" to further tighten and implement food safety primary responsibility. First, clarify the "responsibilities" of the three parties. Platform providers bear overall responsibility for food sales activities within the platform, including establishing a dedicated food safety management agency; equipping management personnel such as food safety supervisors and food safety officers; establishing a full-process management system for online review, risk control, and handling of illegal acts, etc. Online food sellers shall bear the primary responsibility for food safety, including obtaining production and operation licenses or filing in accordance with the law before going online, ensuring the safety of the food sold, standardizing information disclosure, business promotion, storage, and distribution, and establishing a risk prevention and control mechanism of daily monitoring, weekly investigation, and monthly scheduling in accordance with the law. At the same time, regulatory departments shall earnestly fulfill their regulatory responsibilities, with the three parties performing their respective duties and bearing their respective responsibilities, forming a pattern of mutual supervision and collaborative governance. Second, promote two "collaborations." First is the enforcement collaboration mechanism, which requires market regulatory departments across the country to strengthen cross-regional clue notification, evidence collection, and problem handling in regulatory enforcement, achieving a unified national regulatory effort. Second is the integrated collaboration mechanism, which requires platform providers, based on risk monitoring and identification, to promptly push risk warnings and requirements for risk prevention to online food sellers; online food sellers who discover risks in food recommended by the platform shall promptly inform the platform provider; platform providers and online sellers who discover illegal acts in online food sales or potential risks of food safety accidents shall report them to market regulatory departments in accordance with regulations. Third, strengthen integrated "enforcement." It clarifies that if illegal acts occur in areas outside the domicile of the platform provider, the provincial market regulatory department where the illegal act occurred may exercise jurisdiction, focusing on resolving the conflict between the spillover nature of the platform and the limitations of local regulation. In addition, the "Regulations" also strengthen severe punishment, focusing on increasing penalties for illegal and irregular acts by platform providers. Corresponding legal liabilities are added for platform failures to equip food safety management personnel, conduct food safety risk control as required, or handle food safety risks as required. For platform failures to establish selection rules as required, inspect recommended food, or recommend food prohibited by laws and regulations, severe punishment will be imposed in accordance with the law. Food safety has no "zero risk," and regulatory work is always "on the go." The State Administration for Market Regulation will always adhere to the people-centered development philosophy, thoroughly implement the "four strictest" requirements for food safety, and take the implementation of the above two regulations as an opportunity to further consolidate the responsibilities of all parties, innovate regulatory means, and build consensus for joint governance, continuously improve the governance level of online catering and online food sales safety, and make new and greater contributions to safeguarding the health and safety of the people and promoting the high-quality development of the catering and food industries. Wang Qiuping, Spokesperson for the State Administration for Market Regulation and Director of the Department of Publicity and Information: Thank you, Director Sun. We will now proceed to the Q&A session. Before asking questions, please announce your media organization. Reporter from the News Center of China Media Group: Regarding the prominent issues of information opacity and asymmetry in online catering takeout, what specific measures are included in the "Regulations" to ensure consumers can order with confidence and eat with peace of mind? Sun Huichuan, Food Safety Supervisor of the State Administration for Market Regulation: Reassuring takeout hinges on "what you order is what you get." Whether it's merchant operating information or information about dishes, it must be true and reliable for consumers to feel at ease. To this end, the "Regulations" have made a series of system designs from three core dimensions: operating identity, operating model, and processing. By clarifying the information disclosure obligations of platform providers and online catering service providers, a full-chain, visual information disclosure system is established, allowing consumers to "order with understanding and eat with peace of mind." First, standardize information disclosure, so that "store information" is no longer difficult to distinguish. The "Regulations" clearly stipulate that the name of the takeout online store must be consistent with the name on the physical store's signboard; core information such as business qualifications, photos of the physical store, and actual operating address must be continuously displayed in a prominent position on the main page, or a clear link to the information must be provided. To address the problem of "fake addresses," it is clarified that the actual operating address must be consistent with the operating premises indicated on the business qualification certificate. Second, add a special label, so that "no dine-in" is no longer hidden. The "Regulations" stipulate that takeout merchants specializing in takeout services and not providing dine-in must display a "no dine-in" label in a prominent position on their main page, and takeout platforms must also display this label on the merchant list page. This way, consumers can clearly know whether the merchant's operating model includes dine-in before placing an order, and make a rational choice based on their needs and safety expectations for catering services. Third, promote visual disclosure, so that "processing" is no longer a mystery. The "Regulations" establish a "Internet + Transparent Kitchen" disclosure system, advocating for takeout merchants to publicly disclose their meal processing procedures through methods such as "Internet + Transparent Kitchen." Takeout platforms are required to display relevant labels on the list page of online catering service providers, making it clear to consumers at a glance. Fourth, strengthen the platform's technical support, so that "information disclosure" is no longer optional. The "Regulations" require takeout platforms to provide necessary technical support for takeout merchants to fulfill their information disclosure obligations, ensuring that relevant information can be displayed clearly, stably, and conveniently to consumers, and that technical barriers or intentional concealment of information are not allowed; timely disposal of takeout merchants who fail to disclose information as required, or who disclose false or inaccurate information. We believe that by establishing a comprehensive and visual information disclosure system for catering takeout, consumers will be more "informed" and make more "informed" choices when ordering takeout. Xinhua News Agency Reporter: "Ghost takeout" has always been a pain point for food safety in online catering services. What specific measures does the "Regulations" take to address this issue? Yu Lu, Director of the Department of Catering Food of the State Administration for Market Regulation: "Ghost takeout" is a popular online term, which essentially refers to illegal operators without qualifications or fixed premises who operate as legitimate merchants on takeout platforms through means such as faking qualifications, using permits, or fabricating addresses. Their existence seriously disrupts the normal market order of the takeout industry and damages people's confidence in catering food safety. Therefore, to address "ghost takeout," we must get to the root of the problem and build a systematic governance system. First, "substantive review" to rectify the source. The following is the transcript of the press conference: Wang Qiuping, Spokesperson for the State Administration for Market Regulation and Director of the Department of Publicity and Information: Ladies and gentlemen, media friends, good afternoon! The festive atmosphere of the New Year is still strong and warm. First, I would like to extend my New Year greetings to all of you! When families reunite, safety is paramount. Today, we are holding our first special press conference on food safety after the Spring Festival. I am very happy to meet with you all again for a commitment to safeguarding the safety of our "cloud" dining tables. Food safety is the cornerstone of people's well-being and the watchword for every household. Currently, live-streaming e-commerce is booming, and online consumption is vibrant. The rapid development of new business models, while convenient for people's lives, also poses higher requirements and stricter challenges for food safety. As consumption moves to the "cloud," kitchens connect to "fingertips," and delicious food travels through screens to reach dining tables, safeguarding must stay ahead of risks; safety must be the most solid foundation. To reinforce the responsibilities of online business entities, the State Administration for Market Regulation has recently formulated two "Regulations" targeting online catering and food sales. They are the "Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Online Catering Service Providers Implementing Food Safety Primary Responsibility" and the "Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Online Food Sales Operators Implementing Food Safety Primary Responsibility." These two "Regulations" aim to weave a tighter web of responsibility, ensuring that "traffic" and "quality" go hand in hand. Safety on the tip of the tongue, responsibility in the palm of your hand. To help you understand the content of the two "Regulations," we have invited Mr. Sun Huichuan, Food Safety Supervisor of the State Administration for Market Regulation, Mr. Si Guang, Director of the Department of Food Production and Operation, Mr. Yu Lu, Director of the Department of Catering Food, Mr. Liu Songtao, Director of the Department of Special Food, and Ms. Wang Dan, Deputy Director of the Department of Regulations. These officials will provide in-depth interpretations and answer your questions. We look forward to your active participation. First, I would like to invite Mr. Sun Huichuan to introduce the main content and background of the two "Regulations." Sun Huichuan, Food Safety Supervisor of the State Administration for Market Regulation: Dear media friends, good afternoon! First, I will briefly introduce the relevant situation of the "Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Online Catering Service Providers Implementing Food Safety Primary Responsibility." In recent years, the online catering industry has developed rapidly, and "ordering takeout" has become one of the daily dining consumption methods for the public, especially young people. According to data from China's Catering Industry Annual Report, the scale of China's takeout market is expected to exceed 1.4 trillion yuan, with a year-on-year growth rate of over 10%, accounting for about 24% of the total revenue of the catering industry, becoming an important growth pole for the industry. As netizens say, ordering takeout is very simple now, but getting "reassuring takeout" or "quality takeout" is not always easy. Through daily supervision, we have found that some takeout merchants provide fake addresses, upload fake photos, and even have fake qualifications. How can such takeout be reassuring?! At the same time, some takeout platforms are solely focused on expanding their market share, blindly approving merchants, and indiscriminately tolerating dishonest merchants and problematic takeout, disregarding their platform responsibilities and food safety. In response to these situations, to further improve the food safety level of catering takeout, the State Administration for Market Regulation has formulated and issued the "Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Online Catering Service Providers Implementing Food Safety Primary Responsibility," focusing on three aspects to enhance the "reassurance index" of takeout. First, it tightly grips the "key" of the platform's primary responsibility. The "Regulations" detail the platform's management responsibilities for merchant qualification review, information disclosure, process control, and problem handling throughout the entire chain, requiring takeout platforms to be responsible upon registration, managed upon going online, and fulfill their responsibilities during operation. Food safety responsibilities must be embedded in every link, every process, and every decision of platform operations. We want to warn takeout platforms that they cannot just collect commissions and shirk responsibility; they cannot just focus on traffic and ignore quality. Takeout platforms must truly assume the primary responsibility of being the "gatekeeper" of takeout food safety. Second, it focuses on the "key point" of standardized operation by merchants. The "Regulations" clarify that merchants must have a real physical operating store, and their business scope, address, and qualification certificates must be consistent; merchants must strictly implement requirements for raw material control, facility maintenance, and operating procedures, and are not allowed to process food outside the operating area or entrust others to process it; merchants that do not provide dine-in services must be marked with a special label. We want to warn all takeout merchants that "no face-to-face" does not mean "dishonest," and "no door-to-door" does not mean "no one is watching." Food safety is the bottom line for merchants, and legal compliance is their responsibility. Third, it builds a "protective net" for punishing illegal and irregular acts. Takeout platforms are essentially e-commerce platforms. The "Regulations" are linked with the "E-commerce Law," incorporating takeout platforms into the unified regulatory framework for e-commerce platform operators, further strengthening the platform's legal responsibilities in information reporting, data sharing, and consumer rights protection. At the same time, the penalties for illegal and irregular acts by platforms and merchants have been significantly increased, with fines up to 200,000 yuan. If the main responsible person of a platform intentionally violates the law, with serious nature and severe consequences, they may also be fined between one and ten times their income from the previous year. Next, I will briefly introduce the relevant situation of the "Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Online Food Sales Operators Implementing Food Safety Primary Responsibility." Currently, with the vigorous development of the platform economy, food has become one of the main commodities in online "shopping carts," from daily necessities like rice, oil, salt, soy sauce, vinegar, and tea to beverages and fresh meat products. However, at the same time, problems such as counterfeit and shoddy products and false marketing have occurred frequently and have not been eradicated, seriously affecting people's sense of food safety and consumer confidence, and also hindering the high-quality development of the food industry. From a regulatory perspective, current laws and regulations have relatively few specific provisions on the safety of online food sales, especially the specific responsibilities of platform enterprises in food safety management. The relevant requirements are not well-suited to the actual situation of online sales, leading to prominent issues where enterprises have no rules to follow and regulators have no basis for enforcement. In this regard, the State Administration for Market Regulation is committed to "addressing shortcomings" and has specifically formulated the "Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Online Food Sales Operators Implementing Food Safety Primary Responsibility." It focuses on three aspects: platform providers, online food sellers, and regulatory departments, revolving around the three keywords of "responsibility," "collaboration," and "enforcement" to further tighten and implement food safety primary responsibility. First, clarify the "responsibilities" of the three parties. Platform providers bear overall responsibility for food sales activities within the platform, including establishing a dedicated food safety management agency; equipping management personnel such as food safety supervisors and food safety officers; establishing a full-process management system for online review, risk control, and handling of illegal acts, etc. Online food sellers shall bear the primary responsibility for food safety, including obtaining production and operation licenses or filing in accordance with the law before going online, ensuring the safety of the food sold, standardizing information disclosure, business promotion, storage, and distribution, and establishing a risk prevention and control mechanism of daily monitoring, weekly investigation, and monthly scheduling in accordance with the law. At the same time, regulatory departments shall earnestly fulfill their regulatory responsibilities, with the three parties performing their respective duties and bearing their respective responsibilities, forming a pattern of mutual supervision and collaborative governance. Second, promote two "collaborations." First is the enforcement collaboration mechanism, which requires market regulatory departments across the country to strengthen cross-regional clue notification, evidence collection, and problem handling in regulatory enforcement, achieving a unified national regulatory effort. Second is the integrated collaboration mechanism, which requires platform providers, based on risk monitoring and identification, to promptly push risk warnings and requirements for risk prevention to online food sellers; online food sellers who discover risks in food recommended by the platform shall promptly inform the platform provider; platform providers and online sellers who discover illegal acts in online food sales or potential risks of food safety accidents shall report them to market regulatory departments in accordance with regulations. Third, strengthen integrated "enforcement." It clarifies that if illegal acts occur in areas outside the domicile of the platform provider, the provincial market regulatory department where the illegal act occurred may exercise jurisdiction, focusing on resolving the conflict between the spillover nature of the platform and the limitations of local regulation. In addition, the "Regulations" also strengthen severe punishment, focusing on increasing penalties for illegal and irregular acts by platform providers. Corresponding legal liabilities are added for platform failures to equip food safety management personnel, conduct food safety risk control as required, or handle food safety risks as required. For platform failures to establish selection rules as required, inspect recommended food, or recommend food prohibited by laws and regulations, severe punishment will be imposed in accordance with the law. Food safety has no "zero risk," and regulatory work is always "on the go." The State Administration for Market Regulation will always adhere to the people-centered development philosophy, thoroughly implement the "four strictest" requirements for food safety, and take the implementation of the above two regulations as an opportunity to further consolidate the responsibilities of all parties, innovate regulatory means, and build consensus for joint governance, continuously improve the governance level of online catering and online food sales safety, and make new and greater contributions to safeguarding the health and safety of the people and promoting the high-quality development of the catering and food industries. Wang Qiuping, Spokesperson for the State Administration for Market Regulation and Director of the Department of Publicity and Information: Thank you, Director Sun. The "Regulations" clearly stipulate that the name of the takeout online store must be consistent with the name on the physical store's signboard; core information such as business qualifications, photos of the physical store, and actual operating address must be continuously displayed in a prominent position on the main page, or a clear link to the information must be provided. To address the problem of "fake addresses," it is clarified that the actual operating address must be consistent with the operating premises indicated on the business qualification certificate. Second, add a special label, so that "no dine-in" is no longer hidden. title_en: Under the "AI Disruption Theory," Hengke has fallen over 6% this year, with nearly 40 billion yuan in southbound funds buying the dip against the trend.
body_en: "Hiding from the bear market in the Hang Seng Tech Index." This slightly self-deprecating quip is becoming the reality for many investors in the Hang Seng Tech Index. Wind data shows that in the first two months of this year, the SSE Composite Index and the ChiNext Index in the mainland market rose by 4.89% and 3.34% respectively; the S&P 500 Index in the US market rose slightly by 0.49%, while the Nasdaq Index fell by 2.47%; in the Hong Kong market, the Hang Seng Index rose by 3.9%, while the Hang Seng Tech Index fell by 6.86%, ranking last among global asset classes during these two months. "If you look at the trend of the Hang Seng Tech Index in isolation, you can hardly feel the roaring repricing of the AI era; instead, it gives the illusion that technology assets are entering a bear market," wrote CICC in a research report. What is puzzling is why the Hang Seng Tech Index, which includes well-known internet technology giants such as Tencent Holdings (0700.HK), Alibaba-SW (9988.HK), and Meituan-SW (3690.HK), has been "falling non-stop" in a market where technology narratives are the main investment theme? Hang Seng Tech Index Over 20% drawdown in the past six months Looking at a longer time frame, the Hang Seng Tech Index has entered a continuous downward adjustment channel since reaching a cyclical high of 6715 points in early October 2025. As of the end of February this year, the drawdown in the period has exceeded 20%. Especially since entering 2026, the decline of the Hang Seng Tech Index has accelerated. Wind data shows that in the nine trading weeks of the year, the Hang Seng Tech Index recorded six weekly declines, with a year-to-date drop of over 6%, ranking last among global asset classes. CICC analysts Liu Gang and Wang Muyao reviewed the market performance of A-shares, Hong Kong stocks, and US stocks since 2025 and found that the logic of market rotation in Hong Kong stocks is rooted in fundamentals, liquidity, and structural characteristics. "When liquidity tightens, structural characteristics are ignored, or fundamentals are weak, Hong Kong stocks tend to underperform, and vice versa." They believe that the weakening of the Hang Seng Tech Index since February is also due to changes in these three aspects: first, the nomination of "relatively hawkish" and quantitative tightening supporter Worsh as the new Federal Reserve chairman by US President Trump has led investors to worry about tightening global liquidity; second, the sharp fluctuations in precious metal prices have suppressed global risk appetite, coupled with market divergence on the attitude of tech giants towards AI capital expenditure and the slower-than-expected progress of Hong Kong internet companies in deploying core AI capabilities, leading to more pessimistic market sentiment; third, China's economic fundamentals are still in the process of recovery, and historical data shows that Hong Kong stocks usually underperform when fundamentals are weak. "AI Agent Disruption Theory" Shocks the World In addition to macroeconomic factors, the fear of "creative destruction" brought about by AI technological changes has become a new variable suppressing the valuation of Hong Kong internet stocks. Since the beginning of the year, the prophecy that "AI Agents will disrupt software stocks" has triggered multiple rounds of volatility in US tech giants: the open-source project Open Claw, released at the end of January, caused the Nasdaq 100 Index to fall by more than 1% for three consecutive days; on February 23rd, a report titled "The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis" released by research firm Citrini caused all three major US stock indices to fall by more than 1% on the same day, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average falling by 800 points; at the end of February, US company Anthropic announced that its Claude Code can modernize the COBOL programming language, causing investors to worry about the impact on IBM's mainframe business, and IBM's stock price fell by 13% in a single day. Zhao Nianshen, fund manager of Wells Fargo Global Technology and Internet Fund, said that overseas markets are experiencing the theme of large models impacting software. Since September 2025, the gap between the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index and the North American Technology Software ETF has widened rapidly, driven by the significant increase in AI performance such as Gemini 3.0 and the Claude series, which has impacted US SaaS stocks. Dragged down by overseas markets, Hong Kong internet companies have also adjusted accordingly. Due to the fact that their listed companies are mainly To C, their stock price declines are smaller than those overseas. Du Huliang, fund manager of China Europe Information Technology Fund, told Yicai reporter that he believes that in the future distribution of the entire AI world, model/cloud vendors will definitely get a larger share of the pie, while the pie for tool software vendors will shrink. Therefore, overseas markets are showing continuous valuation increases for leading large model companies and collective declines in software stocks. As US and Hong Kong stocks fall simultaneously, capital is flowing heavily into Japan and South Korea. As of February 28th, the Nikkei 225 Index has risen by 16.91% year-to-date, and the Korean KOSPI Index has recorded an astonishing increase of nearly 50%. "Recently, Hong Kong stocks are not underperforming due to their own weakness, but because others are too strong," said Zhang Yidong, chief economist at Haitong International. "Since February of this year, a large amount of capital has flowed from Hong Kong stocks to markets such as Japan, South Korea, and China's Taiwan, especially the South Korean stock market." Zhang Yidong further analyzed that the current surge in the South Korean stock market is essentially a "duet" driven by the two semiconductor giants, Samsung and Hynix. If these two companies are excluded, the South Korean market is more passively rising. Du Huliang believes that this reflects the allocation results of overseas capital based on global comparisons: "Under the logic of 'computing power equals revenue' for large models, the cost-effectiveness of 'hard shovel' assets such as optical modules, storage, and electricity is highlighted, which is also the mainstream logic for current global capital clustering." In addition, the numerous challenges faced by Hong Kong internet companies themselves have further pressured their stock prices. CICC Wealth stated that the "food delivery war" in 2025 led to Meituan's losses and a sharp decline in Alibaba's net profit, directly hitting market confidence; the "red envelope milk tea war" on the eve of this year's Spring Festival was interpreted by the market as short-term KPI-oriented behavior. "The fear of aging internet platforms and the desire to bet on the opportunities of the next era make it unsurprising that capital chooses to reprice. The cruelty of 'advance or retreat' in the AI era is vividly reflected in this round of differentiation." "Weeping and Sowing," Hong Kong Tech Sector Enters Low Valuation Zone Despite facing multiple pressures, many industry insiders point out that the Hang Seng Tech Index, after deep adjustments, has high allocation value from a valuation and trading perspective. CMB International Research believes that the current relative valuation of the Hong Kong technology sector is at its historical lowest level. If we measure the AH premium by the ratio of the Hang Seng Tech Index to the A-share STAR Market Index, it is currently close to its historical extreme. "With the great development of AI and the strategy of strengthening the country through science and technology, Hong Kong technology assets are clearly significantly undervalued." CMB International further analyzed that the price-to-earnings ratios (PE) of some leading internet companies have fallen back to more than ten times, and the narrative implied by this valuation level almost completely excludes expectations for AI business, with extremely limited downside potential in the future. Zhang Yidong also believes that the market's pessimistic sentiment towards Hong Kong stocks is "a bit excessive." He pointed out that the South Korean market has shown characteristics of short-term overbought and crowdedness, and the diversionary impact of the "Korean wave" on Hong Kong stocks may be nearing its end. Zhang Yidong believes that heavyweight stocks such as Tencent and Alibaba have now entered a stage of "short-selling momentum exhaustion." "For 'traditional technology assets' represented by the internet, market disappointment has been released quite thoroughly." From a capital perspective, despite the overall poor performance of Hong Kong stocks, southbound funds have not left the market. Wind data shows that in the first two months of this year, southbound funds had net purchases of 68.971 billion yuan and 90.575 billion yuan respectively. Among them, in the past 20 trading days, Tencent Holdings, Xiaomi Group-W (1810.HK), and Meituan-W were among the top net purchases, attracting nearly 40 billion yuan in total. Regarding the "disruption theory" of AI Agents, Du Huliang holds a relatively optimistic attitude. He believes that AI Agents have a greater impact on tool software in the To B field, but internet platforms themselves are divided into entry-level layers and have user UGC capabilities. "In the era of 'large model democratization,' leading internet platforms can still maintain unique competitiveness." Looking ahead, Zhang Yidong describes the current Hong Kong stock market as a stage of "weeping and sowing." "If we use seasons to describe it, Hong Kong stocks are still in early summer, just experiencing a brief cold snap." He believes that the two sessions in March and subsequent important diplomatic nodes may become key opportunities for market confidence to turn around. title_en: After the 8 billion yuan red envelope wave recedes, major tech companies' AI faces a "retention" test.
body_en: One of the biggest differences this Lunar New Year was undoubtedly AI's transformation from a "new toy" to a real-life "little assistant." As internet giants showered users with red envelopes during the Spring Festival, AI's usability became concrete: AI helped with ordering takeout, buying movie tickets, planning itineraries, and finding coupons; hundreds of millions used AI to write New Year greetings and create images and videos. Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance, Baidu, and JD.com invested over 8 billion yuan to launch the AI "red envelope war" for the Spring Festival. The companies recently announced their results: Alibaba announced that during the Spring Festival, users made nearly 200 million "one-sentence orders" on Qianwen, with one in ten people nationwide ordering through Qianwen on average. ByteDance stated that on New Year's Eve, Doubao AI had a total of 1.9 billion interactions. Tencent announced that Yuanbao's daily active users (DAU) exceeded 50 million, and monthly active users (MAU) reached 114 million. As the Spring Festival holiday concludes, a more pressing challenge emerges: with the red envelope craze subsiding, what will be the user retention rate? Without the stimulus of red envelopes, what will the tech giants rely on to keep users? Several industry insiders interviewed by China Business News reporters expressed pessimism. "Many friends around me have uninstalled some apps after the red envelope promotion ended," said Guo Tao, an angel investor and special researcher at the E-commerce Research Center of the Internet Economy Institute. He predicted that if driven purely by red envelopes, the 7-day retention rate would generally be below 20%; the 30-day retention rate would average around 12%, and for smaller AI applications, the 30-day retention rate might be less than 5%. **Lowest Retention Rate Below 5%** Although the achievements announced by the tech giants mainly include order volume, daily active users (DAU), and monthly active users (MAU), their internal focus extends far beyond these metrics. During the Spring Festival, tech giants distributed 8 billion yuan in AI red envelopes. ByteDance was the first to secure a partnership with the Spring Festival Gala, with Doubao deeply involved in interactive activities, distributing hundreds of millions of yuan in red envelopes and gifts. Tencent's Yuanbao prepared 1 billion yuan in cash red envelope incentives and a new AI social feature, "Yuanbao Pai," to compete. Alibaba launched its AI assistant "Qianwen" with a 3 billion yuan "treat your guests" plan before the Spring Festival Gala began. After the lively red envelope giveaway, user enthusiasm quickly waned. Ms. Zhou from Shanghai noticed that after the first day of the Lunar New Year, fewer red envelope links were being shared in groups. "This kind of red envelope social interaction is mainly concentrated among close friends and family; after a round of excitement, it ends and doesn't extend to work-related social circles." Many users interviewed stated that after grabbing red envelopes, they rarely proactively opened the related AI applications again. "Qianwen's decline might be a bit slower," said Mr. Lu, a user from Shenyang. "Qianwen has two rounds of free order cards with validity periods of February 28th and April 30th. I'll remember to use the free order cards that I couldn't use before due to server lag before they expire." Will user retention experience a cliff-like drop after the red envelope craze fades? Based on an analysis of user behavior logic and past experience with similar marketing activities, Guo Tao predicts that the 7-day retention rate for app promotional activities generally falls within the 20%-30% range. If driven purely by red envelopes, the 7-day retention rate would generally be below 20%. The average 30-day retention rate would be around 12%, and for small AI applications driven purely by red envelopes, the 30-day retention rate might be less than 5%. "Users brought in by red envelope marketing activities are mostly 'short-term benefit sensitive,' with a weak understanding of the product's core functionality, passively participating in activities solely due to cash incentives," Guo Tao further analyzed. "Historical references are more cautionary. Baidu's Spring Festival red envelopes in 2019 only had a 7-day retention rate of about 2% for new users. Out of 100 users who downloaded the app for red envelopes, only two remained after a week," cited Bai Wenxi, vice chairman of the China Enterprise Capital Alliance. However, Guo Tao believes, "Currently, tech giants are not solely relying on red envelope incentives; they are pursuing a 'red envelope incentive + scenario application' route, which will result in higher retention rates than promotion solely through red envelopes." The reporter noted that although the achievements announced by the tech giants mainly include order volume, daily active users (DAU), and monthly active users (MAU), their internal focus extends far beyond these metrics. Wu Jia, president of Qianwen, stated in a media interview, "DAU is not the metric we prioritize. We mainly look at user feedback and user experience. For example, I check every day how many times users say 'Qianwen, help me,' which represents the formation of user mindshare." An insider from Alibaba's Qianwen revealed to reporters that Alibaba was not simply distributing red envelopes in the red envelope war but emphasized user engagement, ensuring users truly experienced the entire purchasing process (ordering takeout, buying movie tickets, event tickets) through the red envelopes, aligning with Wu Jia's emphasis on the "Qianwen, help me" mindshare. **The "Retention" Challenge** After the lively red envelope craze subsides, how to retain users is the real test for the tech giants. The strategies of the tech giants in the Spring Festival AI red envelope war also differed. As Yuanbao AI itself summarized, "This is a battle of path dependency." Bai Wenxi believes that Alibaba's Qianwen used 3 billion yuan to buy "consumption habits" through free orders and an ecological closed loop. Tencent's Yuanbao used 1 billion yuan for social fission to buy "social relationships," strongly promoting "Yuanbao." ByteDance's Doubao bought "brand awareness" through the Spring Festival Gala, further embedding AI capabilities into the entire Douyin product suite. In Bai Wenxi's view, the fundamental difference lies in Alibaba using "free orders" to replace "cash red envelopes," directly drawing users into real consumption scenarios like Taobao Flash Purchase, Fliggy, and Hema. Tencent is betting on social relationship chains. ByteDance relies on the Douyin traffic pool. Baidu continues to leverage the user habits of its search gene. After the lively red envelope craze subsides, how to retain users is the real test for the tech giants. Chen Liteng, an analyst at the E-commerce Research Center of the Internet Economy Institute, believes that the core of whether short-term traffic can be converted into long-term value lies in whether it forms a closed loop with high-stickiness platform scenarios. What truly determines success is not the amount of red envelopes, but the quality of retention and the depth of user behavior conversion in the 30 days after the Spring Festival. "Whether user habits will fade after the red envelope craze subsides depends on whether the AI products are truly integrated into high-frequency life scenarios," said Liang Zhenpeng, a senior industry observer. "Taking Alibaba's Qianwen as an example, if it provides a significantly better experience than traditional methods in scenarios like food delivery and ticket booking (such as more intelligent recommendations, more convenient operations), user retention rates will be higher. Conversely, if it's just a short-term experiment driven by red envelope incentives, users may leave after the craze fades." Each company's retention strategies also differ. According to Bai Wenxi's observations, Alibaba's Qianwen is continuously refining its "AI task completion" capabilities. If the AI task completion experience is inferior to traditional apps (like Meituan or Ctrip), users will still return to traditional apps. ByteDance is deeply embedding AI capabilities into all its core products, including Douyin, Toutiao, and Xigua Video, and is exploring hardware like AI phones and AI earphones to achieve full-scenario coverage of "software + hardware." Tencent's Yuanbao is internally testing the "Yuanbao Pai" social feature, allowing AI to summarize group chats and create interest-based check-in activities, attempting to build a new social scenario of "human-machine symbiosis," which is also Tencent's strongest "relationship chain" moat. "After the red envelopes, the long-term key lies in whether the convenience, accuracy, and scenario adaptability of AI services are strong enough to shift users from 'trying something new' to 'relying on it'," Fu Yifu, a special researcher at Shangshang Bank, told reporters. Several users interviewed stated that at least for now, they have not developed a reliance on AI. For example, using Qianwen to order takeout or place an order on Hema was not smoother than using their existing apps; they were mostly motivated by the red envelopes. Based on current indications, the red envelope war will not stop immediately after the Spring Festival. Alibaba is still trying to extend the popularity of Qianwen's "treat your guests" plan. For example, starting February 17th, Qianwen continues to offer "first order of the day always discounted," which can be combined with existing platform discounts for a "minimum 3.8 yuan" "first order of the day always discounted." "Qianwen's application scenarios will continue to expand," revealed the aforementioned Qianwen insider. Previously, Qianwen mentioned integrating functions like shopping and navigation when connecting to Alibaba's ecosystem, which have not yet been fully implemented. When reporters tried to ask Qianwen to "help me book a ride" or "help me connect to Taobao," Qianwen responded, "I cannot place an order for you directly. I recommend opening a ride-hailing app on your phone," and recommended Didi, Gaode, and Meituan. Regarding the long-term return expectations for the 3 billion yuan investment, Wu Jia responded, "Due to user participation exceeding expectations, the actual investment far exceeded 3 billion yuan." He also emphasized, "AI does not mature overnight; it is continuously refined in the real world." Various signs indicate that the red envelope war is just the prelude, and the battle for the entry point to AI super applications has just begun.

Based on an analysis of user behavior logic and past experience with similar marketing activities, Guo Tao predicts that the 7-day retention rate for app promotional activities generally falls within the 20%-30% range. If driven purely by red envelopes, the 7-day retention rate would generally be below 20%. The average 30-day retention rate would be around 12%, and for small AI applications driven purely by red envelopes, the 30-day retention rate might be less than 5%.
