title_en: Alibaba releases "Wukong," the world's first enterprise-grade AI-native work platform.
body_en: According to a report by our correspondent Chen Cun: "In the past, people used DingTalk to work; in the future, AI will use DingTalk to work." This is how DingTalk founder and CEO Chen Hang describes the upcoming changes. On March 17th, Alibaba held the AI DingTalk 2.0 new product launch conference, where it officially released "Wukong," the world's first enterprise-grade AI-native work platform, aiming to enable every team and company to have a "lobster army" working 24 hours a day. According to introductions, "Wukong" is an independent application that will begin its invite-only testing starting today and will be directly integrated into over 20 million enterprise organizations on DingTalk. "Wukong" will also enter the global market and will subsequently support connections to mainstream global IM platforms such as WeChat and Slack. Users can remotely activate Wukong on their computers and mobile phones to complete work. DingTalk users can directly use Wukong through the Wukong Agent built into the latest DingTalk AI 2.0 version. This is not the first time "Wukong" has appeared in the public eye. If Tongyi Qianwen is Alibaba's answer to C-end demands, then "Wukong" is its crucial step into the B-end market. Just the night before, Alibaba had announced the establishment of the Alibaba Token Hub (ATH) business group, composed of Tongyi Lab, MaaS business line, Qianwen business unit, Wukong business unit, and AI Innovation business unit, directly overseen by Alibaba Group CEO Eddie Wu. In an internal letter, the responsibility of the Wukong business unit was defined as "building a B-end AI-native work platform and deeply integrating model capabilities into enterprise workflows." Chen Hang stated that arbitrarily deploying "lobsters" in enterprises may lead to issues such as fragile permissions, unauthorized execution, data leakage, and malicious skills. However, "Wukong" is different from all other "lobster" Agents on the market; it is naturally embedded within the enterprise organization and can be used safely in real enterprise environments. Chen Hang pointed out that DingTalk began preparing for "lobster" related products as early as 2025, and due to security considerations, it was only officially launched today. It is worth noting that "Wukong" is not positioned as a replica of OpenClaw, nor is it a simple combination of "DingTalk + AI." Chen Hang emphasized that "Wukong" was forged by "shattering DingTalk and rebuilding it with AI." A significant manifestation of this is not making AI adapt to tools, but creating tools for AI. At the press conference, Chen Hang announced a series of AI-native tools. For example, the AI-native file system RealDoc allows AI to operate at the smallest unit, reducing token waste. He also mentioned that the paradigm of human-computer collaboration has evolved from DOS to GUI, and then to LUI. As AI becomes the primary subject of production, the CLI era is about to arrive. DingTalk will rewrite its underlying code to create an AI-native language that comprehensively connects people, AI, and business systems. Chen Hang also shared 10 "Wukong" OPT (One Person Team) industry solutions based on practical applications, covering ten major scenarios including e-commerce, cross-border e-commerce, knowledge bloggers, development, retail stores, design, manufacturing, legal, finance and taxation, and headhunting. These are the world's first solutions to implement AI Skills from a technical concept to industry-level out-of-the-box products. According to introductions, "Wukong" OPT can directly deliver "scenario-based Skill kits + pre-orchestrated workflows + industry data precipitation." Users only need to make decisions and accept, while AI is responsible for execution. Each Skill is no longer an abstract technical capability but an "industry-level capability module" bound to specific scenarios, specific roles, and specific SOPs. In addition, "Wukong" has launched an AI capability market, collaborating with the developer ecosystem to build a complete enterprise-grade Skill ecosystem, providing a full-link system from development, review, listing, to distribution, and fully compatible with the open-source Skill system, aiming to become "the world's largest toB Skill market." Subsequently, Skills for B-end business capabilities from Alibaba Group's Taobao, Tmall, 1688, Alipay, and Alibaba Cloud will be gradually integrated into Wukong. "In the past 11 years, DingTalk has changed our way of working. Today, 'Wukong' is attempting to define a new way of working in the AI era. 'Wukong' is still in its nascent stage, but its evolution speed will be very fast," said Chen Hang.

title_en: Yicai Editorial: Improving Rights Protection is the Best Tool Against "Involution"
body_en: Exposing infringing acts is the most important guarantee for regulating the development of the platform economy. On the 23rd, the Beijing Municipal Administration for Market Regulation, in conjunction with the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Commerce and the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Culture and Tourism, interviewed and provided administrative guidance to twelve platform enterprises in accordance with the law. They collectively announced the first batch of problems discovered since the comprehensive rectification of platform "involutionary" competition and put forward rectification requirements. Protecting the legitimate rights and interests of platform operators and consumers, prohibiting the mandatory or disguised mandatory sale of goods by platform operators at prices below cost according to their pricing rules, and disrupting market competition order are important aspects of the three departments' in-depth comprehensive governance of platform "involutionary" competition. The aim is to establish a multi-party consultation mechanism, organize platforms to solicit opinions from all parties on rule-making, promotional activities, etc., form a long-term prevention mechanism, and promote the healthy development of the platform economy. Currently, some platform enterprises do have problems of directly or indirectly infringing upon the legitimate rights and interests of platform operators and consumers by using their exclusive power in rule-making and commercial negotiation mechanisms, affecting or even interfering with enterprises' pricing autonomy and consumers' free bargaining power. Interviewing these behaviors is completely necessary. Punishing and regulating through interviews highlights the sufficient sensitivity of regulatory authorities in enforcing the law, helps strengthen embedded regulation of platform enterprises through pre-warning, in-process tracking, and post-punishment, and forms a dynamic matching and coordinated regulation effect across the entire ecosystem. Among them, the interviews will focus on the protection of the legitimate rights and interests of all parties, highlighting the public governance characteristics of regulation, and helping to enhance the bargaining power of small and medium-sized operators and consumers on the platform. Platforms are typical bilateral markets, and platform enterprises have absolute power in setting commercial negotiation rules and regulating platform access on the platform. This leads to weak rule and standard bargaining power for small and medium-sized operators and scattered consumers in this three-party transaction structure. Under normal circumstances, platforms use various methods to make it difficult for small and medium-sized operators on the platform to refuse their promotional activities, thereby effectively limiting the freedom of choice and even pricing autonomy of small and medium-sized operators on the platform, forcing them to do things they would not otherwise do. Similarly, for platform consumers, platform enterprises' interface sorting, intelligent content recommendations, sales rules that induce bulk purchases, and even various other hints that involve suspected induced consumption, all interfere with users' consumption autonomy to varying degrees. The most typical is the "full reduction phenomenon." This transaction negotiation rule leads consumers to unwillingly choose goods and services they do not want, bringing about consumption waste and overconsumption to varying degrees. These behaviors are essentially illegal infringing acts, which not only interfere with the market's autonomous pricing power but also infringe upon people's freedom of transaction and also cause cumulative interference to market order. Moreover, as AI begins to enter daily life, the difficulty for platforms to acquire customers and the difficulty of disguised traffic increase, which may force platform enterprises to take bolder and more covert infringing actions to improve platform performance. Therefore, resolutely cracking down on various acts suspected of infringing upon the legitimate rights and interests of platform operators and consumers will help correct the deviation of some platform enterprises, enable platform enterprises to focus more on ecological governance, get rid of the simple model of scale competition and price competition, and cultivate core competitive advantages. It should be emphasized that as AI continues to penetrate, the unique platform commercial negotiation rules and standard evaluation capabilities of platform enterprises are facing systemic reshaping. For example, various Agents such as OpenClaw can achieve localized storage of customers' real preferences and demands. Transactions between supply and demand sides no longer rely solely on platform interface display and search ranking for traffic import. That is, the end-to-end search, matching, and transaction costs for platform operators and consumers are being reconstructed, as are the information structure, communication structure, ranking matching, and transaction structure of consumption and transactions. The cost-effectiveness and price war model of platform enterprises are facing new technological impacts. At this time, regulatory authorities, through interviews, bring platform enterprises back to the track of cooperative game with platform operators and consumers, and frame the core competitiveness of platform operations in how to more effectively leverage service experience, better display participants' intentions, and reduce transaction matching costs within the platform by improving the information structure, communication structure, and transaction structure within the platform. This has a dual effect of addressing the present and planning for the future. Of course, the protection of people's legitimate rights and interests not only requires the standardization of governance by regulatory authorities but also requires maximizing the legal channels and space for every independent market entity to protect its rights. In terms of institutional design, based on the principle of minimizing economic and social costs, a trading scenario and order that creates equal game for all parties to the transaction should be created, so that any legitimate rights and interests can be discovered, respected, and protected.

title_en: Zhejiang Conducts Anti-Monopoly Compliance Guidance for Platform Enterprises
body_en: Reported by (City News Reporter Cao Jigen) Recently, the Zhejiang Provincial Administration for Market Regulation organized over 150 key platform enterprises in the province to conduct anti-monopoly compliance guidance activities. The focus was on proactive prevention, emphasizing the interpretation of 8 types of new monopolistic risks faced by platform enterprises in business scenarios such as data transmission, algorithm application, service pricing, search ranking, recommendation display, and traffic allocation. The 8 types of new monopolistic behaviors are: algorithmic collusion between platforms, organizing and assisting platform merchants in reaching monopoly agreements, unfair high pricing by platforms, selling below cost by platforms, blocking and filtering, "choose one of two," lowest price across the entire network, and differential treatment by platforms. Except for "choose one of two," other situations are relatively unfamiliar to ordinary consumers. Algorithmic collusion between platforms refers to competing platform operators using algorithms to reach monopoly agreements through mutual understanding, exchange of sensitive information, and coordinated actions. Organizing and assisting platform merchants in reaching monopoly agreements refers to platform operators organizing or coordinating competing platform merchants to reach horizontal agreements, or providing substantial assistance by offering necessary support or creating critical conditions. Unfair high pricing by platforms refers to platform operators with a dominant market position abusing their dominance, through platform rules, technology, and algorithms, to charge platform merchants unfairly high fees. Selling below cost by platforms refers to platform operators with a dominant market position abusing their dominance, without justifiable reasons, providing services at prices below cost through excessive subsidies, preferential policies exceeding reasonable limits, etc., to exclude or restrict market competition. Blocking and filtering refers to platform operators with a dominant market position abusing their dominance, without justifiable reasons, blocking or filtering trading counterparts at the application layer, transmission layer, network layer, etc., preventing them from entering relevant markets. Lowest price across the entire network refers to platform operators with a dominant market position abusing their dominance, without justifiable reasons, requiring platform merchants to offer them the lowest price across the entire network. Platform operators without a dominant market position requiring platform merchants to offer them trading conditions equal to or more favorable than those offered to competing platforms in terms of product prices, quantities, etc., may constitute a monopoly agreement. Differential treatment by platforms refers to platform operators with a dominant market position abusing their dominance, without justifiable reasons, implementing differential treatment in prices, policies, etc., towards platform merchants or consumers with the same trading conditions. The Zhejiang Provincial Administration for Market Regulation requires all platform enterprises to integrate anti-monopoly compliance into their daily operations. They are to conduct in-depth risk investigations in accordance with the requirements, and carefully examine platform rules such as account management rules, terminal user policies, agreements and management methods for platform merchants, cooperation agreements with third-party service providers, traffic allocation rules, and promotional activity policies for potential monopolistic issues. They are also to systematically build a long-term mechanism for anti-monopoly compliance.

title_en: Why are Chinese AI large model call token volumes continuously topping the charts?
body_en: The latest data from OpenRouter, the world's largest API aggregation platform for artificial intelligence (AI) models, shows that from March 16th to March 22nd, the total global AI large model call volume reached 20.4 trillion tokens, a 20.7% increase week-on-week. A reporter from Science and Technology Daily noted that among the top ten AI large models, Chinese AI large models had a weekly call volume of 7.359 trillion tokens, a 56.9% increase from the previous week. US AI large models had a weekly call volume of 3.536 trillion tokens, a 7.35% increase week-on-week. This marks the third consecutive week that the weekly call volume of Chinese AI large models has surpassed that of the US. Why has the token call volume of Chinese AI large models continuously surpassed that of the US? The reporter conducted interviews to explore this question. **Question 1: What is a Token?** "A token is the basic unit of text processed by large language models, which can be understood as 'pieces of words in the eyes of AI'," explained Ma Zhiheng, Assistant Professor at the School of Computing and Microelectronics at the Shenzhen Institute of Technology. Before inputting text into a model, it is segmented into tokens and converted into vectors. For example, in Chinese, each character typically corresponds to one to two tokens. Each query and AI response consumes a certain number of tokens. Ou Weijie, Head of Yaishan LAB at the Shenzhen Institute for Computational Science, said that if "computing power" is considered "electricity," then tokens are the "electricity consumed," serving as a core metric for measuring AI activity and processing scale. Ma Chaoliang, Executive Director of the Token Digital Economy Research Center at the China (Shenzhen) Development Institute, believes that tokens reflect a larger trend: humanity is "deconstructing" the world into the smallest units that machines can understand and process. **Question 2: Why is China's Call Volume So High?** According to OpenRouter data, the top four models globally in terms of call volume last week were all Chinese AI large models, including Xiaomi MiMo V2 Pro, Juehu Xingchen Step 3.5 Flash (free), MiniMax M2.5, and DeepSeek-V3.2. "In terms of pricing, domestic models represented by DeepSeek and MiniMax M2.5 have significantly reduced the API usage costs, stimulating the call demand from developers and enterprises," analyzed Ma Zhiheng. "Chinese companies dominate the open-source model field, and the technical gap with top-tier closed-source models has narrowed to about three months, with prices far lower than the latter, making them a significant attraction for widespread adoption." "Chinese developers contribute a substantial amount of token consumption. Applications like WeChat, DingTalk, and Feishu can reach billions of users. These users can invoke AI capabilities with just a simple click, undoubtedly leading to massive model call demand," said Luo Jieping, Executive Director and Chairman of the Board of Yuegangwan Holdings Co., Ltd. "When building AI applications, most enterprises are highly sensitive to costs. Domestic models have made AI as essential as daily necessities like firewood and rice through lower training costs, winning the favor of global developers with their price advantage." Ou Weijie believes that with the continuous optimization of domestic large models in terms of inference costs, response speed, and API costs, a large number of small and medium-sized enterprises and developers have begun to integrate AI into their business processes, triggering a long-tail effect in call volume. **Question 3: What Does This Data Mean?** Last week, Alibaba announced the official establishment of the Alibaba Token Hub business group, aiming to build a complete AI ecosystem around "creating tokens, delivering tokens, and applying tokens." Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA, also proposed "Tokenomics" at GTC 2026, defining data centers as factories for producing AI intelligent tokens and emphasizing that computing power equals revenue. In Ma Zhiheng's view, token call volume is a "thermometer" for measuring the real-world implementation and usage scale of AI. China's continuous leadership in call volume signifies that the focus of AI development is shifting from "model release" to "large-scale application," and the industrialization process is accelerating. Luo Jieping frankly stated that this record-breaking data means China's AI industry is entering a positive cycle of "technology iteration - cost reduction - application explosion," moving from "following" to "leading." Through open-source models and rich application scenarios, China has forged a different path from the closed-source models of other countries, forming an advantage of clustered rise. Ou Weijie cautioned that behind the massive volume of tokens lie larger-scale data throughput and more complex data governance challenges. Every call to a large model relies on the underlying database system for precise management and millisecond-level response to real-time data, historical knowledge, and user interactions. Ma Zhiheng added, "We must also clearly recognize that the US still maintains significant advantages in original model innovation, high-end chips, and computing infrastructure." (Reporter Luo Yunpeng)

title_en: From "AI+" to "New Form of Intelligent Economy," What Do Tax and Finance Experts Think?
body_en: The "Government Work Report" at this year's Two Sessions for the first time proposed "building a new form of intelligent economy." What is the profound meaning of this new proposition? What new possibilities will it bring to China's economy? And what new requirements will it put forward for the fiscal and taxation system and the training of fiscal and taxation talents? A series of questions have attracted the attention and reflection of fiscal and taxation experts. "AI is no longer just a tool, but will become part of the economic organizational structure." "This reflects that the intelligence stage of economic development has become a consensus of the whole society, and it also means that a hybrid economic form that deeply integrates digital and intelligent technologies is accelerating its formation." Xie Bofeng, director of the Institute of Fiscal and Taxation and National Governance at the School of National Governance Engineering, Renmin University of China, believes that after sorting out the relevant statements in the government work reports of recent years, from proposing the "AI+" action in 2024, to continuous promotion in 2025, and then to proposing "building a new form of intelligent economy" this year, the changes behind it are not only an accurate judgment of the trend of technological evolution, but also an active plan for China's economic development path. Zhang Yongji, director of the Department of Accounting at the School of Management, Beijing Institute of Technology, said that "AI+" is more of a tool narrative, emphasizing the penetration of artificial intelligence (AI) into all walks of life; while "new form of intelligent economy" is closer to a structural narrative, meaning that the economic organizational structure and value creation methods are undergoing profound changes. Kou Enhui, director of the Research Center for Smart Taxation at the Central University of Finance and Economics, analyzed that the "new form of intelligent economy" is based on a more macro strategic goal, and its "newness" is mainly reflected in three levels: at the technical level, it shifts from a technological competition of large models to the engineering implementation and large-scale application of intelligent agents; at the industrial level, AI is no longer just a tool, but will become part of the economic organizational structure; at the institutional level, this year's "Government Work Report" simultaneously proposed "improving artificial intelligence governance," which will put the construction of supporting governance systems, including fiscal and taxation systems, on the agenda. Since the beginning of this year, an open-source AI intelligent agent software "Lobster" (OpenClaw) has become a nationwide sensation, quickly triggering a "lobster farming" craze. Experts believe that this phenomenon precisely illustrates the strong and realistic demand of users for intelligent agents. Xie Bofeng said that OpenClaw can run "amphibiously" in the cloud and locally, is more personalized, and is particularly suitable for work that requires strong privacy. It can be regarded as a signal of AI technology moving towards generalization. Kou Enhui said that previous models like DeepSeek, Doubao, and ChatGPT were more like "you ask, it answers," while OpenClaw has achieved a leap from "dialogue" to "execution." Users issue commands in natural language, and under authorized conditions, it can directly control the computer to complete tasks such as file management, email sending and receiving, form filling, and data processing. Zhang Yongji said that OpenClaw represents AI beginning to possess capabilities such as goal decomposition, tool invocation, and cross-step autonomous execution. In economic terms, AI is gradually transforming from a factor of production into a "quasi-economic entity." "Once AI can independently complete a complete workflow, it will no longer just improve human efficiency, but will begin to replace humans as a participating unit in economic activities, which will greatly impact our understanding of production functions, factor distribution, and even the composition of tax bases," Zhang Yongji said. As a series of security risk cases emerged during the "lobster farming" craze, the authorities quickly sounded the alarm, calling for "rational lobster farming." On March 22, the National Internet Emergency Center and the China Cyberspace Security Association jointly released the "OpenClaw Security Usage Practice Guide," providing security protection recommendations for various users. In this regard, Zhang Yongji believes that such intelligent agents are still in a very early stage of development, and market enthusiasm has a considerable degree of bubble component, but in the long run, the era of intelligent agents is coming, and this trend is unavoidable. "The tax system and collection and management models must be adapted to the intelligent economy." Experts believe that improving artificial intelligence governance and reforming China's tax system and collection and management should be advanced in sync with the building of a new form of intelligent economy. Xie Bofeng proposed that the future economic structure may gradually form a layered intelligent economy structure composed of three different levels of intelligence: fully automated, semi-automated with human-machine collaboration, and weakly automated. Fully automated means that production processes require almost no human intervention, achieving both large-scale mass production and high customization. This change will reshape industrial layout, employment patterns, and tax source structures. "Therefore, traditional tax systems and collection and management models need to be adapted, and the degree of adaptation depends on the phased progress of the intelligent economy," he said. Kou Enhui further analyzed that the impact of the intelligent economy on the tax source structure can be summarized as "three reductions and three increases." The so-called "three reductions" are: first, the erosion of traditional tax bases, such as the narrowing of personal income tax bases after intelligent agents replace labor on a large scale; second, the blurring of tax bases for some turnover taxes, where it may be more difficult to define the subject, location, and stage of transactions when intelligent agents complete transactions autonomously; third, the stronger cross-border profit transfer capabilities of capital-intensive artificial intelligence enterprises, making tax base erosion and profit transfer issues more prominent. The so-called "three increases" are: first, the emergence of new tax sources, such as data as a new factor of production, which contains huge tax potential in the process of value creation and circulation; second, as computing power gradually becomes a basic resource similar to water, electricity, and gas, production, transactions, and consumption around computing power may bring new taxation nodes; third, new industries, new business formats, and new models derived from AI will expand tax bases, such as data tax, automation tax, robot tax, etc. Zhang Yongji reminded that the intelligent economy will also bring challenges to corporate tax compliance. The operating logic of intelligent agents like OpenClaw is to obtain as many system permissions as possible to complete automated operations across software and platforms. Once deployed in financial workflows, there is a probability of leakage of core financial data such as bank accounts, tax declaration records, related party transaction information, and internal pricing documents, which can not only cause commercial losses but also lead to tax compliance issues. In addition, when an invoice, a report, or a bill can be automatically generated by AI, the authenticity of financial data will become more complex, posing challenges to tax collection and management and tax inspection. Therefore, he suggested that two issues be studied as soon as possible: first, the legal validity and verification standards of AI-generated financial vouchers; second, the inclusion of AI behavior logs in the evidence chain of tax audits. Not long ago, many regions have introduced support policies such as "Ten Measures for Lobster Farming" to encourage the development of the intelligent agent industry, including fiscal and taxation support measures. Experts generally hold a cautious attitude towards this. Zhang Yongji believes that the problem is that many subsidies subsidize "deployment behavior" rather than "application value." "It is not difficult to install intelligent agents, but it is difficult to truly generate economic value and improve production efficiency after installation. Otherwise, it may lead to resource misallocation or even subsidy fraud," he said. Zhang Yongji also proposed several aspects worth noting for the improvement of relevant tax policies: first, it is suggested to consider extending the scope of application of the R&D expense super-deduction policy to intelligent agent training costs, data annotation costs, and computing power procurement costs; second, it is suggested to establish tax confirmation rules for data elements as soon as possible to solve the long-standing lack of unified standards for value-added tax rates and income tax confirmation points for data transactions; third, it is necessary to be vigilant about the distortion of market competition by fiscal subsidies. He believes that in the long run, the innovation policy system needs systemic reform, shifting from "project-based support" to "institutional empowerment." "China's AI industry lacks not subsidies, but clear data property rights systems, predictable algorithm regulatory frameworks, and digital tax rules that are in line with international standards. The construction of these systems is more difficult and more important than subsidies," he said. "Treating AI as a starting point rather than an answer is the core competitiveness of future fiscal and taxation talents." Will AI lead to massive unemployment or create more jobs? Recently, related discussions have been heating up. Xie Bofeng believes that technological revolutions have a dual impact on employment. As many people say, "It's not AI that replaces you, but people who are better at using AI than you." Whether employment increases or decreases depends on the level of labor quality and changes in product and service structures, which is also the strategic significance of the country's current emphasis on "closely combining investment in things and investment in people." Zhang Yongji's view is that although every technological revolution in history has not caused net unemployment, AI is fundamentally different. The previous round of technological revolutions mainly eliminated manual labor or highly standardized information processing jobs, and new positions were mainly generated in the service industry and knowledge economy. However, this round of AI directly impacts some knowledge workers, such as accountants, lawyers, and programmers, which are precisely the positions that have expanded significantly after the previous round of technological revolutions. In addition, past technological substitution was a gradual process of decades, and society and the labor market had room for adjustment, while the penetration speed of AI far exceeds that of the past. A profession that was in short supply 5 years ago may begin to cool down today, and the education and social security systems may not be able to adapt in time. Overall, with AI empowerment, the flexibility, intelligence, and autonomy of employment have been greatly improved, and labor scenarios and labor relations have undergone profound changes. For example, digital human live streaming, intelligent writing assistants, and automatic customer responses are gradually showing broad prospects. These forms not only improve labor efficiency and work flexibility but also break through the traditional limitations of time and space on labor. Recently, a university's decision to cut 16 undergraduate majors has sparked heated debate, with some attributing it to the impact of AI. Experts remind that "this should not be viewed this way." Kou Enhui said that the dynamic adjustment of university majors is a normal process, and the reason for the cancellation of many majors is the shrinking demand in the job market, and AI is only accelerating this process. Therefore, when cultivating students, we should not only focus on "whether they can find a good job after graduation" but also pay attention to the abilities that will benefit them for decades to come. Experts propose that as AI increasingly becomes an important variable in high-level talent training, many universities have proactively integrated AI into all aspects of education and teaching. Xie Bofeng introduced that Renmin University of China has not only deployed AI basic environments such as DeepSeek internally but also carried out multiple batches of "AI+" curriculum projects, such as the "AI+Chinese Tax System" course. "The scarce fiscal and taxation talents in the AI era are not 'accountants who can use AI,' but 'fiscal and taxation thinkers who can define problems'," Zhang Yongji said. Future talent competitiveness will increasingly focus on judgment, understanding of systems, and the ability to weigh values. Curriculum design should enhance problem awareness, prompting students to think: Which economic activities is AI changing? How do these changes affect existing system rules? Kou Enhui also proposed that we should know what AI is and understand its technical principles and underlying logic, but the goal is not to train everyone into an AI engineer. We should learn to use AI as a tool to promote the application of "AI+Taxation" in scenarios such as risk assessment and compliance auditing. For students, it is important to cultivate irreplaceable abilities, the key is to be able to think independently, master tools, treat AI as a starting point rather than an answer, and maintain higher standards of thinking and academic pursuit. "In the era of the intelligent economy, the fiscal and taxation discipline needs to cultivate high-level professional talents who can design fair and efficient tax systems, build scientific and rigorous collection and management systems, and promote the modernization of national governance. This is something that AI cannot replace, and it is precisely the mission of fiscal and taxation education in this era," he said.

Therefore, he suggested that two issues be studied as soon as possible: first, the legal validity and verification standards of AI-generated financial vouchers; second, the inclusion of AI behavior logs in the evidence chain of tax audits. Not long ago, many regions have introduced support policies such as "Ten Measures for Lobster Farming" to encourage the development of the intelligent agent industry, including fiscal and taxation support measures. Experts generally hold a cautious attitude towards this. Zhang Yongji believes that the problem is that many subsidies subsidize "deployment behavior" rather than "application value." "It is not difficult to install intelligent agents, but it is difficult to truly generate economic value and improve production efficiency after installation. Otherwise, it may lead to resource misallocation or even subsidy fraud," he said. Zhang Yongji also proposed several aspects worth noting for the improvement of relevant tax policies: first, it is suggested to consider extending the scope of application of the R&D expense super-deduction policy to intelligent agent training costs, data annotation costs, and computing power procurement costs; second, it is suggested to establish tax confirmation rules for data elements as soon as possible to solve the long-standing lack of unified standards for value-added tax rates and income tax confirmation points for data transactions; third, it is necessary to be vigilant about the distortion of market competition by fiscal subsidies. He believes that in the long run, the innovation policy system needs systemic reform, shifting from "project-based support" to "institutional empowerment." "China's AI industry lacks not subsidies, but clear data property rights systems, predictable algorithm regulatory frameworks, and digital tax rules that are in line with international standards. The construction of these systems is more difficult and more important than subsidies," he said. "Treating AI as a starting point rather than an answer is the core competitiveness of future fiscal and taxation talents." Will AI lead to massive unemployment or create more jobs? Recently, related discussions have been heating up. Xie Bofeng believes that technological revolutions have a dual impact on employment. As many people say, "It's not AI that replaces you, but people who are better at using AI than you." Whether employment increases or decreases depends on the level of labor quality and changes in product and service structures, which is also the strategic significance of the country's current emphasis on "closely combining investment in things and investment in people." Zhang Yongji's view is that although every technological revolution in history has not caused net unemployment, AI is fundamentally different. The previous round of technological revolutions mainly eliminated manual labor or highly standardized information processing jobs, and new positions were mainly generated in the service industry and knowledge economy. However, this round of AI directly impacts some knowledge workers, such as accountants, lawyers, and programmers, which are precisely the positions that have expanded significantly after the previous round of technological revolutions. In addition, past technological substitution was a gradual process of decades, and society and the labor market had room for adjustment, while the penetration speed of AI far exceeds that of the past. A profession that was in short supply 5 years ago may begin to cool down today, and the education and social security systems may not be able to adapt in time. Overall, with AI empowerment, the flexibility, intelligence, and autonomy of employment have been greatly improved, and labor scenarios and labor relations have undergone profound changes. For example, digital human live streaming, intelligent writing assistants, and automatic customer responses are gradually showing broad prospects. These forms not only improve labor efficiency and work flexibility but also break through the traditional limitations of time and space on labor. Recently, a university's decision to cut 16 undergraduate majors has sparked heated debate, with some attributing it to the impact of AI. Experts remind that "this should not be viewed this way." Kou Enhui said that the dynamic adjustment of university majors is a normal process, and the reason for the cancellation of many majors is the shrinking demand in the job market, and AI is only accelerating this process. Therefore, when cultivating students, we should not only focus on "whether they can find a good job after graduation" but also pay attention to the abilities that will benefit them for decades to come. Experts propose that as AI increasingly becomes an important variable in high-level talent training, many universities have proactively integrated AI into all aspects of education and teaching. Xie Bofeng introduced that Renmin University of China has not only deployed AI basic environments such as DeepSeek internally but also carried out multiple batches of "AI+" curriculum projects, such as the "AI+Chinese Tax System" course. "The scarce fiscal and taxation talents in the AI era are not 'accountants who can use AI,' but 'fiscal and taxation thinkers who can define problems'," Zhang Yongji said. Future talent competitiveness will increasingly focus on judgment, understanding of systems, and the ability to weigh values. Curriculum design should enhance problem awareness, prompting students to think: Which economic activities is AI changing? How do these changes affect existing system rules? Kou Enhui also proposed that we should know what AI is and understand its technical principles and underlying logic, but the goal is not to train everyone into an AI engineer. We should learn to use AI as a tool to promote the application of "AI+Taxation" in scenarios such as risk assessment and compliance auditing. For students, it is important to cultivate irreplaceable abilities, the key is to be able to think independently, master tools, treat AI as a starting point rather than an answer, and maintain higher standards of thinking and academic pursuit. "In the era of the intelligent economy, the fiscal and taxation discipline needs to cultivate high-level professional talents who can design fair and efficient tax systems, build scientific and rigorous collection and management systems, and promote the modernization of national governance. This is something that AI cannot replace, and it is precisely the mission of fiscal and taxation education in this era," he said.

title_en: Domestic AI applications have evolved from "being able to talk" to "being able to do things."
body_en: From "raising lobsters" going viral on social media to DingTalk's "Wukong" upgrading enterprise workflow, Chinese AI applications have once again impressed in the spring of 2026. Computing power monetization, data loops, and entry point reconstruction... Domestic AI is moving from "dialogue" to "execution," and from "being able to do things" to "industrial tools." AI Moves from Dialogue to Execution On March 17th, Alibaba released its enterprise-level AI agent platform "Wukong" in Hangzhou, Zhejiang. Users can handle complex tasks such as document editing, spreadsheet updates, meeting minutes, and research through a unified interface. DingTalk CEO Chen Hang stated at the press conference: "Today, we have shattered DingTalk and rebuilt it with AI to create 'Wukong.' In the past, humans used DingTalk to work; in the future, AI will use DingTalk to work." According to reports, DingTalk, with its 800 million users, will rewrite its underlying code and undergo a comprehensive command-line interface transformation to achieve "communication as execution." "Wukong" can natively operate thousands of DingTalk capabilities, rather than simulating human clicks on a graphical interface. On the same day, DingTalk, in conjunction with the Hangzhou Future Sci-Tech City Management Committee, simultaneously launched the AI Innovation Factory plan, publicly recruiting AI startup teams, solo teams, and AI SaaS companies. By providing preferential policies, talent training, startup spaces, and capability empowerment, they aim to help developers build innovative products in the AI era. ByteDance, on the other hand, has leveraged Lark and the Douyin ecosystem to lower the barrier to entry for its Lark Daily agent platform to a "click and get" level. Simultaneously, relying on the Doubao 2.0 large model, it has formed a production loop of "instruction entry + cloud execution + secure hosting." At the recent Huawei China Partner Conference 2026, Huawei also officially announced "raising lobsters." In the second half of the year, Huawei Cloud will launch a series of industry and scenario-specific "lobsters" based on the AgentArts one-stop enterprise-level intelligent agent development platform, further improving the enterprise-level AI application ecosystem. On March 22nd, WeChat officially launched the WeChat ClawBot plugin, supporting access to OpenClaw. Users can call lobsters for interaction in WeChat chats by scanning a QR code or copying a command link. The so-called "lobster" is an open-source AI agent named OpenClaw that has rapidly gained popularity in the global tech community this year, named after its lobster icon design. In just one week, Alibaba, Huawei, and Tencent have all made moves, continuously innovating. These AI tools, capable of executing tasks in the real world and acting on behalf of users, have attracted widespread attention. Liu Liehong, Party Secretary and Director of the National Data Administration, stated at the China Development Forum 2026 that Chinese enterprises are accelerating the implementation of intelligent agent applications through a unique path of "open-source frameworks + Chinese models + full-stack data security strategies." Unlike purely pursuing functional realization, the solutions introduced by Chinese enterprises use domestic large models as the "brain" and innovatively embed full-link security mechanisms such as tool compliance detection, data isolation, permission control, and operation auditing. "This also makes us recognize the standard of a 'good intelligent agent': it should not only be a showy 'all-around executor' but also an honest risk communicator and a reliable solution provider," said Liu Liehong. Token Consumption Grows Rapidly The underlying logic of "raising lobsters" is hidden in a steep curve – Token consumption. Data shows that at the beginning of 2024, China's average daily Token calls were 100 billion; by the end of 2025, it had surged to 100 trillion; and in March of this year, it exceeded 140 trillion, a more than thousandfold increase in two years. Liu Liehong stated that behind these numbers, a new business logic based on Token billing is accelerating its evolution. OpenClaw is a major consumer of Tokens. While ordinary AI consumes hundreds of Tokens for a single question-and-answer, OpenClaw can consume tens to hundreds of times more for the same task. The ability to quickly pivot is tested by market judgment. On March 16th, Alibaba completed a key architectural adjustment internally. The newly established Alibaba Token Hub business group, directly managed by CEO Eddie Wu, includes the Tongyi Laboratory, the Qianwen Business Unit, the Wukong Business Unit, and the AI Innovation Business Unit. In an internal announcement, Alibaba redefined Token from a technical unit of measurement to a strategic core asset. Core Kernel Ensures Security In this race, security has become an unavoidable focus. Liu Liehong pointed out that as AI becomes deeply integrated into production and life, security and compliance have become governance priorities. Copyright disputes over training data and generated content can lead AI products into legal battles and trust crises; risks such as data poisoning attacks, permission loss, and cybersecurity vulnerabilities can all lead to distorted system outputs and biased decision-making. "Intelligent agent applications represented by 'lobsters' must continuously carry out security protection in accordance with the principles of 'least privilege, active defense, and continuous auditing'," said Liu Liehong. How can intelligent agents ensure maximum security in their work? DingTalk CTO Zhu Hong explained the security operation logic of their products in six layers during an interview: The first layer is basic security rules, including control over computer system operation permissions and basic access rules for personal computers. The second layer is unified identity authentication. The use of intelligent agents requires enterprise-level account authorization, and the permissions of the intelligent agent are less than or equal to those of the employee account. All operations are performed within the scope of employee authorization. The third layer is enterprise-exclusive capabilities. Enterprises can develop skills for internal systems and deploy them to intelligent agents, avoiding security risks for employees during tedious operations. The fourth layer is network proxy and supervision. Intelligent agents have the ability to access the external network, and for this purpose, layers of network policies are set up for supervision, ensuring that every network access is traceable. The fifth layer is an AI-native file system. A dedicated file system is created for intelligent agents, ensuring that all data changes are traceable and auditable. The final layer is runtime environment control. Enterprises have complete control over the runtime environment of intelligent agents, ensuring that the entire usage process complies with enterprise-level security standards. In the spring of 2026, domestic AI is crossing the watershed from "being able to talk" to "being able to do." This "lobster" craze, ignited by OpenClaw, is pushing artificial intelligence from a conversational tool to a true productivity engine.

title_en: Hong Kong Stock AI New Narrative: Embracing "Token Economics"
body_en: In early spring 2026, Hong Kong's AI sector is becoming a focal point for global capital with a redefinition of valuation logic. As of the midday session on March 24th, the Hang Seng Tech Index stood at 4779.52 points, up 1.42%. Notably, the Hang Seng Hong Kong Stock Connect AI Thematic Index, which reflects the overall performance of the AI industry, has risen approximately 15% year-to-date, indicating an acceleration of capital into the AI sector. Amidst this wave, the "twin stars" of domestic AI large models in Hong Kong have been particularly outstanding. As of the midday session on March 24th, MiniMax's latest stock price was HK$999, up 9%, with a total market capitalization of approximately HK$313.322 billion; while Zhipu's latest stock price reached HK$627, up 6.27%, with a total market capitalization of HK$279.544 billion. Since their listing, the year-to-date stock price increases for both companies have exceeded 400%. Behind the market's enthusiasm, a clear valuation theme is emerging: as AI agents like OpenClaw ignite a wave of "application implementation," the Token consumption generated by each task grows exponentially. As the smallest unit of information processed by AI large models, Tokens are becoming the core pricing unit for measuring the depth of AI business implementation and commercialization potential. In this competitive landscape reshaped by the AI large model wave, Hong Kong stock investors and analysts are also searching for a new "ruler" to measure value. The shift in the valuation anchor for Hong Kong's AI sector began with changes in the competitive landscape of the Hong Kong stock market. Market analysis suggests that the Hang Seng Tech Index is still heavily weighted towards traditional internet and software companies. However, in this AI revolution, large models are becoming new traffic entry points and value centers, continuously eroding the user time and commercial space of traditional platforms and software. In January 2026, MiniMax and Zhipu became the world's first publicly listed companies in large model research and development. After their stock prices multiplied several times, the market capitalization of these "twin stars" of domestic AI large models has reached parity with Baidu and is comparable to JD.com. "The listing of tech companies like MiniMax and Zhipu allows investors to directly participate in China's AI development, while also escaping the limitations of being passively exposed to traditional business risks like e-commerce and food delivery when investing in the eight major tech giants," said Chen Mingkang, Senior Equity Strategist at Bloomberg Industry Research. He added that the large language models developed by these two companies rank among the top globally, and their products demonstrate strength in both performance and cost-effectiveness. Chen Mingkang believes that the multi-fold increase in stock prices of the "twin stars" of domestic AI large models since their listing may reflect market optimism about early adoption prospects and the demand for high-performance and cost-effective models. The market expects that both MiniMax and Zhipu will see year-on-year revenue growth exceeding 150%, far surpassing the single-digit high growth levels of China's eight major tech giants and the low double-digit growth levels of the seven major US tech giants. If the story of new AI forces is "from 0 to 1," then traditional internet giants are performing a "from 1 to 10" leap. This year, the capital expenditure plans of established tech giants like Tencent, Alibaba, and Baidu have frequently attracted market attention. To compete for AI entry points, these cash-rich players are investing heavily in computing infrastructure and model development. "Old players are encountering new opportunities. Increasing capital expenditure must mean they are optimistic about the sector's development. Combining new business models with existing ones to achieve geometric growth is a mode that traditional internet giants are actively pursuing or are compelled to develop," noted Wang Xin Jie, Chief Investment Strategist at Wealth Solutions, Standard Chartered China. He believes that various application scenarios will emerge within the current industry business models. For internet giants, increasing capital expenditure and rapidly monetizing is the current development direction. Chen Mingkang predicts that cloud service giants, which control full-stack AI infrastructure and may adopt service bundling strategies, will gain advantages in pricing and profit margins, potentially intensifying industry competition. With AI agents like OpenClaw igniting the "application implementation" wave, major internet companies are accelerating their shift from "model competition" to "scenario positioning." Tencent quickly launched WorkBuddy, an all-scenario AI agent compatible with OpenClaw skills; Alibaba Cloud launched exclusive image services; and JD Cloud is piloting in business lines such as retail and logistics. These established players with vast user ecosystems are attempting to open up new growth spaces through OpenClaw. This collective embrace of OpenClaw quickly yielded results in the capital market. Tencent emerged as one of the biggest winners. On March 10th, the day after WorkBuddy's launch, its stock price surged at the opening, reaching a high of HK$556 intraday, a daily increase of 7.27%, marking the largest single-day gain in nearly three months, with a turnover exceeding HK$30 billion. Market expectations for its AI commercialization were fully ignited. Alibaba, which owns Alibaba Cloud, did not experience a single-day surge, but its stock price steadily recovered during the mid-March tech stock rebound wave, thanks to its Baixian MaaS business achieving its highest historical growth rate driven by a surge in Token consumption, validating market recognition of its Token business strategy. Following the news of pilot programs in retail and logistics scenarios, JD.com's stock price also broke its previous sideways trend, rising for five consecutive trading days from March 12th to 16th, with its Hong Kong stock price gradually recovering from HK$108.6 to HK$111.5. As OpenClaw pushes AI from "question-answering interaction" to "task execution," the Token consumption per task grows exponentially. Tokens are no longer just a computational unit at the technical level but have become the core pricing unit for measuring the depth of AI business implementation and commercialization potential. This is the key logical starting point for the migration of AI valuation anchors to Tokens. In March 2026, at NVIDIA's GTC conference, founder and CEO Jensen Huang introduced a new concept that reshaped industry perception: the "Token factory." In his view, data centers are undergoing a fundamental role transformation: no longer just "electronic warehouses" for storing files and data, but intelligent production lines operating day and night. These factories input electricity and data, and output Tokens. As Huang stated, Tokens have become the "hard currency" of the digital economy, and their generation efficiency will directly determine the survival capability and revenue curve of technology companies. What are Tokens? Simply put, a Token is the smallest unit of measurement for every interaction between a user and a model: every word and punctuation mark you input to the AI, and every word the model replies to you, is broken down and consumes a certain number of Tokens. For investors, Tokens have become a focus because they unify the revenue and cost sides of AI companies onto a single quantifiable scale for the first time. "For the AI sector, traditional PE valuation is actually not very effective. For such potentially high-growth industries, investors primarily focus on their future potential profitability," said Wang Xin Jie. Wang Xin Jie pointed out that at the current stage of development, significant capital expenditure may make it difficult for these companies to achieve immediate profitability. Therefore, in the AI industry, current user traffic and Token consumption are of greater concern to investors, as they can increase the probability of future profitability. For example, when analysts prepare valuation reports for AI companies, they are beginning to look beyond traditional income statements and attempt to calculate the company's share of global large model subscription and API market Token consumption, as well as the gross profit achievable per Token. This shift in valuation logic is driven by a renewed understanding of the fundamental nature of AI companies' business models: growth in Token consumption signifies increased user activity and deeper business penetration, while an increase in the monetization capability per Token represents the maturation of the business model. Specifically, native large model companies command high valuations due to their technological foundations, as investors believe their Token consumption is expected to grow exponentially. Traditional platform giants with vast scenarios are given higher monetization imagination because existing businesses like e-commerce recommendations, food delivery dispatch, and content distribution naturally provide channels to convert Token calls into actual revenue. Yang Delong, Chief Economist at Qianhai Kaiyuan Fund, pointed out that Hong Kong stocks are placing greater emphasis on new metrics like customer traffic in the AI era. This change in valuation logic will also have a significant impact on the valuation of Hong Kong tech stocks, with investors paying more attention to tech companies' advantages in Tokens and big data. Under this trend, Tokens are becoming the new valuation anchor for AI companies. Song Weiwei, fund manager of the CICC CSI Robotics Index Fund, stated that OpenClaw represents a paradigm shift in AI from "dialogue" to "execution," and Token consumption is the first principle of the entire investment chain. The business models of pure AI companies are highly dependent on Token consumption, and the underlying logic for benefiting sectors is the transmission of this multiplier effect. The business data of Hong Kong's AI "twin stars" provides the best evidence: MiniMax, driven by the explosive growth of its M2 series text models, saw its average daily Token consumption increase more than sixfold compared to December 2025, leading to a 158.9% year-on-year surge in full-year 2025 revenue to $79.04 million. Its gross profit margin also jumped significantly from 12.2% to 25.4%, demonstrating excellent commercialization efficiency. Zhipu, relying on the rapid commercialization of its GLM-5 flagship model API services, has seen continuous growth in Token consumption. By November 2025, its average daily Token consumption reached 4.2 trillion, driving a multi-fold increase in 2025 revenue. Its MaaS platform has attracted over 3 million enterprises and application developers, and API prices were cumulatively increased by 83% in the first quarter of 2026, showing a clear trend of both volume and price increases. The common characteristic of these two companies is that Token call volume has become a direct revenue indicator, and performance realization has driven the valuation shift from "concept-driven" to "revenue-driven." Duan Nairong, Senior Investment Strategist at RBC Wealth Management, stated that most "new AI forces" are not yet profitable, and the market is more focused on their dynamic growth potential. Duan Nairong believes that against the backdrop of "Token inflation," the value anchor for Hong Kong tech stocks can be referenced from several dimensions: first, the conversion efficiency of Token consumption to revenue, i.e., how much revenue is generated per Token, which determines the true profitability of the business; second, the monetization rate of traffic and customer stickiness, including customer retention rates and paid renewal rates, which reflect the sustainability of revenue; third, the locking ability of prepaid models, i.e., the extent to which companies lock in future revenue through prepaid and subscription models, which better reflects business stability. It is worth noting that the performance and cost-effectiveness advantages of domestic AI models are supporting Token competitiveness, and Token pricing and cost advantages are also a basis for building valuation premiums. Data from OpenRouter, a third-party API aggregation platform, shows that in late February 2026, the usage of API Tokens from Chinese AI models surpassed that of US AI models for the first time. A recent research report from Goldman Sachs obtained by reporters indicates that the performance gap between China's new-generation AI models and US models has significantly narrowed, supporting ultra-long context windows of up to 1 million Tokens and powerful agent capabilities. Secondly, the Token pricing of Chinese AI models is only 5% to 10% of that of US flagship models, making them more cost-effective. Finally, Chinese AI models perform excellently in multimodal areas such as text, video, and audio, further expanding Token application scenarios. In the research report, Goldman Sachs analyzes that the surge in Token demand will bring revenue breakthroughs for Chinese AI model companies and drive growth in cloud service revenue. In terms of competitive landscape, independent AI model companies are expected to rise rapidly through the Token business, competing with internet giants. Leading internet companies will also consolidate their advantages in Token-related infrastructure through capital expenditure. A research report from Bloomberg Industry Research points out that the surge in stock prices of companies like MiniMax and Zhipu AI is essentially market recognition of their "low Token cost + high demand growth rate" combination, leading to their market capitalization rapidly reaching parity with tech giants like JD.com and Baidu. For investors, it may be necessary to accept a reality: in the rapidly iterating AI industry, there may be no eternal value anchor. Today's Tokens may be replaced by new measurement units tomorrow; today's leaders may be disrupted by cross-industry players tomorrow. What is certain is that Hong Kong is becoming the core stage for connecting China's AI industry with global capital. On this stage, the story has just begun. Amidst this wave, the "twin stars" of domestic AI large models in Hong Kong have been particularly outstanding. As of the midday session on March 24th, MiniMax's latest stock price was HK$999, up 9%, with a total market capitalization of approximately HK$313.322 billion; while Zhipu's latest stock price reached HK$627, up 6.27%, with a total market capitalization of HK$279.544 billion. Since their listing, the year-to-date stock price increases for both companies have exceeded 400%. Behind the market's enthusiasm, a clear valuation theme is emerging: as AI agents like OpenClaw ignite a wave of "application implementation," the Token consumption generated by each task grows exponentially. As the smallest unit of information processed by AI large models, Tokens are becoming the core pricing unit for measuring the depth of AI business implementation and commercialization potential. In this competitive landscape reshaped by the AI large model wave, Hong Kong stock investors and analysts are also searching for a new "ruler" to measure value. The shift in the valuation anchor for Hong Kong's AI sector began with changes in the competitive landscape of the Hong Kong stock market. Market analysis suggests that the Hang Seng Tech Index is still heavily weighted towards traditional internet and software companies. However, in this AI revolution, large models are becoming new traffic entry points and value centers, continuously eroding the user time and commercial space of traditional platforms and software. In January 2026, MiniMax and Zhipu became the world's first publicly listed companies in large model research and development. After their stock prices multiplied several times, the market capitalization of these "twin stars" of domestic AI large models has reached parity with Baidu and is comparable to JD.com. "The listing of tech companies like MiniMax and Zhipu allows investors to directly participate in China's AI development, while also escaping the limitations of being passively exposed to traditional business risks like e-commerce and food delivery when investing in the eight major tech giants," said Chen Mingkang, Senior Equity Strategist at Bloomberg Industry Research. He added that the large language models developed by these two companies rank among the top globally, and their products demonstrate strength in both performance and cost-effectiveness. Chen Mingkang believes that the multi-fold increase in stock prices of the "twin stars" of domestic AI large models since their listing may reflect market optimism about early adoption prospects and the demand for high-performance and cost-effective models. The market expects that both MiniMax and Zhipu will see year-on-year revenue growth exceeding 150%, far surpassing the single-digit high growth levels of China's eight major tech giants and the low double-digit growth levels of the seven major US tech giants. If the story of new AI forces is "from 0 to 1," then traditional internet giants are performing a "from 1 to 10" leap. This year, the capital expenditure plans of established tech giants like Tencent, Alibaba, and Baidu have frequently attracted market attention. To compete for AI entry points, these cash-rich players are investing heavily in computing infrastructure and model development. "Old players are encountering new opportunities. Increasing capital expenditure must mean they are optimistic about the sector's development. Combining new business models with existing ones to achieve geometric growth is a mode that traditional internet giants are actively pursuing or are compelled to develop," noted Wang Xin Jie, Chief Investment Strategist at Wealth Solutions, Standard Chartered China. He believes that various application scenarios will emerge within the current industry business models. For internet giants, increasing capital expenditure and rapidly monetizing is the current development direction. Chen Mingkang predicts that cloud service giants, which control full-stack AI infrastructure and may adopt service bundling strategies, will gain advantages in pricing and profit margins, potentially intensifying industry competition. With AI agents like OpenClaw igniting the "application implementation" wave, major internet companies are accelerating their shift from "model competition" to "scenario positioning." Tencent quickly launched WorkBuddy, an all-scenario AI agent compatible with OpenClaw skills; Alibaba Cloud launched exclusive image services; and JD Cloud is piloting in business lines such as retail and logistics. These established players with vast user ecosystems are attempting to open up new growth spaces through OpenClaw. This collective embrace of OpenClaw quickly yielded results in the capital market. Tencent emerged as one of the biggest winners. On March 10th, the day after WorkBuddy's launch, its stock price surged at the opening, reaching a high of HK$556 intraday, a daily increase of 7.27%, marking the largest single-day gain in nearly three months, with a turnover exceeding HK$30 billion. Market expectations for its AI commercialization were fully ignited. Alibaba, which owns Alibaba Cloud, did not experience a single-day surge, but its stock price steadily recovered during the mid-March tech stock rebound wave, thanks to its Baixian MaaS business achieving its highest historical growth rate driven by a surge in Token consumption, validating market recognition of its Token business strategy. Following the news of pilot programs in retail and logistics scenarios, JD.com's stock price also broke its previous sideways trend, rising for five consecutive trading days from March 12th to 16th, with its Hong Kong stock price gradually recovering from HK$108.6 to HK$111.5. As OpenClaw pushes AI from "question-answering interaction" to "task execution," the Token consumption per task grows exponentially. Tokens are no longer just a computational unit at the technical level but have become the core pricing unit for measuring the depth of AI business implementation and commercialization potential. This is the key logical starting point for the migration of AI valuation anchors to Tokens. In March 2026, at NVIDIA's GTC conference, founder and CEO Jensen Huang introduced a new concept that reshaped industry perception: the "Token factory." In his view, data centers are undergoing a fundamental role transformation: no longer just "electronic warehouses" for storing files and data, but intelligent production lines operating day and night. These factories input electricity and data, and output Tokens. As Huang stated, Tokens have become the "hard currency" of the digital economy, and their generation efficiency will directly determine the survival capability and revenue curve of technology companies. What are Tokens? Simply put, a Token is the smallest unit of measurement for every interaction between a user and a model: every word and punctuation mark you input to the AI, and every word the model replies to you, is broken down and consumes a certain number of Tokens. For investors, Tokens have become a focus because they unify the revenue and cost sides of AI companies onto a single quantifiable scale for the first time. "For the AI sector, traditional PE valuation is actually not very effective. For such potentially high-growth industries, investors primarily focus on their future potential profitability," said Wang Xin Jie. Wang Xin Jie pointed out that at the current stage of development, significant capital expenditure may make it difficult for these companies to achieve immediate profitability. Therefore, in the AI industry, current user traffic and Token consumption are of greater concern to investors, as they can increase the probability of future profitability. For example, when analysts prepare valuation reports for AI companies, they are beginning to look beyond traditional income statements and attempt to calculate the company's share of global large model subscription and API market Token consumption, as well as the gross profit achievable per Token. This shift in valuation logic is driven by a renewed understanding of the fundamental nature of AI companies' business models: growth in Token consumption signifies increased user activity and deeper business penetration, while an increase in the monetization capability per Token represents the maturation of the business model. Specifically, native large model companies command high valuations due to their technological foundations, as investors believe their Token consumption is expected to grow exponentially. Traditional platform giants with vast scenarios are given higher monetization imagination because existing businesses like e-commerce recommendations, food delivery dispatch, and content distribution naturally provide channels to convert Token calls into actual revenue. Yang Delong, Chief Economist at Qianhai Kaiyuan Fund, pointed out that Hong Kong stocks are placing greater emphasis on new metrics like customer traffic in the AI era. This change in valuation logic will also have a significant impact on the valuation of Hong Kong tech stocks, with investors paying more attention to tech companies' advantages in Tokens and big data. Under this trend, Tokens are becoming the new valuation anchor for AI companies. Song Weiwei, fund manager of the CICC CSI Robotics Index Fund, stated that OpenClaw represents a paradigm shift in AI from "dialogue" to "execution," and Token consumption is the first principle of the entire investment chain. The business models of pure AI companies are highly dependent on Token consumption, and the underlying logic for benefiting sectors is the transmission of this multiplier effect. The business data of Hong Kong's AI "twin stars" provides the best evidence: MiniMax, driven by the explosive growth of its M2 series text models, saw its average daily Token consumption increase more than sixfold compared to December 2025, leading to a 158.9% year-on-year surge in full-year 2025 revenue to $79.04 million. Its gross profit margin also jumped significantly from 12.2% to 25.4%, demonstrating excellent commercialization efficiency. Zhipu, relying on the rapid commercialization of its GLM-5 flagship model API services, has seen continuous growth in Token consumption. By November 2025, its average daily Token consumption reached 4.2 trillion, driving a multi-fold increase in 2025 revenue. Its MaaS platform has attracted over 3 million enterprises and application developers, and API prices were cumulatively increased by 83% in the first quarter of 2026, showing a clear trend of both volume and price increases. The common characteristic of these two companies is that Token call volume has become a direct revenue indicator, and performance realization has driven the valuation shift from "concept-driven" to "revenue-driven." Duan Nairong, Senior Investment Strategist at RBC Wealth Management, stated that most "new AI forces" are not yet profitable, and the market is more focused on their dynamic growth potential. Duan Nairong believes that against the backdrop of "Token inflation," the value anchor for Hong Kong tech stocks can be referenced from several dimensions: first, the conversion efficiency of Token consumption to revenue, i.e., how much revenue is generated per Token, which determines the true profitability of the business; second, the monetization rate of traffic and customer stickiness, including customer retention rates and paid renewal rates, which reflect the sustainability of revenue; third, the locking ability of prepaid models, i.e., the extent to which companies lock in future revenue through prepaid and subscription models, which better reflects business stability. It is worth noting that the performance and cost-effectiveness advantages of domestic AI models are supporting Token competitiveness, and Token pricing and cost advantages are also a basis for building valuation premiums. Data from OpenRouter, a third-party API aggregation platform, shows that in late February 2026, the usage of API Tokens from Chinese AI models surpassed that of US AI models for the first time. A recent research report from Goldman Sachs obtained by reporters indicates that the performance gap between China's new-generation AI models and US models has significantly narrowed, supporting ultra-long context windows of up to 1 million Tokens and powerful agent capabilities. Secondly, the Token pricing of Chinese AI models is only 5% to 10% of that of US flagship models, making them more cost-effective. Finally, Chinese AI models perform excellently in multimodal areas such as text, video, and audio, further expanding Token application scenarios. In the research report, Goldman Sachs analyzes that the surge in Token demand will bring revenue breakthroughs for Chinese AI model companies and drive growth in cloud service revenue. In terms of competitive landscape, independent AI model companies are expected to rise rapidly through the Token business, competing with internet giants. Leading internet companies will also consolidate their advantages in Token-related infrastructure through capital expenditure. A research report from Bloomberg Industry Research points out that the surge in stock prices of companies like MiniMax and Zhipu AI is essentially market recognition of their "low Token cost + high demand growth rate" combination, leading to their market capitalization rapidly reaching parity with tech giants like JD.com and Baidu. For investors, it may be necessary to accept a reality: in the rapidly iterating AI industry, there may be no eternal value anchor. Today's Tokens may be replaced by new measurement units tomorrow; today's leaders may be disrupted by cross-industry players tomorrow. What is certain is that Hong Kong is becoming the core stage for connecting China's AI industry with global capital. On this stage, the story has just begun.
